Drishti Current Affairs 2026 (2)

Current Affairs for UPPCS

All 656 one-line questions with their answers, and every article, news item and table of the issue, with a short memory card on top of each.

Everything here comes from the supplied Drishti Current Affairs 2026 (2) PDF (241 pages). Dates, ranks and figures are as that issue printed them; this is not a live news feed. Page references are PDF file pages. Practice questions are built from the issue's own facts: they are not UPPSC previous-year questions.
1. Read once, with the answers showing. Questions are in normal text, answers are green; key facts the magazine printed in bold are highlighted. The green box above each article is the short version to memorise.
2. Turn on Test mode and recall. Answers and highlighted facts turn into grey boxes. Say the answer out loud, then tap the box to check. Retrieving from memory fixes facts far better than re-reading.
3. Practise. Each chapter has multiple-choice practice built from the issue's own facts. Wrong answers are remembered and come back in "Your weak questions" until you get them right twice (spaced repetition).
4. Use the memory aids. Purple "Memory aid" lines link a fact to a picture, pattern or number; red "Don't confuse" lines separate look-alike facts. They are learning aids, not extra facts.

  144. Ch 2 Internet Access and Children’s Rights: The Supreme Court held that internet access is a fundamental right, including for children, and rejected blanket bans on children's internet use.
    • Case: Just Rights for Children Alliance v. S. Harish; order delivered on October 15, 2026.
    • Bench: Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K. Vinod Chandran.
    • Right flows from Article 21 read with Article 19(1)(a); children have it irrespective of age.
    • Blanket limits called disproportionate; Court suggested parental supervision, child modes, private-by-default accounts.
    • Limits on inherently harmful content and services remain allowed.
    • Centre must build a National Hash & URL List Database to detect and remove CSEAM.

  145. Ch 2 RTI Act Completes 21 Years: The Right to Information Act, 2005 completed 21 years of full implementation on 12 October 2026; it supports transparency and accountability in government.

    • PUCL v. Union of India (2003): voters' right to information about candidates upheld.
    • The RTI Act replaced the Freedom of Information Act, 2002.
    • It set up the Central Information Commission and State Information Commissions.

  172. Ch 2 Mines and Minerals Development and Regulation Amendment Act 2026: The MMDR Amendment Act, 2026 brings mineral-bearing land under central control and limits State taxes on mineral rights.

    • Amends the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957; it is Act No. 20 of 2026.
    • Background: July 2024, nine-judge bench (8:1) held royalty is a contractual payment, not a tax.

  173. Ch 2 Protection for Women in Live-in Relationships: The Supreme Court held that Section 498A IPC protection against cruelty can extend to women in live-in relationships 'in the nature of marriage'.
    • Case: Dr. Lokesh B.H. & Others v. State of Karnataka & Another; decided 3 August 2026.
    • Two conditions: relationship in the nature of marriage, and a genuine intention to marry.
    • The woman bears the initial burden of proving both conditions.
    • Section 498A IPC punished cruelty by husband or his relatives: up to three years and fine.
    • Under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), the matching offence is Section 85.
    • Indra Sarma v. V.K.V. Sarma (2013): live-in between consenting adults is not an offence.

  176. Ch 2 The Public Examinations Prevention of Unfair Means Amendment Act 2026: The Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Act, 2026 sharply raises penalties for exam cheating and sets fast-track trials.
    • Introduced by Dr. Jitendra Singh (27 July); passed both Houses by 30 July; assent 31 July 2026.
    • Amends the 2024 Act; covers UPSC, SSC, Railway Recruitment Boards, IBPS, NTA and central ministries.
    • Individuals: jail raised from 3–5 to 5–10 years; maximum fine ₹10 lakh to ₹50 lakh.
    • Service providers: fine up to ₹5 crore (from ₹1 crore); debarment up to eight years (from four).
    • Organised crime: 7–10 years' jail and a minimum ₹10 crore fine.

    • GLOF = flood when a glacial lake's ice or moraine dam fails.

    • ChaSTE (Chandra's Surface Thermophysical Experiment) is a lunar thermometer, re-inserted into the regolith (moon soil).
    • Found a two-layer structure in the top 6.5 cm of soil at the post-hop site.
    • Soil gets denser and stickier with depth; craters made temperatures drop faster (shadowing effect).
    • The engine firing blew away the top 3 cm of regolith.

  354. Ch 6 The Kigali Amendment marked its 10th anniversary: The Kigali Amendment to the Montreal Protocol, which phases down climate-warming HFCs used in cooling, marked its 10th anniversary on October 15, 2026.

    • India ratified in 2021: freeze by 2028, 10% cut by 2032, 85% cut by 2047.

    October 25, 2026 · National · PDF p. 4 Must know

    1. How many Farmer IDs had been created by October 23, 2026?11 crore
    2. Under which mission is the Farmer ID initiative implemented?Digital Agriculture Mission
    3. What was the deadline for creating 11 crore Farmer IDs?March 31, 2027
    4. What is the main purpose of a Farmer ID?To provide a unique digital identity for easier access to government schemes, bank credit, crop insurance and disaster relief

    Remember: Farmer ID (Digital Agriculture Mission): 11 crore created by 23 Oct 2026; deadline for 11 crore IDs was 31 March 2027. Gives farmers one digital identity.

    Memory aid Farmer ID = one digital identity that opens four doors: government schemes, bank credit, crop insurance, disaster relief.

    हिंदी: Crop insurance (फसल बीमा) · Digital identity (डिजिटल पहचान)

    Political / National Affairs

    Chinmaya Amrit Mahotsav Global Sammelan PDF p. 18

    PM Modi inaugurated the Chinmaya Amrit Mahotsav Global Sammelan in New Delhi, closing year-long celebrations of 75 years of the Chinmaya Mission.

    • Inaugurated on October 23, 2026 at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi; event ran 23–25 October.
    • Over 9,000 participants from India and abroad were expected.
    • PM interacted with a 'Holobot' (holographic image) of Swami Chinmayananda; recalled their 1993 Vadodara meeting.
    • Swami Chinmayananda (born Balakrishna Menon, 8 May 1916; died 3 August 1993) founded Chinmaya Mission in 1953.
    • His Gita Gyana Yagnas took Bhagavad Gita, Upanishads and Vedanta teachings to the public.
    • PM's focus: culture, social unity, self-reliance and youth role in Viksit Bharat by 2047.

    Check Mission founded in 1953, yet 75 years are celebrated in 2026 (1953 + 75 would be 2028).

    हिंदी: Spiritual teacher (आध्यात्मिक गुरु)

    From the magazine

    • Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurated the Sammelan on October 23, 2026 at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi.
    • The 23–25 October event marks the culmination of year-long celebrations commemorating 75 years of the Chinmaya Mission.
    • It was expected to bring together over 9,000 participants from India and abroad.
    • The Prime Minister interacted with a holographic representation, or “Holobot,” of Swami Chinmayananda.
    • He recalled their 1993 meeting in Vadodara, which focused on youth empowerment and building a strong India.
    • He highlighted Swami Chinmayananda’s Gita Gyana Yagna, which brought the teachings of the Bhagavad Gita, Upanishads and Vedanta to the public.
    • His address emphasised cultural preservation, social unity, self-reliance and youth participation in achieving Viksit Bharat by 2047.
    • Swami Chinmayananda Saraswati was a spiritual teacher who spread the teachings of Vedanta, the Upanishads and the Bhagavad Gita.
    • Born on May 8, 1916, as Balakrishna Menon, he passed away on August 3, 1993.
    • Founded the Chinmaya Mission in 1953 to spread the timeless wisdom of Advaita Vedanta.
    • He launched Gita Gyana Yagnas to make spiritual knowledge accessible to the public.

    UDAN Completes 10 Years Must knowPDF p. 18

    UDAN, the regional air-connectivity scheme launched on 21 October 2016, completed 10 years of bringing flights to unserved and underserved areas.

    • RCS-UDAN = Regional Connectivity Scheme – Ude Desh ka Aam Nagrik; follows National Civil Aviation Policy, 2016.
    • First UDAN flight: Shimla–Delhi, April 2017.
    • By October 2026: 687 routes and 95 aerodromes (including 17 heliports, two water aerodromes).
    • Over 3.68 lakh flights carried 1.72 crore passengers.
    • Operational airports rose from 74 (2014) to 166 (2026); India is world's third-largest domestic aviation market.
    • Modified UDAN (4 July 2026): ₹28,840 crore, FY 2026–27 to 2035–36; 100 airports, 200 helipads.

    Memory aid UDAN = 'Ude Desh ka Aam Nagrik' – let the common citizen of the country fly.

    Don't confuse Don't confuse the launch (21 October 2016) with the first flight (Shimla–Delhi, April 2017).

    हिंदी: Regional connectivity (क्षेत्रीय संपर्क) · Civil aviation (नागर विमानन)

    From the magazine

    • RCS–UDAN completed 10 years on October 21, 2026.
    • RCS-UDAN stands for Regional Connectivity Scheme -Ude Desh ka Aam Nagrik.
    • Launched on October 21, 2016, it follows the National Civil Aviation Policy, 2016.
    • It promotes affordable and economically viable air connectivity to unserved and underserved regions.
    • The first UDAN flight connected Shimla and Delhi in April 2017.
    • By October 2026, the scheme had operationalised 687 regional routes and 95 aerodromes, including 17 heliports and two water aerodromes.
    • It facilitated over 3.68 lakh flights, carrying 1.72 crore passengers.
    • India’s operational airports increased from 74 in 2014 to 166 in 2026. India is the world’s third-largest domestic aviation market.
    • Modified UDAN, launched on 4 July 2026, has an outlay of ₹28,840 crore for FY 2026–27 to FY 2035–36.
    • It envisages developing 100 airports and 200 modern helipads.
    • Its priorities include sustainable regional operations, stronger infrastructure and indigenous aircraft manufacturing.

    Internet Access and Children’s Rights Must knowPDF p. 18

    The Supreme Court held that internet access is a fundamental right, including for children, and rejected blanket bans on children's internet use.

    • Case: Just Rights for Children Alliance v. S. Harish; order delivered on October 15, 2026.
    • Bench: Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K. Vinod Chandran.
    • Right flows from Article 21 read with Article 19(1)(a); children have it irrespective of age.
    • Blanket limits called disproportionate; Court suggested parental supervision, child modes, private-by-default accounts.
    • Limits on inherently harmful content and services remain allowed.
    • Centre must build a National Hash & URL List Database to detect and remove CSEAM.

    हिंदी: Fundamental right (मौलिक अधिकार)

    From the magazine

    • On October 15, 2026, the Supreme Court delivered its order in Just Rights for Children Alliance v. S. Harish.
    • The Bench comprised Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K. Vinod Chandran.
    • It recognised internet access and use as a fundamental right under Article 21 read with Article 19(1)(a).
    • Children enjoy this right irrespective of age.
    • The Court rejected blanket restrictions on children’s internet access as disproportionate and unproven.
    • It suggested parental supervision, dedicated child modes, private-by-default accounts and restrictions on messages from unknown adults.
    • Restrictions on inherently harmful content and services remain permissible.
    • The Centre must create a National Hash & URL List Database to detect and remove Child Sexual Exploitation and Abuse Material (CSEAM).

    RTI Act Completes 21 Years Must knowPDF p. 19

    The Right to Information Act, 2005 completed 21 years of full implementation on 12 October 2026; it supports transparency and accountability in government.

    • Presidential assent: 15 June 2005; fully operational: 12 October 2005.
    • Right to Know comes from Article 19(1)(a) – freedom of speech and expression.
    • State of U.P. v. Raj Narain (1975): SC recognised citizens' right to know about public acts.
    • PUCL v. Union of India (2003): voters' right to information about candidates upheld.
    • The RTI Act replaced the Freedom of Information Act, 2002.
    • It set up the Central Information Commission and State Information Commissions.

    Don't confuse Don't confuse assent (15 June 2005) with full operation (12 October 2005), the date used for the anniversary.

    हिंदी: Right to Information (सूचना का अधिकार) · Transparency (पारदर्शिता)

    From the magazine

    • The Right to Information (RTI) Act, 2005 completed 21 years of full implementation on October 12, 2026.
    • It received Presidential assent on 15 June 2005 and became fully operational on 12 October 2005.
    • The Right to Know derives from Article 19(1)(a), which guarantees freedom of speech and expression.
    • In State of U.P. v. Raj Narain (1975), the Supreme Court recognised citizens’ right to know about public acts of government.
    • In PUCL v. Union of India (2003), it upheld voters’ right to information about electoral candidates.
    • The Act replaced the Freedom of Information Act, 2002.
    • It enables citizens to obtain information held by public authorities, subject to statutory exemptions.
    • It established the Central Information Commission and State Information Commissions.
    • Its central objectives are transparency, accountability, informed participation and prevention of corruption.

    100 Years of the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) Must knowPDF pp. 20–21

    UPSC completed 100 years on 1 October 2026; India's first Public Service Commission was set up on 1 October 1926.

    • Centenary event 'Manthan': Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi, 30 September–1 October 2026.
    • Lee Commission (1924, Arthur Hamilton Lee) recommended it; set up under PSC (Functions) Rules, 1926.
    • First Chairman: Sir Ross Barker; office at Metcalfe House, Delhi.
    • Renamed Federal PSC (1 April 1937), then Union PSC (26 January 1950).
    • 1947: H.K. Kripalani first Indian Chairman; 1979: three-stage exam; 2011: CSAT introduced.
    • Satyendranath Tagore first Indian in ICS (joined 1864); ICS exam first held in India 1922 at Allahabad.

    Memory aid 1926 → 1937 → 1950: PSC → Federal PSC → Union PSC.

    Don't confuse Sir Ross Barker = first Chairman (1926); H.K. Kripalani = first Indian Chairman (1947). Tagore passed in 1863 but joined in 1864.

    हिंदी: Public Service Commission (लोक सेवा आयोग) · Centenary (शताब्दी)

    From the magazine

    The Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) completed 100 years on 1 October 2026. Its institutional journey began on 1 October 1926, when India’s first Public Service Commission was established.

    • At that time, it was an advisory body whose Chairman and members were appointed by the Secretary of State for India in London.
    • Various programmes and activities were organised throughout the year to mark the UPSC’s centenary. The year-long celebrations began on 1 October 2025 and continued until 1 October 2026.

    Key Facts

    • The UPSC organised a two-day centenary event titled ‘Manthan’ at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi, from 30 September to 1 October 2026.

    The Journey

    • The Indian Civil Service (ICS) examination began in London in 1855, replacing the East India Company’s nomination system with open competition.
    • In 1862, 21-year-old Satyendranath Tagore, the elder brother of Rabindranath Tagore, passed the examination in 1863 and joined the service in 1864.
    • He thus became the first Indian to join the ICS. The British referred to it as the ‘heaven-born service’.
    • The Government of India Act, 1919, enacted following the Montagu–Chelmsford Reforms, provided for the establishment of a Public Service Commission.
    • In 1922, the ICS examination was held in India for the first time, alongside London. Its Indian examination centre was Allahabad, now Prayagraj.
    • In 1924, the Lee Commission, chaired by Arthur Hamilton Lee, recommended the immediate establishment of a statutory Public Service Commission.
    • The Commission was established under the Public Service Commission (Functions) Rules, 1926, framed under Sections 96B and 96C(2) of the Government of India Act, 1919.
    • Sir Ross Barker, a member of the United Kingdom’s Home Civil Service, was its first Chairman.
    • The Commission’s office was located at Metcalfe House in Delhi.
    • The Indian examination centre was shifted to Delhi in 1928.

    Major Milestones

    YearMajor milestone
    1937On 1 April, the Commission was renamed the Federal Public Service Commission.
    1938Combined competitive examinations were introduced for several services, marking the beginning of integrated recruitment to multiple services.
    1947Shri H. K. Kripalani became the first Indian Chairman following independence; the first examination was held in December and the IAS replaced the ICS.
    1950On 26 January, the Federal Public Service Commission was renamed the Union Public Service Commission. Shri R.N. Banerjee assumed charge on January 14, 1949, and continued as Chairman following the Institution’s Constitutional transition on January 26, 1950.
    1951The All India Services Act was enacted.
    1979The three-stage Civil Services Examination— Preliminary Examination, Main Examination and Interview—was introduced.
    2011The Civil Services Aptitude Test (CSAT) was introduced. A Single Window System was launched on 1 September.

    Planning framework and digital support

    • Three levels of planning: Gram Panchayats prepare Gram Panchayat Development Plans (GPDPs), Block Panchayats prepare Block Panchayat Development Plans (BPDPs) and District Panchayats prepare District Panchayat Development Plans (DPDPs). Block and district plans support coordination, convergence and the scaling of local initiatives.

    • Planning coverage: More than 2.55 lakh Gram Panchayats prepare participatory GPDPs and upload them on eGramSwaraj.
    • As of 29 July 2025, more than 18.13 lakh Panchayat Development Plans had been uploaded for 2019–20 to 2025–26: over 17.73 lakh GPDPs, 35,755 BPDPs and 3,469 DPDPs.

    Lakshadweep and Jammu & Kashmir Declared Fully Literate State Must knowPDF p. 22

    Lakshadweep (11 October 2026) and Jammu & Kashmir (September 2026) were declared fully literate under the ULLAS adult literacy programme.

    • Lakshadweep (11 Oct 2026, by Administrator Praful Patel) became fully literate; J&K was 10th since June 2024.
    • ULLAS = Understanding Lifelong Learning for All in Society; for people aged 15+ who missed school.

    Don't confuse Himachal was the fifth State/UT (fourth state, September 2025); Sikkim was the fifth state (May 2026).

    हिंदी: Literacy (साक्षरता) · Adult education (प्रौढ़ शिक्षा)

    From the magazine

    • Lakshadweep was declared a 100% literate Union Territory under ULLAS Scheme on October 11, 2026. Declaration was made by Administrator Praful Patel.
    • The UT of Jammu and Kashmir was declared fully literate in September 2026, becoming the 10th state or Union Territory (UT) to do so since June 2024, under the Centre’s adult literacy programme ULLAS, for people aged 15 and above who missed formal schooling.
      • The other states and Union Territories are Ladakh, Mizoram, Goa, Tripura, Himachal Pradesh, Chandigarh, Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Sikkim, Uttarakhand, Jammu and Kashmir, and Lakshadweep.
    • Under ULLAS, a state or UT is considered fully literate once at least 95% of its population aged 15 and above can read and write.
    • Uttarakhand officially became India's sixth fully literate state on July 8, 2026, after achieving an adult literacy rate of 98.7%.
    • Sikkim on May 27, 2026 was declared India’s fifth fully literate state after achieving the literacy benchmarks prescribed under the ‘Understanding Lifelong Learning for All in Society (ULLAS) programme.
    • Himachal Pradesh was declared to be a ‘fully literate’ state (September, 2025), becoming the fifth such State/Union Territory in India (fourth among states). Himachal claims to have a literacy rate of 99.3% as per ULLAS Programme. According to the Census of India 2011, the total literacy rate for Himachal Pradesh was 82.80%.
      • Earlier on May 20, 2025, Chief Minister of Mizoram, Lalduhoma, officially declared Mizoram as a fully literate state under ULLAS.
      • Mizoram becomes the first state in India to attain the status of full literacy.
      • Prior to Mizoram, on June 24, 2024, Ladakh became the first administrative unit (non-state) to declare full literacy.

    Sikkim Declared India’s First Paperless Judiciary

    • Sikkim marked an important milestone in India’s judicial digitalisation when it was officially declared the first paperless State judiciary in the country on May 1, 2026. The declaration was made by Justice Surya Kant, Chief Justice of India, during the Conclave on Technology and Judicial Education held in Gangtok.
    • The event was held at Chintan Bhawan, Gangtok, with Chief Minister Prem Singh Tamang as the Guest of Honour.
    • Sikkim’s judiciary has achieved the distinction of becoming the first State judiciary in the country to move fully towards a paperless system.

    Cheetah Population in India Must knowPDF p. 23

    Five cheetah cubs born at Kuno on 5 October 2026 took India's cheetah count to 60; after one cub died, it fell to 59.

    • Mother KJP21 (32 months, Indian-born) is the third Indian-born female to give birth; father from Botswana.
    • Indian-born cheetahs: 41 after the births, 40 after the Aasha cub died (12 October 2026).
    • Project Cheetah launched at Kuno on 17 September 2022 with eight Namibian cheetahs.
    • Imports: eight from Namibia, 12 from South Africa (2023), nine from Botswana (2026); total 29.
    • Programme expanded to Gandhi Sagar Wildlife Sanctuary (Madhya Pradesh) in 2025.
    • Project uses African cheetah (A. j. jubatus); India's native Asiatic subspecies (A. j. venaticus) is Critically Endangered.

    Don't confuse Total population 60 → 59, but Indian-born 41 → 40; cumulative imports are 29.

    Check Botswana is said to have handed over eight cheetahs in November 2025, but nine arrived from Botswana on 28 February 2026.

    हिंदी: Critically Endangered (गंभीर रूप से संकटग्रस्त) · Wildlife (वन्यजीव)

    From the magazine

    On October 5, 2026, five healthy cheetah cubs were born at Kuno National Park in Madhya Pradesh. The births increased India’s cheetah population to 60, including 41 Indian-born individuals.

    • The announcement by Union Environment Minister Bhupender Yadav marked another breeding milestone under Project Cheetah but after the death of an Aasha Cub on October 12, 2026 total population is now 59.

    Key Details of the New Births

    • The mother, KJP21, is a 32-month-old Indian-born female. She became the third Indian-born female cheetah to give birth, after Mukhi and KGP12.
    • The father was brought from Botswana.
    • The remaining 19 animals in the reported population were born outside India, calculated as 60 minus 41. The Indian born population is now stands at 40 (59 – 19 = 40).
    • Reproduction by females born in India shows that the programme is producing another generation on Indian soil.

    Fact Box: Project Cheetah

    • Scientific name of the cheetah: Acinonyx jubatus. The subspecies native to India was the Asiatic cheetah, A. j. venaticus. Project Cheetah uses African cheetahs, identified as A. j. jubatus.
    • The NTCA booklet identifies the cheetah species as Vulnerable and the Asiatic subspecies as Critically Endangered.

    Key Chronology

    Date or periodDevelopment
    20 July 2022India signed a wildlife conservation agreement with Namibia.
    17 September 2022Project Cheetah was launched at Kuno. Prime Minister Narendra Modi released eight Namibian cheetahs, five females and three males, into quarantine enclosures.
    17 January 2023India signed the cheetah cooperation agreement with South Africa.
    18 February 2023Twelve cheetahs arrived from South Africa, five females and seven males, taking cumulative imports to 20.
    March and April 2023The first Indian-born litter arrived in March. By 20 April, four Namibian cheetahs were already free ranging in the wild.
    2025The programme expanded to Gandhi Sagar Wildlife Sanctuary in Madhya Pradesh.

    28 February 2026Nine cheetahs from Botswana, six females and three males, entered quarantine enclosures at Kuno. Cumulative imports from the three countries reached 29.

    Special Constitutional Safeguards for Ladakh Must knowPDF pp. 25–26

    The Home Ministry reportedly proposed Article 371-K to give Ladakh special constitutional safeguards with a directly elected UT-level body; it remains a proposal.

    • Proposed at a 9 September 2026 meeting with Leh Apex Body (LAB) and Kargil Democratic Alliance (KDA).
    • Body would make laws on land, culture, language, forests, environment and natural resources.
    • 'Sui generis' model = unique arrangement; no automatic statehood or regular UT legislature.
    • Ladakh became a UT without a legislature on October 31, 2019 (J&K Reorganisation Act, 2019).
    • Local demands: statehood, Sixth Schedule, job safeguards, separate Lok Sabha seats for Leh and Kargil.
    • Sixth Schedule (Articles 244(2), 275(1)) covers tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram.

    Memory aid Sixth Schedule states = 'AMTM': Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram.

    Don't confuse Article 371-K is only a proposal; it is not statehood and not Sixth Schedule status.

    हिंदी: Union Territory (केंद्र शासित प्रदेश) · Sixth Schedule (छठी अनुसूची)

    From the magazine

    • At a meeting on September 9, 2026, the Union Home Ministry reportedly proposed Article 371- K to provide special constitutional safeguards for Ladakh. Representatives of the Leh Apex Body (LAB) and Kargil Democratic Alliance (KDA) participated in the discussions.
    • The proposed arrangement envisages a directly elected Union Territory-level body with legislative powers over specified local matters, including land, culture, language, forests, environment and natural resources.
    • It would follow a “sui generis” model, meaning a unique governance arrangement tailored to Ladakh’s circumstances. It would not automatically grant statehood or create a conventional Union Territory legislature.
    • Ladakh became a Union Territory without a legislature on October 31, 2019, following the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019.
    • Local organisations seek stronger protection for tribal identity, land, employment, culture and natural resources, alongside greater participation in governance.
    • Their principal demands include statehood, Sixth Schedule protection, employment safeguards and separate Lok Sabha constituencies for Leh and Kargil.
    • The Sixth Schedule, linked to Articles 244(2) and 275(1), provides special administrative arrangements for tribal areas in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.
    • It provides for Autonomous District and Regional Councils, with legislative, administrative, judicial and financial powers over specified subjects. Extending this framework to Ladakh would require appropriate constitutional changes.
    • Article 371-K remains a proposal; its final constitutional structure and distribution of powers require agreement and parliamentary approval.

    Assam Uniform Civil Code Act, 2026 Must knowPDF pp. 26–27

    Assam's Uniform Civil Code Act, 2026 got Presidential assent on 29 September 2026, making Assam the first Northeast state with a UCC.

    • Bill introduced 25 May 2026 by Atul Bora; passed by voice vote on 27 May 2026.
    • Assam is the third state, after Uttarakhand and Gujarat, to adopt a state UCC law.
    • Linked to Article 44; STs excluded; repeals Assam Compulsory Registration of Muslim Marriages and Divorces Act, 2024.
    • Monogamy compulsory; bigamy/polygamy up to seven years' jail; marriage age 21 (men), 18 (women).
    • Marriage memorandum within 60 days; live-in registration within one month; live-in children fully legitimate.
    • Gujarat UCC: assent 17 September 2026; committee led by Justice Ranjana Prakash Desai.

    Memory aid UCC order: Uttarakhand → Gujarat → Assam (first in the Northeast).

    Don't confuse Assam: passed 27 May, assent 29 September 2026. Gujarat: passed 24 March, assent 17 September 2026.

    हिंदी: Uniform Civil Code (समान नागरिक संहिता) · Monogamy (एकविवाह)

    From the magazine

    The Uniform Civil Code, Assam, Bill, 2026, was introduced in the Assam Legislative Assembly on May 25, 2026, by Parliamentary Affairs Minister Atul Bora on behalf of Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma

    • The Assam Legislative Assembly passed the Bill by voice vote on 27 May 2026.
    • Presidential assent was given on September 29, 2026.
    • With this, Assam became the first state in the Northeast and the third state in India after Uttarakhand and Gujarat to adopt such UCC legislation at the state level.
    • The idea of a Uniform Civil Code is linked to Article 44 of the Constitution, which directs the State to endeavour to secure a uniform civil code for citizens throughout India.
    • It also repeals the Assam Compulsory Registration of Muslim Marriages and Divorces Act, 2024.
    • STs are excluded from the application of Assam’s UCC.

    Marriage-Related Provisions

    • The Act mandates monogamy as the legal rule for marriage.
    • Bigamy and polygamy shall attract imprisonment of seven years. up to
    • The act fixes the legal age of marriage at 21 years for grooms and 18 years for brides.
    • Couples must submit a marriage memorandum to the Sub-Registrar within 60 days of the marriage ceremony and within 90 days outside Assam.

    Divorce-Related Provisions

    • The Act codifies uniform grounds for divorce.
    • Grounds for divorce include cruelty, desertion, and mutual consent.
    • The Act ensures that custody of children below five years of age remains with the mother (However, the Court remains free to consider the best interests of the child).
    • Class-1 heirs will include the spouse, children, and parents of the deceased.

    Live-In Relationship Provisions

    • The Act makes registration of live-in relationships mandatory within one month, including for non-residents.
    • Failure to register a live-in relationship within one month may attract imprisonment of up to three months or a fine of up to ₹10,000 (and continued failure may attract six months of imprisonment or ₹25,000 or both).
    • Any child born out of a live-in relationship will be considered fully legitimate.

    Penalties Under the Act

    • Marriage within prohibited relationships, unless protected by valid customs, shall be punishable with imprisonment of up to six months and a fine of up to ₹50,000.
    • Non-registration of marriage or divorce within the prescribed period shall attract a penalty of ₹10,000 (and ₹25,000 after first notice).
    • Forged documents in registration matters may lead to imprisonment of up to three months, or a fine of up to ₹25,000, or both.

    Gujarat Uniform Civil Code 2026

    President Droupadi Murmu assented to the Gujarat Uniform Civil Code Bill on 17 September 2026. Gujarat became the second state after Uttarakhand to adopt a new UCC framework.

    • The Gujarat Assembly passed the Bill on March 24, 2026.
    • The committee chaired by retired Supreme Court judge Justice Ranjana Prakash Desai made recommendation for UCC.
    • Scheduled Tribes and groups with constitutionally protected customary rights are exempt.

    Major provisions

    • Monogamy is compulsory: neither party may have a living spouse. The framework therefore prohibits bigamy.
    • Minimum marriage age: men 21 years; women 18 years.
    • Marriages covered by the Act after its commencement require a registration memorandum within 60 days; wilful non-compliance attracts monetary penalties.
    • Grounds for divorce include adultery, cruelty, desertion for at least two years, etc.
    • Live-in relationships: Partners living within Gujarat must declare their relationship to the Registrar.

The Bill was introduced in the Lok Sabha on 10 August 2026 and passed by the Lok Sabha on 11 August and the Rajya Sabha on 12 August. The President assented to the Act on 14 August 2026. Section 1(2) requires a separate commencement notification, which was not located in official sources examined up to August 22, 2026.

    • The amendment provides flexible financing for diversified cooperative-sector needs and widens institutional channels for infrastructure, technology, processing and marketing.

    • NCDC is a statutory organisation established in 1963 under the 1962 Act and administered by the Ministry of Cooperation. It plans, promotes and finances cooperative development, including agriculture, dairy, fisheries, processing, storage and marketing.

    Major Provisions of the Amended Act

    • The amended Act allows direct loans and grants to any cooperative society or eligible entity engaged in cooperative development, alongside State Government financing. Share-capital investment in single-State cooperatives and other eligible entities requires prior Central Government approval.
    • It expands “foodstuffs” to include processed food, other edible products and notified items, removes the rural-area restriction on eligible cooperative industrial activities, permits credit-information exchange with the Central Government, RBI, banks and notified financial institutions, and authorises activities addressing emerging technological and sectoral needs.
    • The 97th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2011, recognised the right to form cooperative societies under Article 19(1)(c), introduced Article 43B and added Part IXB. Article 43B promotes voluntary formation, autonomy, democratic control and professional management.

    • Section 2 of the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Act, 1956, initially permitted 10 judges excluding the CJI, giving a total strength of 11.

    Background to the Bill

    • The Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, approved four additional puisne judges on 5 May 2026.
    • The Lok Sabha passed the Bill by a voice vote without debate on 3 August 2026. Presidential assent was given on 11 August 2026.

    Need for Increasing Judicial Strength

    • The government cited increasing case pendency as the main reason for expansion. On 1 January 2026, the Court had 92,101 pending cases.
    • During 2025, it received 75,410 cases but disposed of 65,615, leaving a gap of 9,795. By 30 April 2026, pendency had reached 92,823, according to the National Judicial Data Grid.
    • This gap continued despite the Court functioning close to its sanctioned strength. The increase seeks to improve disposal capacity and deliver speedy justice.

    The Tribunals Reforms Act, 2026 Must knowPDF pp. 29–30

    The Tribunals Reforms Act, 2026 creates a judiciary-led National Tribunals Commission to keep tribunals independent of the executive, replacing the 2021 Act.

    • Introduced by Law Minister Arjun Ram Meghwal; Lok Sabha passed it by voice vote on August 10, 2026.
    • Assent: August 13, 2026; in force from August 25, 2026.
    • Repeals the 2021 Act; applies to 16 tribunals, appellate tribunals and authorities.
    • Implements Madras Bar Association v. Union of India principles; SC had struck down 2021 Act provisions.
    • National Tribunals Commission: headquarters New Delhi; one Chairperson and four members (total five).
    • NTC members serve five years or till age 70, whichever is earlier.

    Don't confuse Assent on 13 August 2026, but in force from 25 August 2026.

    हिंदी: Tribunal (न्यायाधिकरण) · Judicial independence (न्यायिक स्वतंत्रता)

    From the magazine

    • The Tribunals Reforms Act, 2026 seeks to establish an independent, transparent, efficient and professionally administered tribunal system through a judiciary-led National Tribunals Commission (NTC).
    • It seeks to reduce executive discretion, establish uniform service conditions and implement the Supreme Court’s Madras Bar Association principles.
    • Introduced by Union Law Minister Arjun Ram Meghwal, the Bill passed the Lok Sabha by voice vote on August 10, 2026, without detailed debate amid Opposition protests.
    • It received presidential assent on August 13, 2026, and came into force on August 25, 2026.
    • The Act repeals and replaces the 2021 Act and applies to 16 tribunals, appellate tribunals and authorities without altering their jurisdiction or adjudicatory powers.

    Background and Objectives

    • The Supreme Court has repeatedly emphasised that tribunals performing judicial functions must remain independent of the executive.
    • In Madras Bar Association v. Union of India, (2026) 2 SCC 1, the Supreme Court struck down provisions of the 2021 Act for violating judicial independence, separation of powers and earlier judicial standards.
    • The new Act seeks uniform appointments, financial and administrative autonomy, expert assessment and institutional accountability.

    National Tribunals Commission

    • The Act establishes the National Tribunals Commission as the central institutional body responsible for appointments and oversight in the tribunal system.
    • The Commission will replace the fragmented and predominantly executive-controlled administrative framework established under the 2021 Act.
    • Its headquarters will be located in New Delhi.
    • The Commission will consist of one Chairperson and four members, producing a total strength of five.
    • The NTC Chairperson and members will serve for five years or until the age of 70, whichever is earlier.

    Search cum Selection Committees

    • Section 13 provides separate committees for selecting tribunal Chairpersons and members. The NTC Chairperson heads the committee for Chairpersons, which includes a retired High Court Chief Justice nominated by the NTC Chairperson.
    • An NTC Judicial Member heads the committee for Members, which includes a retired High Court Judge nominated by the NTC Chairperson.
    • The committee Chairperson has a casting vote when votes are equal. The Member-Secretary and empanelled experts have no voting rights.

    Mines and Minerals Development and Regulation Amendment Act 2026 Must knowPDF pp. 31–32

    The MMDR Amendment Act, 2026 brings mineral-bearing land under central control and limits State taxes on mineral rights.

    • Passed by both Houses on August 13, 2026; assent August 17, 2026; in force August 22, 2026.
    • Amends the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957; it is Act No. 20 of 2026.
    • Background: July 2024, nine-judge bench (8:1) held royalty is a contractual payment, not a tax.
    • That case: Mineral Area Development Authority v. Steel Authority of India; States may tax under Entry 50.
    • Section 9D restricts State taxes, cesses and levies on mineral rights and mineral-bearing land.
    • Unpaid past State levies become invalid; amounts already paid will not be refunded.

    Don't confuse Royalty is a contractual payment, not a tax (8:1 ruling, July 2024).

    हिंदी: Mineral (खनिज) · Mining (खनन)

    From the magazine

    The Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026 was passed by both Houses of Parliament on August 13, 2026. The Act amends the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957. The President assented to Act No. 20 of 2026 on August 17, 2026. The Act came into force August 22, 2026.

    • The MMDR Act, 1957, is the principal mining legislation. The Centre regulates major minerals, conservation and royalty rates.
    • In Mineral Area Development Authority v. Steel Authority of India, a nine-judge bench ruled by 8:1 in July 2024 that royalty is a contractual payment, not a tax.
    • States may tax mineral rights under Entry 50, subject to parliamentary restrictions absent from the existing MMDR Act.

    Major Provisions of the Act

    • Union Regulation of Mineral Bearing Land: The amendment to Section 2 brings mineral-bearing land, defined as land containing minerals under Central parameters, within Central regulatory control.
    • Restrictions on State Levies: Section 9D restricts State taxes, cesses and similar levies on mineral rights and mineral-bearing lands, including levies based on mineral quantity, value or royalty. States may impose them only under Central conditions or restrictions.
    • Treatment of Past Dues: Unpaid or unrecovered State levies for periods before commencement will become invalid. Amounts already deposited or recovered will not be refunded.
    • Central Rule Making Power: The amendment to Section 13 authorises Central rules prescribing conditions and restrictions for future State levies.

    Evolution of the MMDR Framework

    • The 2015 amendment introduced mandatory auctions, the District Mineral Foundation and the National Mineral Exploration Trust. The 2016 amendment defined the leased area and permitted certain captive lease transfers.
    • The 2020 reforms opened coal and lignite auctions to companies without prior coal-mining experience. In 2021, captive mines could sell up to 50% of their annual output after meeting linked end-use requirements.

    Protection for Women in Live-in Relationships Must knowPDF p. 32

    The Supreme Court held that Section 498A IPC protection against cruelty can extend to women in live-in relationships 'in the nature of marriage'.

    • Case: Dr. Lokesh B.H. & Others v. State of Karnataka & Another; decided 3 August 2026.
    • Two conditions: relationship in the nature of marriage, and a genuine intention to marry.
    • The woman bears the initial burden of proving both conditions.
    • Section 498A IPC punished cruelty by husband or his relatives: up to three years and fine.
    • Under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), the matching offence is Section 85.
    • Indra Sarma v. V.K.V. Sarma (2013): live-in between consenting adults is not an offence.

    Memory aid 498A IPC = 85 BNS (cruelty to a woman).

    हिंदी: Cruelty (क्रूरता) · Live-in relationship (सहजीवन संबंध)

    From the magazine

    In Dr. Lokesh B.H. & Others v. State of Karnataka & Another, decided on 3 August 2026, the Supreme Court held that protection against domestic cruelty under Section 498A of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) is not confined to women in legally valid marriages.

    • The protection may extend to a woman in a live-in relationship when the relationship is “in the nature of marriage” and the parties have the intention to marry.

    What Is Section 498A of the IPC?

    • Section 498A of the IPC criminalised cruelty committed against a woman by her husband or a relative of her husband.
    • The provision prescribed imprisonment for up to three years and a fine.
    • Following the replacement of the IPC by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), the corresponding offence is contained in Section 85 of the BNS.

    Supreme Court’s Ruling

    • The Supreme Court held that Section 498A is not restricted exclusively to relationships based on a legally valid marriage.
    • It can apply to a live-in relationship that legally qualifies as a relationship in the nature of marriage.
    • However, the woman must also establish that the relationship involved a genuine intention to marry.
    • The relationship must be between consenting adults and must satisfy the legal characteristics of a marriage-like domestic partnership.

    Essential Conditions for Invoking Section 498A

    • A woman in a live-in relationship must initially establish two essential requirements:
      • The live-in arrangement must constitute a relationship in the nature of marriage.
      • The relationship must involve an intention to marry.
    • The initial burden rests on the woman seeking protection under Section 498A.
    • In Indra Sarma v. V.K.V. Sarma (2013), the Supreme Court recognised that a live-in relationship between consenting adults is not an offence.

    The Public Examinations Prevention of Unfair Means Amendment Act 2026 Must knowPDF pp. 33–34

    The Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Act, 2026 sharply raises penalties for exam cheating and sets fast-track trials.

    • Introduced by Dr. Jitendra Singh (27 July); passed both Houses by 30 July; assent 31 July 2026.
    • Amends the 2024 Act; covers UPSC, SSC, Railway Recruitment Boards, IBPS, NTA and central ministries.
    • Individuals: jail raised from 3–5 to 5–10 years; maximum fine ₹10 lakh to ₹50 lakh.
    • Service providers: fine up to ₹5 crore (from ₹1 crore); debarment up to eight years (from four).
    • Organised crime: 7–10 years' jail and a minimum ₹10 crore fine.
    • Investigation within two months; Special Fast Track Courts to finish trials within three months of charge sheet.

    Don't confuse Individual's maximum fine ₹50 lakh; service provider's maximum ₹5 crore; organised crime minimum ₹10 crore.

    हिंदी: Unfair means (अनुचित साधन) · Public examination (सार्वजनिक परीक्षा)

    From the magazine

    The Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Act, 2026, amends the 2024 Act, which came into force on June 21, 2024.

    • Dr. Jitendra Singh introduced the Bill in the Lok Sabha on July 27, 2026. It passed the Lok Sabha on July 29 and the Rajya Sabha on July 30, and received presidential assent on July 31, 2026.

    Public examination authorities covered

    • The Act covers examinations conducted by the Union Public Service Commission, Staff Selection Commission, Railway Recruitment Boards, Institute of Banking Personnel Selection, National Testing Agency, Central Government ministries and attached offices, and other authorities notified by the Central Government.

    Major provisions

    Enhanced penalties

    • For individuals using unfair means, imprisonment increases from 3–5 to 5–10 years, and the maximum fine increase from ₹10 lakh to ₹50 lakh. For service providers, the maximum fine rises from ₹1 crore to ₹5 crore and debarment expands from up to four years to eight years. Proportionate examination costs shall also be recovered.
    • Directors, senior managers or persons in charge who consent to or connive in an offence face 5–10 years’ imprisonment and a ₹5 crore fine, compared with 3–10 years of imprisonment and a fine of ₹1 crore earlier. Organised crime attracts 7–10 years’ imprisonment and a minimum ₹10 crore fine, compared with 5–10 years of imprisonment and a fine of a minimum ₹1 crore fine under the 2024 Act.

    Investigation

    • The amendment introduces a two-month investigation period, counted from the date of recording information for police investigations, referral for central agencies, and the date of the notification constituting a Special Task Force (STF).

    Special Fast Track Courts

    • Every state and Union Territory must designate one or more Courts of Session as Special Fast-Track Courts in consultation with Chief Justice of the relevant High Court. Trials must be completed within three months of filing the charge sheet, or within three months of transfer in pending cases. State governments and UT administrations must appoint Special Public Prosecutors under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023.

    Appeals

    • Appeals lie before a two-judge High Court bench, normally within 30 days, with an absolute 90-day limit. Appeals should be disposed of, as far as possible, within three months of admission.

    The Union Ministry of Education released the reports of the All India Survey on Higher Education (AISHE) for the years 2022-23 and 2023-24 on July 8, 2026.

    • The AISHE 2023–24 is the 14th edition of the nationwide survey conducted by the Ministry of Education.
    • The reference period of the survey was the academic session 2023–24 (and the 2022-23 session in some cases).
    • The AISHE report for 2021-22 was released in January 2024. The survey was initiated to collect data for the academic year 2010–11.

    Key Finding

    • A total of 64,756 Higher Educational Institutions formed part of the AISHE 2023–24 survey frame.
      • These included: 1,289 universities and university-level institutions, 48,246 colleges, 15,221 standalone institutions.
    • India had 18 universities exclusively for women in 2023–24.
    • There were 19 open universities in India during 2023–24.
    • The number of registered colleges increased from 38,498 in 2014–15 to 48,246 in 2023–24.
    • Total enrolment in higher education reached approximately 4.5 crore students in 2023–24.
    • Total enrolment had increased from approximately 3.4 crore in 2014–15 to 4.5 crore in 2023–24.
    • Approximately 76.8% of students were enrolled at the undergraduate level.
    • Undergraduate enrolment was approximately 3.5 crore students.
    • Postgraduate programmes accounted for 12.9% of total enrolment.
    • Female enrolment reached approximately 2.2 crore students in 2023–24.
    • Women accounted for around 49.7% of total higher education enrolment.

    • Scheduled Caste enrolment increased from 69.1 lakh in 2022–23 to 69.7 lakh in 2023–24.
    • SC student enrolment increased by 23.2% between 2019–20 and 2023–24.
    • SC female enrolment increased from 33.9 lakh in 2022–23 to 35.1 lakh in 2023–24.
    • Compared with 2014–15, SC female enrolment increased by 66.9%.
    • Scheduled Tribe enrolment increased marginally from 28.72 lakh in 2022–23 to 28.8 lakh in 2023-24.
    • Compared with 2014–15, ST student enrolment rose by 75.7%.
    • ST female enrolment increased from 14.7 lakh in 2022–23 to 15.1 lakh in 2023–24.
    • Compared with 2014–15, ST female enrolment increased by 101.8%.
    • Other Backward Classes (OBC) student enrolment increased from approximately 1.74 crore in 2022–23 to around 1.8 crore in 2023–24.
    • Compared with 2014–15, OBC student enrolment rose by 60.2%.
    • OBC female enrolment increased from 85.3 lakh in 2022–23 to 90.1 lakh in 2023–24.
    • Compared with 2014–15, OBC female enrolment increased by 72%.
    • Minority student enrolment increased from 21.8 lakh in 2014–15 to 33.3 lakh in 2023–24.

    States with the Highest Enrolment

    • The seven States with the highest student enrolment were: Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka, Bihar and Rajasthan.

    Overall GER (Gross Enrolment Ratio)

    • India’s higher education GER increased to 30.0 in 2023–24.
    • It was 29.5 in 2022–23 and 23.7 in 2014–15.
    • The male GER in 2023–24 was 28.9.
    • The female GER was 31.2, which was higher than the male GER.
    • The GER of Scheduled Caste students increased from 27.3 in 2022–23 to 27.8 in 2023–24.
    • The GER of Scheduled Tribe students stood at 22.8 in 2023–24.

    Gender Parity Index

    • The Gender Parity Index is calculated as the ratio of female GER to male GER.
    • The all-India GPI in higher education stood at 1.08 in 2023–24.
    • A GPI above one indicates that the GER of female students is higher than that of male students.

    Enrolment by Academic Discipline

    Undergraduate Level

    • Based on actual institutional responses, the distribution of undergraduate enrolment was: Arts (32.1%); Science (13.5%); Engineering and Technology (12.9%).

    Postgraduate Level

    • The leading postgraduate disciplines were:
      • Social Sciences: 18.6%; Management: 18.2%.
    • Total enrolment in universities stood at approximately 1.09 crore students in 2023–24.
    • A total of 58,134 foreign students (from 173 countries) were enrolled in Indian higher education institutions during 2023–24.
    • Nepal accounted for the highest share of foreign students in India.

    Teachers and Faculty

    • The total number of teachers and faculty members in higher education institutions stood at approximately 17.3 lakh in 2023–24.
    • Male teachers constituted 55.1% of total faculty.
    • The Pupil-Teacher Ratio represents the average number of students per teacher.
    • For the regular mode of study in universities and colleges, the PTR was 23 students per teacher.

    हिंदी: Electric vehicle (विद्युत वाहन) · Air quality (वायु गुणवत्ता)

    From the magazine

    The Delhi Government has notified the Delhi Electric Vehicle Policy 2.0, effective from July 1, 2026 to March 31, 2030. Chief Minister Rekha Gupta defended the decision to stop fresh registrations of petrol two-wheelers from April 2028. The policy was approved by the Cabinet on June 29, 2026.

    About the Policy and Its Objectives

    • Delhi EV Policy 2.0 promotes electric mobility in the National Capital Territory to reduce vehicular emissions, improve air quality and make Delhi a leading electric mobility hub.
    • It builds on the 2020 policy, under which EVs accounted for around 14% of newly registered vehicles in 2025.

    Vehicle Registration and School Bus Targets

    • From 1 January 2027, only electric three-wheelers and N1-category trucks will be registered in Delhi.
    • From 1 April 2028, only electric two-wheelers will be registered. Existing petrol and other fossil-fuel vehicles may complete their full life cycle, allowing a gradual transition.
    • School buses must convert at least 10% of their fleet to EVs within two years of policy notification. The target is to electrify at least 30% of the school-bus fleet by 31 March 2030.
    • The government is committing a direct investment of over ₹7,000 crore for implementation.
    • The overall investment plan is ₹15,000 crore, covering charging infrastructure, purchase incentives and scrapping incentives.
    • EV buyers receive purchase incentives, road-tax exemptions and registration-fee waivers.
    • Electric two-wheeler incentives are up to ₹30,000, ₹20,000 and ₹10,000 in the first, second and third years, respectively. Electric three-wheelers receive ₹50,000, ₹40,000 and ₹30,000, respectively (No incentive shall be given to e-autos with a battery capacity of less than 4 kWh.). N1 commercial trucks receive up to ₹1 lakh in the first year.
    • The government targets 32,000 public EV charging points, with around 9,000 already operational, and has allocated around ₹1,000 crore for charging infrastructure.

    Scrapping Incentives

    • Vehicles complying with BS-IV or earlier emission standardes receive scrapping incentives of around ₹10,000 for two-wheelers, ₹25,000 for three-wheelers, ₹1 lakh for new non-transport electric four-wheelers and ₹50,000 for N1 trucks.

    • Even then it stays below the 0.27% weighted average of high-income countries.
    • Proposes a National Health Research Agenda and a National Health Research Stewardship Committee.

    Memory aid 0.024 → 0.072 (2037) → 0.15 (2047): triple first, then over six times.

    हिंदी: Health research (स्वास्थ्य अनुसंधान) · Draft policy (मसौदा नीति)

    From the magazine

    The Department of Health Research (DHR), under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, released the draft policy in July 2026, inviting public comments until July 27, 2026. It updates the 2011 policy.

    • The policy seeks to establish a trusted, inclusive, self-reliant, ethical and impact-oriented research ecosystem aligned with India’s disease burden, healthcare needs and equity concerns.
    • Publicly funded health-research expenditure is approximately 0.024% of GDP in 2026–27. The draft proposes increasing it to 0.072% by 2037 and 0.15% by 2047, more than six times the present level but remaining below for the reported weighted average of 0.27% for thigh-income countries.
    • The proposed National Health Research Agenda would set periodically reviewed priorities based on disease burden, scientific opportunities, health-system needs, equity, pandemic preparedness, emerging threats and national interests.
    • A National Health Research Stewardship Committee would provide strategic direction and coordination.

    Ken-Betwa River Link Project Must knowPDF p. 38

    Ken-Betwa project-affected tribal families and farmers renewed protests on 3 July 2026 near Chhatarpur, saying promises made in April were unfulfilled.

    • Protest by the Barana River near Kupi village, Chhatarpur; included Jal, Faansi and Mitti Satyagrahas.
    • MP Cabinet raised the package by about ₹202.50 crore; compensation ₹5 lakh to ₹12.5 lakh per family.
    • Project launched by PM Modi on 25 December 2024; first of 30 river-linking projects (National Perspective Plan).
    • Moves surplus Ken water to the Betwa basin; helps Bundelkhand in MP and UP; both are Yamuna tributaries.
    • Phase I: 77-metre Daudhan Dam, two powerhouses, 216.46-km link canal with a 2-km tunnel.
    • Canal will irrigate 1,93,899 hectares en route; 50.93 MCM reaches Betwa for Lalitpur.

    Memory aid Ken (surplus) → Betwa (deficit); both rivers end up in the Yamuna.

    Don't confuse Phase I = Daudhan Dam and link canal; Phase II = Lower Orr Dam, Kotha Barrage and Bina Complex.

    हिंदी: River linking (नदी जोड़ो) · Rehabilitation (पुनर्वास)

    From the magazine

    Tribal families and farmers renewed their protest on July 3, 2026 beside the Barana River near Kupi village, Chhatarpur, alleging that assurances made in April remained unfulfilled. Participants included people affected by the Ken-Betwa, Majhgawan, Runjh, Neguwan or Naiguwa, and NTPC-linked projects.

    • Protesters stood in the river during the Jal Satyagraha, women lay on symbolic pyres during the Chita Andolan and wore symbolic nooses during the Faansi Satyagraha, while soil represented their attachment to ancestral land during the Mitti Satyagraha. Activists began an indefinite hunger strike.

    Revision of the Rehabilitation Package

    • After the April protest, a fresh survey added around 750 families to rehabilitation plans for the Majhgaon and Runjh projects.
    • The Madhya Pradesh Cabinet approved an increase of approximately ₹202.50 crore increase in the package.
    • Compensation rose from ₹5 lakh to ₹12.5 lakh per affected family. Protesters were advised to raise remaining concerns with Panna’s administration.

    Background of the Project

    • Launched by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on 25 December 2024, the Ken-Betwa Link Project is the first of 30 proposed river-linking projects under the National Perspective Plan.
    • It seeks to transfer surplus Ken basin water to the water-deficit Betwa basin, addressing shortages in Bundelkhand across Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh.
    • The Ken and Betwa rivers are tributaries of the Yamuna River.

    Phase I

    • Phase I proposes the 77-metre-high Daudhan Dam, two powerhouses and a 216.46-kilometre link canal, including a 2-kilometre tunnel.
    • The reservoir’s dead and full reservoir levels will be 240 and 288 metres; respectively, dead and gross storage capacities will be 169 and 2,853 million cubic metres respectively.
    • Annual gross water yield up to Daudhan is estimated at 6,590 million cubic metres (MCM) at 75% dependability.
    • The canal will divert 1,377 million cubic metres annually. Of this, 220.77 million cubic metres will be used at the RD 18-kilometre pumping station, 1,010.51 million cubic metres for irrigating 1,93,899 hectares en route and 94.79 million cubic metres for drinking.
    • The remaining 50.93 million cubic metres will enter the Betwa upstream of Parichha Weir for drinking water and irrigation in Lalitpur.

    Phase II

    • Phase II includes the Lower Orr Dam, Kotha Barrage and Bina Complex. These will meet water requirements in water-deficit areas of the Betwa basin within Madhya Pradesh’s allocated share at Rajghat Dam.

    NCRB's ADSI 2024 report (released 6 May 2026) shows accidental deaths rose to 4,67,857 while suicides fell slightly to 1,70,746.

    • Accidental deaths: 4,44,104 (2023) to 4,67,857 (2024); rate 31.9 to 33.3.

    • Maharashtra had the largest share of accidental deaths (16.2%); Uttar Pradesh 9.2%.

    हिंदी: Accidental death (आकस्मिक मृत्यु) · Suicide (आत्महत्या)

    From the magazine

    Accidental Deaths and Suicides in India 2024 (ADSI 2024) is an annual report published by the National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) on May 6, 2026 under the Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India.

    Key Findings of the Report

    Accidental Deaths in India

    • In 2023, the total number of accidental deaths in India was 4,44,104.
    • In 2024, the total number of accidental deaths in India increased to 4,67,857.
    • The rate of accidental deaths was 31.9 in 2023.
    • The rate of accidental deaths increased to 33.3 in 2024.
    • The maximum number of accidental deaths in 2024 was reported in the age group of 30 to below 45 years.
    • This age group accounted for 1,46,370 deaths, which represented 31.3% of total accidental deaths.

    Major Causes of Deaths Due to Forces of Nature

    • Out of the 7,903 accidental deaths attributable to forces of nature, 35.7% were due to lightning.
    • Out of the 7,903 accidental deaths attributable to forces of nature, 23.2% were due to heat or sunstroke. Percentage Share of States/UTs in Accidental Deaths

    during in 2024 Haryana (3.9%) Madhya Pradesh (9.8%) Uttar Pradesh (9.2%) Maharashtra (16.2%) Tamil Nadu (7.2%) Rajasthan (6.6%) Gujarat (5.1%) Karnataka (6.6%) Odisha (5.0%) Bihar (4.2%) Other State/UTs (26.2%)

    Cases, Deaths, and Injuries Due to Other Causes

    • A total of 7,54,441 cases of under accidents due to other causes were reported.
    • These cases resulted in 4,59,954 deaths.
    • The male-female ratio among fatalities during 2024 was 82.4:17.6.
    • Traffic accidents were the leading cause of accidental deaths due to other causes and accounted for 43.4% of such deaths.

    Fire Accidents

    • A total of 5,971 fire accident case were reported in the country during 2024.
    • These fire accidents resulted in 5,888 deaths.
    • Drowning caused 40,044 deaths during 2024.

    Total Traffic Accidents

    • A total of 4,95,256 traffic accidents were reported during 2024.
    • These traffic accidents included 4,67,967 road accidents.

    Deaths by Type of Traffic Accident

    • Road accidents accounted for 87.8% of deaths in traffic accidents.
    • Road accidents caused 1,75,142 deaths.

    Rural and Urban Road Accidents

    • Rural areas reported 59.7% of road accidents.
    • Rural areas reported 2,79,412 road accident cases.
    • Urban areas reported 40.3% of road accidents.
    • Urban areas reported 1,88,555 road accident cases.

    Total Suicides and Suicide Rate

    • In 2023, the total number of suicides in India was 1,71,418.
    • In 2024, the total number of suicides in India decreased to 1,70,746.
    • The suicide rate was 12.2 in 2024.
    • The suicide rate refers to the number of suicides per lakh of the population.

    Suicide Rate in Cities

    • The suicide rate in cities was 16.3.
    • The suicide rate in megacities was higher than the all-India suicide rate of 12.2.

    Major Causes of Suicides

    • Family problems, other than marriage-related problems, accounted for 33.5% of total suicides in the country during 2024.
    • Illness accounted for 18.0% (~ 17.9%) of total suicides in the country during 2024.
    • Drug abuse or addiction accounted for 7.6% of total suicides in the country during 2024.
    • Family problems other than marriage-related problems, illness, and drug abuse or addiction together accounted for 59.0% of total suicides in the country during 2024.
    • The overall male-female ratio of suicide victims was 73.5:26.5.
    • A total of 10.1% of suicide victims were illiterate.
    • A total of 14.4% of suicide victims were educated up to the primary level.
    • A total of 17.7% of suicide victims were educated up to the middle level.
    • A total of 25.6% of suicide victims were educated up to the matriculation level.
    • Only 5.6% of total suicide victims were graduates or had higher qualifications.

    Election Commission Announces Special Intensive Revision Phase III Must knowPDF p. 40

    The Election Commission announced Phase III of the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls on 14 May 2026, covering 16 States and 3 Union Territories.

    • Began on May 30, 2026; about 3.94 lakh Booth Level Officers cover 36.73 crore electors.
    • Not covered in Phase III: Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir, and Ladakh.
    • Legal basis: Articles 324 and 326; Sections 16, 19, 21 and 22 of RP Act, 1950.
    • SC (ADR v. ECI, 27 May 2026) held SIR is within ECI's statutory mandate.

    Don't confuse Phase III = 16 States + 3 UTs; the first two phases together covered 13 States/UTs.

    Check Text says Odisha, Mizoram, Sikkim and Manipur publish final rolls on 6 September, but the table gives Odisha 21 September and Mizoram 7 September.

    हिंदी: Electoral roll (मतदाता सूची) · Booth Level Officer (बूथ स्तरीय अधिकारी)

    From the magazine

    • The Election Commission of India announced Phase III of the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls to be conducted in a phased manner on May 14, 2026 beginning on May 30, 2026.
    • As of September 2026, Special Intensive Revision (SIR) was being implemented in phases across India. Phase III covered 16 States and 3 Union Territories. Odisha, Mizoram, Sikkim and Manipur were scheduled to publish their final electoral rolls on September 6, while other regions had later deadlines extending into October, November and December 2026.

    Constitutional and Legal Basis

    • The SIR exercise is based on the Election Commission’s constitutional and statutory powers. Article 324 and 326 of the Constitution gives the Election Commission superintendence, direction and control over the preparation of electoral rolls and the conduct of elections. Section 16, 19, 21 and 22 of Representation of the People Act 1950 are also invoked.
    • On May 27, 2026, the Supreme Court in Association for Democratic Reforms & Ors. vs. Election Commission of India & Ors. (2026) held that SIR falls within the ECI’s statutory mandate and is consistent with its constitutional responsibility to ensure free and fair elections.

    Key Highlights

    • More than 3.94 lakh Booth Level Officers is participating in the revision process during Phase III.
    • These Booth Level Officers visit households covering 36.73 crore electors.
    • The Special Intensive Revision Phase III will not cover Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir, and Ladakh.

    Crime in India Report 2024 Must knowPDF pp. 42–43

    NCRB's Crime in India 2024 report (6 May 2026) shows total crime fell about 6%, but cybercrime rose 17.9% to 1,01,928 cases.

    • Total cases: 58,85,867 in 2024, down from 62.41 lakh in 2023; crime rate 448.3 to 418.9.
    • Cybercrime: 1,01,928 cases (+17.9%); financial fraud 73,987 cases (72.6%).
    • Crimes against women fell 1.5% to 4.41 lakh; Uttar Pradesh highest with 66,398 cases.
    • 'Cruelty by husband or his relatives' formed 27.2% (1,20,227 cases) of crimes against women.
    • UP also highest in crimes against SCs (14,642) and dowry deaths (2,057 victims); MP highest against STs (3,165).
    • Drug overdose deaths up 50% to 978 (Tamil Nadu highest, 313); Kerala top charge-sheeting (94.5%).

    From the magazine

    The National Crime Records Bureau released the Crime in India Report 2024 on May 6, 2026. It is also significant because 2024 was the year in which the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita was used along with the Indian Penal Code framework.

    Key Highlights

    • According to the report, India recorded 58,85,867 criminal cases in 2024 (a declined of ~ 6% compared with 2023).

    • A total of 23.41 lakh cases were registered under Special and Local Laws.

    Impact of Legal Reclassification

    • Cases under the hurt category declined sharply by 30.58 percent.
    • The number of cases under IPC Sections 325,326 and 329–335 declined from 6.36 lakh in 2023 to 4.41 lakh in 2024.

    • Cybercrime continued to rise sharply in 2024.
    • India recorded 1,01,928 cybercrime cases in 2024.
    • This was a 17.9 percent increase over 86,420 cases in 2023.

    • Out of 1,01,928 cybercrime cases, 73,987 cases were related to financial fraud.
    • Financial fraud accounted for 72.6 percent of all registered cybercrime cases in 2024.
    • Sexual exploitation accounted for 3.1 percent, with 3,190 cases.

    Economic Offences

    • Economic offences increased by 4.6 percent in 2024.
    • India reported 2,14,379 economic offence cases in 2024.

    • 1,92,382 cases were related to forgery, cheating and fraud.

    • Crimes against women declined slightly by 1.5 percent in 2024.

    • This category acconted for 27.2 percent of total crimes against women.

    • Nagaland, Sikkim and Manipur recorded the lowest numbers of such cases.
    • Uttar Pradesh also recorded the highest number of dowry deaths cases (2038) with 2,057 victims.

    Crimes Against Children

    • Crimes against children increased by 5.9 percent in 2024.
    • India recorded 1,87,702 cases of crimes against children.

    Atrocities Against Scheduled Tribes

    • Cases fell from 12,960 in 2023 to 9,966 in 2024.

    • Madhya Pradesh recorded the highest number of crimes against ST communities with 3,165 cases.

    Atrocities Against Scheduled Castes

    • Crimes against Scheduled Caste communities declined by 3.6 percent in 2024.
    • Cases fell from 57,789 in 2023 to 55,698 in 2024.
    • The crime rate for crimes against Scheduled Castes stood at 27.7.
    • Rape accounted for 7.6 percent of cases.
    • Uttar Pradesh recorded the highest number of crimes against Scheduled Castes with 14,642 incidents.

    Murder Cases

    • India recorded 27,049 murder cases in 2024.
    • This was a marginal decline of 2.4 percent from 2023.
    • Murder cases had also declined by 2.8 percent in 2023 compared to 2022.

    Deaths by Suicide

    • The farming sector recorded 10,546 suicide deaths.

    • Tamil Nadu recorded the highest number of drug overdose deaths with 313 cases.

    Crimes Against the State

    • Cases under offences against the State increased by 6.6 percent in 2024.
    • These cases rose from 4,873 in 2023 to a higher level in 2024.
    • About 84.6 percent of these cases were registered under the Prevention of Damage to Public Property Act.

    • Kerala filed charge-sheets in 94.5 percent of cases.
    • Puducherry followed with 91 percent charge-sheeting efficiency.

    Arrests and Convictions

    • More than 10.71 lakh people were convicted.

    The Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026 was introduced in the Lok Sabha on 16 April 2026, but on 17 April 2026, it failed to pass in the Lok Sabha as it could not secure the required special majority.

    • During the vote, 298 members voted in favour and 230 members voted against.
    • A total of 528 members were present and voting, therefore 352 votes were required for its passage.
    • The central idea of this Bill was to bring representation closer to population.
    • If the population of a state has increased significantly, then the representation of its voters should increase proportionately.
    • On the one hand, it strengthened the idea of “one person, one vote, one value”, and on the other hand, it raised concerns among those states that had made serious efforts towards population control.

    Main Objectives of the Bill

    • The Bill was based on four major objectives:
      • To increase the strength of the Lok Sabha
      • To restart delimitation on a new basis
      • To give Parliament the power to decide which census would be used
      • To implement one-third reservation for women at an earlier stage
    • An amendment to Article 81 was proposed.
    • The maximum strength of the Lok Sabha was proposed to be increased from 550 to 850.
    • Of these a maximum of 815 members would be from the states and 35 members from Union Territories.
    • A new definition of “population” was proposed in Articles 55, 81,170, 330,332 etc.
    • Population would mean the census determined by Parliament through law.
    • An amendment to Article 82 was proposed.
    • Under the new proposal, delimitation would be done census determined by Parliament. based on the
    • This work would be carried out by the Delimitation Commission.
    • An amendment to Article 170 was proposed.
    • The total number of seats and constituencies in State Legislative Assemblies would be re-determined.

    Plastic Waste Management (Amendment) Rules, 2026 Must knowPDF p. 45

    MoEFCC notified the Plastic Waste Management (Amendment) Rules, 2026 on 31 March 2026, refining definitions and making recycled-content labels mandatory.

    • They amend, not replace, the Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016.
    • End-of-Life Disposal now includes co-processing, waste-to-energy, waste-to-oil and road construction.
    • Turning plastic into feedstock or new plastic counts strictly as recycling, not disposal.
    • Plastic Waste Processors now include recyclers and end-of-life disposal entities.
    • New terms: Registered Environment Auditor, Reuse and Seller.
    • Recycled plastic packaging must meet IS 14534:2023 and carry recycled-content labels.

    Don't confuse Feedstock or new plastic = recycling; energy recovery (waste-to-energy, road building) = end-of-life disposal.

    हिंदी: Plastic waste (प्लास्टिक अपशिष्ट) · Recycling (पुनर्चक्रण)

    From the magazine

    The Plastic Waste Management (Amendment) Rules, 2026 are an important step in India’s plastic-waste governance. They do not replace the Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016; rather, they further amend them.

    • The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change notified the amendment on March 31, 2026.

    Revised Definitions and Scope

    • The definition of End-of-Life Disposal has been expanded to include energy recovery methods such as co-processing, waste-to-energy, waste-to-oil, and road construction.
    • Processes converting plastic into feedstock or new plastic are now classified strictly as recycling, not disposal.
    • The definition of Plastic Waste Processors has been broadened to include both recyclers and end-of-life disposal entities.
    • New terms such as Registered Environment Auditor, Reuse, and Seller have been introduced to improve regulatory clarity.
    • The scope of local governance has been widened to include all relevant authorities beyond traditional local bodies.
    • All recycled plastic packaging must comply with Indian Standard IS 14534:2023.
    • Packaging must carry mandatory labeling indicating recycled content.

    The Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) released India’s first national counter-terrorism policy, and strategy, PRAHAAR, on 23 February 2026.

    • The policy comes after the government announced in November 2024 that a comprehensive national counter-terrorism strategy would be framed, and it follows recent security concerns including the April 2025 Pahalgam terror attack.
    • It seeks to provide a uniform, coordinated and technology-aware framework to deal with terrorism, terror financing, radicalisation, cyber-attacks, drone-based threats, and attacks on critical infrastructure.

    Key Highlights

    • The policy states that India faces terrorist threats across land, air and water, along with growing risks in the cyber domain.
    • It specifically warns that criminal hackers and nation-states are targeting India through cyber-attacks.
    • The document underlines that India continues to face sponsored terrorism from across the border.
    • The policy identifies groups such as Al-Qaeda and ISIS as entities trying to incite violence in India through sleeper cells and extremist propaganda.
    • PRAHAAR notes the use of drones, encrypted messaging apps, social media, dark web platforms, and crypto wallets by terrorist groups for communication, propaganda, recruitment and financing.
    • It also flags the danger of misuse of CBRNED materials—Chemical, Biological, Radiological, Nuclear, Explosive and Digital—as well as robotics and drone systems.

    The Raksha Mantri, Rajnath Singh, released “Defence Forces Vision 2047: A Roadmap for a Future-Ready Indian Military” on 10 March 2026 in South Block, New Delhi. Prepared by the Headquarters Integrated Defence Staff (HQ IDS), the document presents a long-term blueprint for transforming India’s armed forces into a modern, integrated, technologically advanced, and self-reliant military by the centenary of Independence.

    • In 2025, the Ministry of Defence declared the year as the “Year of Reforms” to push jointness, integration and future-readiness.
    • The Ministry’s Year End Review 2025 had also said that the Armed Forces Vision 2047 was prepared in two parts and that Part I would be released publicly soon.

    Phased Roadmap to 2047

    One of the major strengths of the document is that it sets out a calibrated timeline for transformation. 1. Era of Transition (till 2030)

    • This phase focuses on restructuring the military and strengthening deterrence.
    • It gives importance to rapid adoption of indigenous technologies, especially in areas such as drones and surveillance. 2. Era of Consolidation (2030–2040)
    • This phase aims to deepen integration of cyber and space capabilities.
    • It seeks to operationalise layered air and missile defence systems. 3. Era of Excellence (2040–2047)
    • This final phase envisions a fully integrated, self-reliant, all-domain military force.
    • It aims to make India’s armed forces globally respected, technologically advanced, and combat ready.
