    हिंदी: Drinking water (पेयजल) · Tap connection (नल कनेक्शन)

    From the magazine

    Under the chairmanship of Narendra Modi, the Union Cabinet approved Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) 2.0 on 10 March 2026. Its objective is to transform Jal Jeevan Mission from being limited to infrastructure creation into a service-based model.

    Key Facts

    • The Cabinet has approved an increase in the total expenditure for this restructuring to ₹8.69 lakh crore, of which the central government’s contribution will be ₹3.59 lakh crore.
    • This amount is higher than the earlier approved ₹2.08 lakh crore by the Centre in 2019–20, meaning that an additional ₹1.51 lakh crore of central assistance has been included.
      • In this direction, an integrated national digital platform named “Sujalam Bharat” was developed by March, 2026.
      • Under this, each village will be assigned a unique Sujal village/service area ID, through which a complete digital mapping of the supply system from water source to household tap will be prepared.
    • To enhance transparency and accountability, active participation of Gram Panchayats and Village Water and Sanitation Committees will be ensured through the “Jal Arpan” initiative.
    • Gram Panchayats will certify project completion only when adequate arrangements for operation and maintenance have been ensured by the state government; only thereafter will a village be declared as “Har Ghar Jal”.
    • To strengthen community participation, “Jal Utsav” will be developed as an annual programme.

    Progress and Coverage

    • The Functionality Assessment 2024 covered 19,812 Har Ghar Jal Villages and 2,37,608 househoulds; 76% received water meeting prescribed quality standards.
    • It is noteworthy that in 2019, only 3.23 crore (about 17%) rural households had tap water connections, whereas now more than 12.56 crore additional households have been provided this facility.
    • At present, out of a total of 19.36 crore rural households, approximately 15.80 crore (about 81.61%) households have access to tap water (as on March, 2026).

    Targets and Implementation

    • Under JJM 2.0, the target is to provide tap water connections to all 19.36 crore rural households by December 2028 and to ensure that all Gram Panchayats receive “Har Ghar Jal” certification.
    • This mission is now moving beyond an infrastructure-based approach towards a utility-based service delivery model, which will ensure 24×7 rural drinking water supply and strengthen the goal of “Viksit Bharat @2047”.

    Quick Facts

    • Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) was launched by Narendra Modi on 15 August 2019.
    • It had an ambitious target of providing tap water supply to every rural household by 2024.
    • At the time of its launch, only 3.23 crore (17%) rural households had access to tap water connections.

    • The major components of the scheme are as follows:
    • Under the Revised UDAN scheme, it is proposed to develop 100 airports from existing unserved airstrips to enhance regional connectivity.

    • Considering the high recurring O&M costs and limited revenue of airports operated under the Regional Connectivity Scheme (RCS), the scheme proposes O&M support for three years.

    Supreme Court stays 2026 UGC Equity Regulations Must knowPDF pp. 47–48

    On 29 January 2026 the Supreme Court put the UGC Equity Regulations, 2026 in abeyance, keeping the 2012 regulations in force for now.

    • Court flagged vagueness, possible misuse and exclusion in the 2026 Regulations.
    • The Regulations followed SC directions in Abeda Salim Tadvi v. Union of India (2019).
    • A Bench of Justices Surya Kant and Ujjal Bhuyan had directed UGC to notify enforceable rules.
    • Caste discrimination defined to cover SCs, STs and OBCs.
    • Every institution must set up an Equal Opportunity Centre with an Equity Committee headed by the institution head.
    • Equity Committee meets within 24 hours, reports in 15 working days; head acts within 7 days.

    Memory aid 24 hours – 15 working days – 7 days: meet, report, act.

    हिंदी: Discrimination (भेदभाव) · Equity (समता)

    From the magazine

    In a significant order affecting India’s higher education governance, the Supreme Court on 29 January 2026 has kept in abeyance the newly notified UGC (Promotion of Equity in Higher Education Institutions) Regulations, 2026.

    • These Regulations were designed to create a time-bound, enforceable anti-discrimination framework on campuses. The Court raised concerns about vagueness, possible misuse, and exclusion, and has directed that the older 2012 UGC Equity Regulations would continue to operate for now.
    • The UGC Equity Regulations, 2026, were framed pursuant to the Supreme Court’s directions in Abeda Salim Tadvi v. Union of India (2019).
    • A Bench of Justices Surya Kant and Ujjal Bhuyan had directed the UGC to notify enforceable regulations to:
      • Address caste-based discrimination
      • Prevent student suicides
      • Rectify the ineffective implementation of the 2012 regulations.

    Key Provisions of the UGC Regulations, 2026

    • Broad Coverage of Caste-Based Discrimination: The regulations define caste-based discrimination as any unfair or biased treatment against Scheduled Castes (SCs), Scheduled Tribes (STs), and Other Backward Classes (OBCs), thereby explicitly extending legal protection to OBCs and correcting a major omission in the earlier draft framework.
    • Mandatory Equal Opportunity Centres Every higher education institution (EOCs): is required to establish an Equal Opportunity Centre (EOC) to promote equity, social inclusion, and equal access, and to address complaints related to discrimination on campus.
      • Each institution must form an Equity Committee under the EOC, chaired by the head of the institution, with mandatory representation from SCs, STs, OBCs, persons with disabilities, and women, ensuring inclusive decision-making.
      • The Equity Committee is required to meet within 24 hours of receiving a complaint and submit its report within 15 working days, after which the head of the institution must initiate action within 7 days.
    • The UGC will establish a national monitoring committee comprising representatives from statutory bodies and civil society to oversee implementation, review complaints, and suggest preventive measures, with the committee meeting at least twice a year.

    NITI Aayog and GIZ India released 'Water Budgeting in Aspirational Blocks', studying water supply and demand in 18 blocks to improve local water security.

    • Kotri and Abu Road (Rajasthan) over-extract groundwater beyond recharge.

    हिंदी: Groundwater (भूजल) · Water security (जल सुरक्षा)

    From the magazine

    NITI Aayog, in collaboration with GIZ India, has released a report titled “Water Budgeting in Aspirational Blocks”, aimed at enhancing water security at the local level, improving resource planning, and aligning with the vision of Viksit Bharat@2047. The report provides a comprehensive analysis of water availability, demand, and sector-specific challenges across 18 Aspirational Blocks in 10 states and a UT (11 states and UT), using a digital platform for water budgeting.

    Key Findings

    • Water Deficits: Several blocks are facing severe water shortages. Notable examples include:
      • Namchi (94% deficit)
      • Gangiri (60% deficit)
      • Baldeogarh (53% deficit)
    • Over-extraction of Groundwater: Blocks like Kotri and Abu Road in Rajasthan are over-extracting groundwater beyond recharge levels, leading to unsustainable water use.
    • Under-utilization of Runoff: Some regions, such as Fatehpur in Bihar, generate runoff but fail to utilize the stored water effectively.

    Union Cabinet Approves 2027 Census Must knowPDF pp. 49–50

    The Cabinet approved Census 2027 on 12 December 2025 at ₹11,718.24 crore; it will be India's 16th Census and the first by digital means.

    • Eighth Census since Independence; the last completed Census was in 2011.
    • Census is a Union subject: Entry 69, Union List, Seventh Schedule; Census Act, 1948.
    • Phase I Houselisting: 1 April–30 September 2026; Phase II Population Enumeration: February 2027.
    • Reference date: 00:00 hours, 1 March 2027 (Ladakh and snow-bound areas enumerated September 2026).
    • Caste enumeration included (CCPA decision, April 30, 2025); 40-question schedule, Question 10 on caste.
    • Registrar General (under MHA) runs it; Android/iOS apps; about 30 lakh field staff; optional online self-enumeration.

    Memory aid 16th Census, 8th after Independence; the count 'freezes' at midnight, 1 March 2027.

    Don't confuse Approval date (12 December 2025) is not the reference date (00:00 hours, 1 March 2027). Census 2021 was postponed after COVID-19.

    हिंदी: Census (जनगणना) · Caste enumeration (जाति गणना)

    From the magazine

    • India is conducting Census 2027 after the last completed Census of 2011. It will be the sixteenth Census of India and the eighth since Independence.
    • The Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, approved the scheme on 12 December 2025, at an estimated cost of ₹11,718.24 crore.
    • The Census is a Union subject under Entry 69 of the Union List in the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution. Its legal framework comprises the Census Act, 1948, and the Census Rules, 1990, as amended.
    • The Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner, India, under the Ministry of Home Affairs, conducts the Census with state governments and Union Territory administrations.
    • The initial declaration under Section 3 of the Census Act was issued on 16 June 2025. A notification dated 5 September 2026 superseded it and introduced an additional regional reference date.
    • Census operations will take place across 2026 and 2027 in two phases: Houselisting and Housing Census, followed by Population Enumeration.
    • Phase I records housing conditions, household amenities and assets. Its original national window was 1 April–30 September 2026, normally involving 30 days of fieldwork in each state or Union Territory.
    • Subsequent notifications deferred Phase I in Manipur until a further declaration and extended houselisting in Assam’s Charaideo and Sivasagar districts until 31 October 2026.
    • Phase II—Population Enumeration generally remains scheduled for February 2027, with separate schedules for specified regions.
    • In the entire Union Territory of Ladakh and specified snow-bound non-synchronous areas of Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand, Population Enumeration was scheduled for 1–30 September 2026, followed by revision on 1–5 October 2026. Self-enumeration was scheduled for 17–31 August 2026.
    • The reference date, meaning the point in time to which the population count relates, is generally 00:00 hours on 1 March 2027.
    • Population Enumeration covers demography, religion, language, literacy, education, economic activity, migration and fertility. Its notified schedule contains 40 questions, including questions on disability and digital literacy.
    • The Cabinet Committee on Political Affairs decided on April 30, 2025 to include caste enumeration. Caste information will be collected electronically during Population Enumeration, and Question 10 concerns SC, ST and caste.
    • Census 2027 will be India’s first Census conducted by digital means, using enumerator mobile applications available on Android and iOS, while continuing house-to-house visits.
    • Optional online self-enumeration enables households to submit information before the enumerator’s visit. For Phase I, the normal window is 15 days before fieldwork, and the generated Self-Enumeration ID helps enumerators confirm submitted details.
    • About 30 lakh field functionaries are envisaged.
    • Census 2021 was postponed following the COVID-19 outbreak.

    From the magazine

    Unlocking Growth in Tourism and Hospitality Sector

    • NITI Aayog, in collaboration with the Ministry of Tourism, launched a report titled “Unlocking Growth in Tourism and Hospitality Sector” on June 30, 2026 at New Delhi.

    • The report is aligned with the vision of Viksit Bharat 2047 and aims to strengthen tourism’s contribution to economic growth, employment generation and regional development.

    12th International Yoga Day 2026

    • The 12th International Yoga Day was officially celebrated in Kolkata on June 21, 2026.
      • Prime Minister Narendra Modi participated in the main event at Red Road in Kolkata, West Bengal.
      • Around 35,000 people joined the yoga session with the Prime Minister.

    • The campaign “100 Days, 100 Cities, 100 Organisations” encouraged regular yoga practice across India.

    Ahmedabad Metro Rail Project Phase 2A

    • The Union Cabinet approved Phase 2A of the Ahmedabad Metro Rail Project on June 10, 2026.

    • Phase 2A will connect Koteshwar Road to the Airport corridor.

    Yuge Yugeen Bharat National Museum

    • The first gallery of the Yuge Yugeen Bharat National Museum “Time and Timelessness,” is expected to open by end-2026.

    • Located in the North and South Blocks, Raisina Hill, under the Central Vista Redevelopment Project.

    Ministry of Mines Reclassifies Limestone as Major Mineral

    • Effective from October 10, 2025, all limestone reclassified as “major mineral” under MMDR Act, 1957.
    • Removes previous distinction between lime stone (minor) and industrial (major) uses.
    • Simplifies regulation, improves mining transparency, and enables freer sale and usage.

    • India’s first AI hub with gigawatt-scale compute capacity for AI, cloud, and HPC services.

    India’s First Cooperative Multi-Feed CBG Plant – Maharashtra

    • Inaugurated on October 5, 2025 at Kopargaon, Ahilyanagar district, by the Union Home and Cooperation Minister.
    • Produces ~12 tonnes of CBG and ~75 tonnes of potash granules daily from sugarcane and molasses waste.

    Approval of Proposal to Rename ‘Kerala’ as ‘Keralam’

    • The Kerala Legislative Assembly passed a resolution on June 24, 2024 to change the name of the state from “Kerala” to “Keralam.” Under the chairmanship of Narendra Modi, the Union Cabinet approved the proposal on 24 February 2026 to change the name of the state “Kerala” to “Keralam.”

    BCCI Is Not a Public Authority Under RTI Act

    • The Central Information Commission has held that the Board of Control for Cricket in India is not a “public authority” under the Right to Information Act, 2005.
    • The CIC held that the BCCI is not covered under the definition of “public authority” under Section 2(h) of the RTI Act (May, 2026).
    • The Commission observed that the BCCI is registered as a private association under the Tamil Nadu Societies Registration Act, 1975.
    • It has argued that it is not “State” under Article 12 of the Constitution.

    ‘One Case One Data’ and ‘Su Sahayak’

    • The Supreme Court of India has taken another step towards technology-enabled justice delivery through two digital initiatives: ‘One Case One Data’ and ‘Su-Sahayak’.
    • Chief Justice of India Justice Surya Kant announced the move on May 11, 2026, with the stated purpose of improving judicial data integration, case management and public access to court services.
    • ‘One Case One Data’ is a digital initiative to streamline case management across different levels of the judiciary.
    • ‘Su Sahayak’ is an Artificial Intelligence (AI) powered chatbot integrated with the Supreme Court website.

    Internationalisation of Higher Education in India

    • NITI Aayog has released a comprehensive report titled “Internationalisation of Higher Education in India: Prospects, Potential, and Policy Recommendations.”
    • The report identifies internationalisation as a strategic imperative for India’s economic growth, research competitiveness, and global influence.
    • India inbound–outbound student ratio was 1: 24 in 2021 and 1: 19 in 2022.
    • Indian students’ overseas education expenditure is projected to reach about ₹6 lakh crore by 2025, which is nearly 2% of India’s GDP and approximately 75% of India’s trade deficit (FY 2024–25).

    8th Poshan Pakhwada 2026

    • Poshan Pakhwada 2026 is a nationwide campaign of the Ministry of Women and Child Development to strengthen nutrition awareness, early childhood care and development and community participation under Mission Poshan 2.0.
    • The Ministry of Women and Child Development celebrated the 8th Poshan Pakhwada from 9th to 23rd April 2026.
    • The national launch took place on 9 April 2026 at Vigyan Bhavan, New Delhi under the leadership of Union Minister Annpurna Devi and Minister of State Savitri Thakur and Secretary Anil Malik.
    • The theme for 2026 was “Maximizing Brain Development in the First Six Years of Life.”
    • POSHAN Abhiyan was launched on March 8, 2018 in Jhunjhunu district, Rajasthan.

    NCERT Granted Status of an Institution Deemed to be University (2026)

    • The Union Government on March 30, 2026 has granted National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT) the status of an “Institution Deemed to be University under distinct category”.
    • The decision aligns with the vision of National Education Policy 2020 (NEP 2020).
    • NCERT is now empowered to independently offer degree programmes for undergraduate, postgraduate, doctoral, and specialised courses etc.

    PM-RAHAT Scheme

    • To reduce fatalities due to road accidents, the scheme was launched by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on February 13, 2026, and it was officially named “Prime Minister – Road Accident Victims’ Hospitalisation and Assured Treatment (PM-RAHAT) Scheme” through a notification issued on February 19, 2026.
    • As per the statutory provisions provided under Section 162 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, this scheme was notified on 5 May 2025.
    • Under this scheme, each eligible victim will be provided treatment cover up to ₹1.5 lakh, which will be applicable for a maximum period of 7 days from the date of the accident, and it will apply to all types of roads.

    AI-based Bharat VISTAAR’ Scheme

    • Bharat-VISTAAR is a farmer-centric, AI-powered agricultural Digital Public Infrastructure launched on February 17, 2026 in Jaipur by Union Minister for Agriculture and Farmers’ Welfare, and Rural Development, Shivraj Singh Chouhan, in the presence of Rajasthan Chief Minister Bhajanlal Sharma.
    • In Phase-1, this facility will start in Hindi and English and will reach lakhs of farmers in several states including Maharashtra, Bihar, Gujarat.
    • Bharat-VISTAAR is a single digital gateway for farmers.

    Motion Against Om Birla and Gyanesh Kumar

    • The Lok Sabha rejected the no-confidence motion against Speaker Om Birla by a voice vote after an extensive debate.
    • The notices of impeachment motion against Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar were refused for admission by the Lok Sabha speaker and Rajya Sabha chairman.
    • The decision was taken after evaluation by Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla and Rajya Sabha Chairman C. P. Radhakrishnan.
    • The primary allegation behind this was that the proceedings of the House were not being conducted in accordance with the standards of impartiality and that the opposition was not being given adequate opportunities.
    • The constitutional provision for the removal of the Speaker of the Lok Sabha is contained in Article 94.

    BHASHINI and Voice-First Multilingual AI

    • The Digital India BHASHINI Division (DIBD) under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) showcased its voice-first multilingual Artificial Intelligence platform at the AI-Led Innovation and Capacity Building Conference held on January 20, 2026 in Lucknow.
    • The conference was organised by the Centre for e-Governance (CeG), IT and Electronics Department, Government of Uttar Pradesh, and focused on strengthening AI adoption, digital skilling, and innovation capacity at the State level.

    About the BHASHINI Platform

    • BHASHINI is a national initiative aimed at enabling multilingual, voice-enabled digital public services across India.
    • BHASHINI expands to ‘BHASHa INterface for India’.
    • The platform supports more than 36 languages in text and over 22 languages in voice.
    • It has deployed over 350 AI language models to facilitate translation, speech recognition, and conversational AI services.

    Uttar Pradesh “Gharauni Act” 2025

    • The Uttar Pradesh Rural Abadi Records Act (popularly called the “Gharauni Act”) was taken up and passed by the Uttar Pradesh Legislature (assented to by the Governor on January 2, 2026), to provide a clear legal framework for rural residential (“abadi”) property records created under the SVAMITVA programme.
    • The law is designed to institutionalise rural property cards/records prepared through drone-based surveys under the SVAMITVA Scheme (Ministry of Panchayati Raj).
    • SVAMITVA status in Uttar Pradesh
    • As per a Lok Sabha annexure (answer dated 29 July 2025), Uttar Pradesh shows:
      • Targeted villages: 90,573
      • Drone flying completed: 90,573
      • Property cards prepared (villages): 68,377
      • Number of property cards prepared: 10,486,961
    • As on January 2026, 3.06 crore property cards have been prepared across 1.86 lakh villages under SVAMITVA (all-India).

    Gyan Bharatam National Manuscript Survey

    • The Ministry of Culture launched the Gyan Bharatam National Manuscript Survey on March 16, 2026 under the broader Gyan Bharatam initiative (announced in the Union Budget 2025-26).
    • It is being described as India’s first comprehensive national map of manuscript repositories to identify, document, and prepare for the preservation and digitisation of manuscript collections across the country.
    • The survey is a nationwide exercise aimed at identifying manuscript repositories across India and preparing a geo-tagged national inventory of manuscript presence.
      • The survey seeks to map manuscripts located in private homes, temples, monasteries, libraries, and institutions.
      • It will help create a national “Manuscript Presence Map” across districts and states.

    Indian Maritime Doctrine 2025

    • On December 2, 2025, the Chief of the Naval Staff released the updated Indian Maritime Doctrine 2025. The Indian Navy Day was celebrated December 4, 2025. The theme for Indian Navy Day 2025 is “Combat Ready, Cohesive, Credible, and Aatmanirbhar Force,” highlighting the Navy’s role in safeguarding the seas for a Viksit, Samriddha Bharat (Developed and Prosperous India).

    Flag Hoisting at Ram Temple in Ayodhya

    • On November 25, 2025, Prime Minister Narendra Modi attended the Dhwajarohan Utsav at Shri Ram Janmbhoomi Mandir, hoisted the Dharma Dhwaja on the Shikhara.
    • .The flag is right-angled triangular, measuring 10 feet in height and 20 feet in length, featuring powerful symbols like:
      • Radiant Sun, representing the brilliance and valour of Lord Ram evokes the Suryavansha tradition.
      • Om, symbolizing the spiritual connection.
      • Kovidara Tree, an emblem of ancient wisdom and strength. The flag’s saffron color is associated with the Sun dynasty (Suryavansh) and reflects the ideals of Ram Rajya.

    India and It’s Neighbours; Other Asian Countries

    India–Switzerland Must knowPDF p. 53

    Swiss President Guy Parmelin's State Visit to India (October 5–7, 2026) marked one year of the India–EFTA TEPA trade deal.

    • Visit October 5–7, 2026; talks at Hyderabad House; focus on 3Ts — Trade, Technology, Talent.
    • EFTA (set up 1960): Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, Switzerland; Switzerland is not in the EEA.
    • TEPA: signed 10 March 2024, entered into force 1 October 2025.
    • TEPA goal: US$100 billion investment and one million direct jobs in India over 15 years.
    • Young Professionals pact: 300 professionals a year from each country, expandable to 500.
    • Second India–EFTA Prosperity Summit: Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi, 7 October 2026.

    Memory aid EFTA's four = 'I Like Nice Sweets': Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, Switzerland.

    Don't confuse TEPA was signed on 10 March 2024 but came into force on 1 October 2025; don't swap the two dates.

    हिंदी: Free Trade Association (मुक्त व्यापार संघ) · State Visit (राजकीय यात्रा)

    From the magazine

    President Guy Parmelin’s State Visit to India

    Swiss Confederation President Guy Parmelin visited India from October 5–7, 2026, marking the first anniversary of the India–European Free Trade Association (EFTA) Trade and Economic Partnership Agreement (TEPA). On 5 October, he paid tribute to Mahatma Gandhi at Rajghat, New Delhi, held bilateral talks with Prime Minister Narendra Modi at Hyderabad House, and met President Droupadi Murmu at Rashtrapati Bhavan. Both countries emphasised cooperation in the 3Ts—Trade, Technology and Talent, alongside developing resilient global supply chains.

    • India–EFTA Agreement: Established in 1960, EFTA comprises Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland. Switzerland is not a member of the European Economic Area (EEA).
    • India–EFTA TEPA was signed on 10 March 2024 and entered into force on 1 October 2025. It aims to facilitate US$100 billion in investments and one million direct jobs in India over 15 years.
    • Five Major Agreements and Arrangements: 1. Migration and Mobility Partnership Memorandum of Understanding (MoU): Promotes legal migration and professional mobility, including multiple-entry visas valid for up to five years. 2. Young Professionals Exchange Agreement: Provides for the exchange of 300 professionals annually from each country, expandable to 500, through temporary employment. 3. Transport Technology MoU: Signed between India’s Ministry of Road Transport and Highways and Switzerland’s Federal Department of Economic Affairs, Education and Research

    (EAER) to promote sustainable transport, electric vehicles, ropeways and tunnel technologies. 4. Research Letter of Intent (LoI): Signed between India’s Department of Science and Technology (DST) and the Swiss National Science Foundation (SNSF) to strengthen long-term scientific research. 5. Innovation Implementation Arrangement: Signed between DST and the Zurich University of Applied Sciences (ZHAW) to promote technology transfer, entrepreneurship and the Indo-Swiss Academia–Industry Training (AIT India) programme for early-stage startups.

    • The inaugural Indo-Swiss Research Flagship Event was held in New Delhi on 6 October 2026, attended by President Parmelin and Union Minister Dr. Jitendra Singh.
    • The Indo-Swiss Research Framework (ISRF) aims to strengthen scientific networks, knowledge exchange and academia–industry collaboration. Bilateral scientific cooperation began in 2003, followed by the Indo-Swiss Joint Research Programme in 2005.
    • The Second India–EFTA Prosperity Summit was held at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi, on 7 October 2026, reviewing TEPA implementation and investment opportunities.
    • India–Switzerland relations are rooted in the Treaty of Friendship signed on 14 August 1948.

    India-Japan Must knowPDF pp. 53–54

    Abe Memorial Corridor opened in Varanasi (7 October 2026), and the 16th India–Japan Annual Summit (July 2026) widened defence, AI and energy ties.

    • Abe Memorial Corridor (Rudraksh Centre, Varanasi) opened 7 October 2026 by CM Yogi Adityanath and Akie Abe.
    • Rudraksh Centre (Japanese-aided) opened by Modi on 15 July 2021; Abe received Padma Vibhushan in 2021.
    • UP: 500-acre Japan City planned in YEIDA region; Yamanashi Prefecture partners UP on green hydrogen.
    • 16th Annual Summit: Japanese PM Sanae Takaichi in New Delhi, 1–3 July 2026; 16 official outcomes.
    • UNICORN = Unified Complex Radio Antenna, a naval defence co-development, announced outside the 16 outcomes.
    • ISRO–JAXA LUPEX = Chandrayaan-5; 2027 = Year of Shared Horizons (75 years of diplomatic ties).

    Memory aid 16th Summit → 16 official outcomes: the summit number equals the outcome count.

    Don't confuse UNICORN was announced separately; it is NOT one of the 16 official outcomes.

    हिंदी: Special Strategic and Global Partnership (विशेष रणनीतिक और वैश्विक साझेदारी) · Green hydrogen (हरित हाइड्रोजन)

    From the magazine

    Shinzo Abe Memorial Corridor Inaugurated in Varanasi

    On October 7, 2026, Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath and Akie Abe, wife of former Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe, jointly inaugurated the Abe Memorial Corridor at the Rudraksh International Cooperation and Convention Centre in Varanasi.

    • The corridor commemorates Shinzo Abe’s contribution to India–Japan relations and his association with Varanasi.
    • It displays photographs and memories of his visits to India and his friendship with Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
    • In December 2015, Abe visited Varanasi with Prime Minister Modi and participated in the Ganga Aarti.
    • The visit strengthened cultural cooperation between Varanasi and Japan’s ancient city of Kyoto.
    • Rudraksh Convention Centre: Inaugurated by Prime Minister Modi on 15 July 2021, the centre was constructed with Japanese assistance.
    • Its concept was discussed during Abe’s 2015 Varanasi visit, making it a symbol of India–Japan cultural cooperation.
    • Abe served as Japan’s Prime Minister during 2006– 07 and 2012–20.
    • India honoured him with the Padma Vibhushan in 2021 in the field of Public Affairs.
    • Uttar Pradesh plans to develop a 500-acre Japan City in the Yamuna Expressway Industrial Development Authority (YEIDA) region to attract Japanese investment.
    • Cooperation with Japan’s Yamanashi Prefecture also includes green hydrogen, research and skill development, with a proposed Centre of Excellence involving IIT (BHU), IIT Kanpur and other institutions.
    • Japan supports major Indian projects, including the Mumbai–Ahmedabad High-Speed Rail, Dedicated Freight Corridor and Delhi–Mumbai Industrial Corridor.

    16th India–Japan Annual Summit 2026

    Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi visited New Delhi from 1 to 3 July, 2026 for the 16th India–Japan Annual Summit. The main meeting with Narendra Modi was held on 2 July. The visit marked 20 years of annual, alternating leadership visits.

    • The summit strengthened the Special Strategic and Global Partnership established in 2014, focusing on defence and security, economic partnership and people-to-people exchanges.
    • It produced 16 official outcomes. The separately announced UNICORN defence co-development initiative was outside this list.
    • Mineral cooperation focuses on upstream exploration, technical knowledge and collaboration between the Geological Survey of India and the Japan Organization for Metals and Energy Security (JOGMEC).
    • Japan’s Free and Open Indo-Pacific (FOIP) approach broadly aligns with India’s Indo-Pacific Oceans Initiative (IPOI) and Mutual and Holistic Advancement for Security and Growth Across Regions (MAHASAGAR), supporting sovereignty, international law and a rules-based region.
    • The fourth 2+2 Foreign and Defence Ministers’ Meeting is scheduled to be held in Tokyo before the end of 2026.
    • Cooperation covers JAIMEX 25, satellite-based maritime awareness, naval maintenance in India and defence technology under Make in India.
    • The Unified Complex Radio Antenna (UNICORN) combines communication antennas into one structure, reducing radar signature and improving naval communication.
    • AI outcomes included a joint statement and IndiaAI Mission–Japan’s Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry cooperation with GENIAC.
    • IIT Bombay, BharatGen and Japan’s National Institute of Informatics will develop large language models with scientific-reasoning capabilities.
    • SarvamAI and Preferred Networks will cooperate on foundation models and the complete AI technology stack.
    • The target is to invite 500 highly skilled Indian AI professionals to Japan by 2030.
    • AI cooperation will be guided by the Hiroshima AI Process and New Delhi Declaration on AI Impact.
    • Digital cooperation includes the proposed FOIP Digital Corridor and the NIXI–JPNIC agreement on internet registries, IPv6, security, capacity building and exchanges.
    • Energy cooperation involves Indian national oil companies, Indian Strategic Petroleum Reserves Limited, JOGMEC and the Japan Bank for International Cooperation.
    • The Cooperative Biogas for Growth Initiative supports approximately 1,000 biogas and organic-fertiliser plants through dairy cooperatives.
    • The leaders supported the proposed clean-ammonia project in Odisha and recognised hydrogen and ammonia as important for decarbonisation and energy security.
    • The Joint Crediting Mechanism under Article 6.2 of the Paris Agreement can facilitate bilateral carbon-credit cooperation and low-carbon investment.
    • Cooperation will continue on the Mumbai– Ahmedabad High-Speed Rail project and Japan’s latest E10-series Shinkansen technology.
    • The Centre for Cellular and Molecular Platforms (C-CAMP) and RIKEN will cooperate in translational research, deep technology, start-ups, healthcare, agriculture and environmental applications.
    • The National Centre for Biological Sciences–Tata Institute of Fundamental Research and RIKEN will cooperate in biological and neuroscience research, researcher exchanges and joint projects.
    • The leaders welcomed research exchanges and progress in the ISRO–JAXA Lunar Polar Exploration Mission, or LUPEX, also called Chandrayaan-5.
    • India and Japan will celebrate 2027 as the Year of Shared Horizons, marking 75 years of diplomatic relations through cultural, academic, youth, business and public-diplomacy events.
    • Modi accepted an invitation to Japan for the 17th Annual Summit in 2027.
    • The leaders supported state–prefecture partnerships, including Yamanashi–Uttar Pradesh, and the India–Japan Governors’ Network for Friendship and Exchange.
    • Yamanashi (a leader in hydrogen technology) partnered with Uttar Pradesh (via UPNEDA) on hydrogen production, storage, and clean energy pilot projects.

    PM Modi’s State Visit to Uzbekistan Must knowPDF p. 55

    PM Modi's Uzbekistan visit (29–30 August 2026) upgraded ties to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership, focusing on uranium, minerals and trade.

    • Visit: 29–30 August 2026, on the invitation of President Shavkat Mirziyoyev.
    • Strategic Partnership (2011) upgraded to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership.
    • Modi received the 'Oliy Darajali Do‘stlik' Order, Uzbekistan's highest state award.

    हिंदी: Comprehensive Strategic Partnership (व्यापक रणनीतिक साझेदारी) · Landlocked country (स्थलरुद्ध देश)

    From the magazine

    Prime Minister Narendra Modi visited Uzbekistan on 29–30 August, 2026 at the invitation of President Shavkat Mirziyoyev. The two countries upgraded their Strategic Partnership (established in 2011) to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership. President Mirziyoyev conferred Uzbekistan’s highest state award, the “Oliy Darajali Do‘stlik” Order, on Modi.

    • Uzbekistan, a double-landlocked Central Asian country, remains strategically important to India because of its location and mineral resources.
    • Both countries discussed a framework for long-term uranium supplies to India and expanded cooperation in peaceful nuclear energy, geological exploration, mining, mineral processing and value-added products.
    • Uzbekistan produced approximately 7,000 tonnes of uranium in 2025, with proven reserves estimated at 139,000 tonnes. Cooperation also supports India’s National Critical Mineral Mission.
    • The countries set a bilateral trade target of US$5 billion by 2030, compared with trade exceeding US$1 billion previously.
    • Both sides supported multimodal transport corridors and reduced freight costs.
    • Iran’s Chabahar Port and the International North– South Transport Corridor (INSTC) offer alternative routes to overcome India’s limited overland connectivity with Central Asia.
    • An agreement between NPCI International Payments Ltd. (NIPL) and Uzbekistan’s National Interbank Processing Centre (NIPC) will enable Indian UPI applications to scan Uzbekistan’s UZQR codes for merchant payments.
    • Their joint military exercise DUSTLIK (7th edition) was last conducted in Uzbekistan’s Namangan Region in April 2026.
    • An MoU on Ayurveda and other traditional medicines was signed.
    • India announced 100 Lal Bahadur Shastri Hindi Scholarships and an ICCR Sanskrit Chair at Tashkent State University of Oriental Studies.
    • Both countries signed a Letter of Intent to conserve the ancient Buddhist sites of Fayaz Tepa and Kara Tepa near Termez.
    • India also announced a US$1 million grant for afforestation and ecological rehabilitation in the Aral Sea region.

    India–Uzbekistan Business Forum 2026

    • The forum was attended by India’s Union Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal and Uzbekistan’s Minister of Investment, Industry and Trade, Laziz Kudratov.
    • Piyush Goyal called for doubling bilateral trade from approximately US$1.5 billion to about US$3 billion within three years.
    • The forum involved India’s Ministry of Commerce and Industry, Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade, and the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FICCI).
    • Cooperation focused on mining, textiles, pharmaceuticals, healthcare, agriculture, food processing, information technology, digital infrastructure and advanced manufacturing.

    • The major outcome was the MoU on Strategic Collaboration between Indian Strategic Petroleum Reserves Limited and Abu Dhabi National Oil Company.

    • The next outcome was an MoU between Cochin Shipyard Limited and Drydocks World to set up a Ship Repair Cluster at Vadinar, including offshore fabrication, under the Maritime Development Fund Scheme launched by the Government of India.

    • In 2026, India and Canada completed 79 years of diplomatic relations.

    India-UK CETA and DCC Must knowPDF p. 58

    The India–UK CETA trade deal and Double Contribution Convention became operational on July 15, 2026, boosting trade, mobility and social-security relief.

    • Operational: July 15, 2026; CETA concluded 6 May 2025, signed in London 24 July 2025.
    • DCC signed 10 February 2026; ends double social-security payments for posted workers.
    • Took 14 negotiation rounds; built on Enhanced Trade Partnership and Roadmap 2030 (May 2021).
    • CETA has 30 chapters; UK gives zero duty on nearly 99% of Indian tariff lines.
    • UK service commitments: 12 sectors and 137 sub-sectors.
    • India kept dairy, cereals, millets, apples, edible oils and oilseeds out of major concessions.

    Don't confuse CETA = trade agreement; DCC = social-security convention. DCC does not automatically give host-country pensions.

    हिंदी: Free Trade Agreement (मुक्त व्यापार समझौता) · Social security (सामाजिक सुरक्षा)

    From the magazine

    The India–United Kingdom Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) and Double Contribution Convention (DCC) became operational on July 15, 2026. They aim to expand trade and investment, facilitate temporary professional mobility and eliminate duplicate social-security contributions for eligible workers.

    • The Enhanced Trade Partnership and Roadmap 2030, launched in May 2021, laid their foundation.
    • After 14 negotiation rounds, CETA was concluded on 6 May 2025 and signed in London on 24 July 2025. DCC was signed on 10 February 2026.
    • CETA is a next-generation free trade agreement with 30 chapters covering goods, services, investment, digital trade, intellectual property, government procurement, competition, innovation, sustainability and MSMEs.
    • The UK provides zero-duty access to nearly 99 per cent of Indian tariff lines, covering almost the entire value of Indian exports to the UK.
    • Major beneficiary sectors include textiles, leather, footwear, gems, jewellery, marine products, engineering goods, pharmaceuticals, chemicals, processed food and automobile components.
    • India excludes dairy products, cereals, millets, apples, edible oils and oilseeds from major tariff concessions.
    • This protects small producers, domestic prices and rural livelihoods while balancing liberalisation with policy space for vulnerable sectors.
    • UK commitments cover 12 service sectors and 137 sub-sectors, including IT, finance, engineering, healthcare, education and telecommunications.
    • CETA facilitates temporary movement of business visitors, intra-corporate transferees, contractual service suppliers, independent professionals and investors.
    • It also creates opportunities for Indian chefs, yoga instructors and classical musicians.
    • DCC prevents dual social-security contributions for eligible temporarily posted or detached workers.
    • Ordinary overseas employees generally contribute in their country of employment.
    • It concerns contribution liability and does not automatically grant host-country pensions or other contributory benefits.

    India–Liberia Must knowPDF p. 59

    India and Liberia launched GoF on S4, a UN group on shipping safety and seafarers, on 25 September 2026 in New York.

    • GoF on S4 = Group of Friends on Safety and Security of Shipping and Seafarers.
    • Launched 25 September 2026 at UN HQ during the 81st UNGA; about 25 countries attended.
    • Co-chairs: Dr. S. Jaishankar and Liberian Foreign Minister Sara Beysolow Nyanti.
    • Liberia has the world's largest ship registry by Gross Tonnage; India is a major seafarer supplier.

    Memory aid S4 = four S-words: Safety, Security, Shipping, Seafarers.

    हिंदी: Seafarers (नाविक) · Maritime security (समुद्री सुरक्षा)

    From the magazine

    On September 25, 2026, India and Liberia launched the Group of Friends on Safety and Security of Shipping and Seafarers (GoF on S4) at UN Headquarters, New York, during the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA). The meeting was co-chaired by Dr. S. Jaishankar and Liberia’s Foreign Minister Sara Beysolow Nyanti, with representatives from approximately 25 countries. India and Liberia serve as co-chairs.

    • India–Liberia Partnership: India is a major supplier of merchant seafarers, while Liberia maintains the world’s largest ship registry by Gross Tonnage (GT).
    • Global Significance: Over 80% of global merchandise trade by volume moves by sea, supporting nearly two million seafarers.
    • Security Concerns: Maritime attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, Red Sea, Gulf region and Black Sea threaten global trade and seafarers.
    • Three Priorities: Shipping safety (vessel standards and compliance), maritime security (piracy and armed attacks), and seafarers’ welfare (labour rights, medical care and repatriation).
    • Nature: A voluntary cooperation platform supporting the International Maritime Organization (IMO) and International Labour Organization (ILO).

    Important Legal Frameworks

    • UNCLOS, Article 94: Flag-state jurisdiction and control.
    • SOLAS Convention, 1974: Ship safety standards.
    • Maritime Labour Convention (MLC), 2006: Seafarers’ rights, welfare and repatriation.

    WJP Rule of Law Index 2026 Must knowPDF p. 61

    WJP Rule of Law Index 2026 (October 21, 2026) ranked India 88th of 143, down two places; Denmark topped.

    • Released by World Justice Project on October 21, 2026; India 88th of 143, score 0.48.
    • India was 86th in 2025 (score 0.49); slipped two places.
    • Rule of law declined in 62% of countries — ninth straight year decline beat improvement.
    • Index uses eight factors, 44 sub-factors; score 0 (weakest) to 1 (strongest).
    • India: 3rd of six in South Asia; best in Open Government (45th), worst in Civil Justice (116th).
    • Top: Denmark (0.90), Norway, Finland; last: Venezuela (143rd).

    Don't confuse India's 2026 score 0.48 and rank 88th vs 2025 score 0.49 and rank 86th.

    हिंदी: Rule of Law (विधि का शासन)

    From the magazine

    The World Justice Project (WJP) released the Rule of Law Index 2026 on October 21, 2026, ranking India 88th among 143 countries and jurisdictions, with an overall score of 0.48. India slipped two positions from 86th in 2025, when its score was 0.49. Globally, the rule of law declined in 62% of countries, marking the ninth consecutive year in which deterioration exceeded improvement.

    Key Highlights

    • About WJP: The World Justice Project is an independent, nonpartisan, multidisciplinary organisation promoting the rule of law worldwide.
    • Methodology: The Index uses eight factors and 44 sub-factors, drawing on household and expert surveys. Scores range from 0 (weakest) to 1 (strongest adherence to the rule of law).
    • Four Fundamental Principles: Accountability, Just Law, Open Government, and Accessible and Impartial Justice.
    • Regional Performance: India ranked 3rd among six South Asian countries and 6th among 33 lower-middle-income economies. Its strongest global factor ranking was in Open Government (45th), while its lowest was in Civil Justice (116th).

    Global Rankings

    • Top Seven Countries: Denmark (1st; 0.90), Norway (2nd; 0.89), Finland (3rd; 0.87), Sweden (4th; 0.86), Luxembourg (5th; 0.83), Germany (6th; 0.83) and New Zealand (7th; 0.83).
    • Bottom Five Countries: Venezuela (143rd; 0.26), Afghanistan (142nd; 0.31), Haiti (141st; 0.31), Cambodia (140th; 0.31) and Nicaragua (139th; 0.32).
    • South Asian Rankings: Nepal (71st), Sri Lanka (74th), India (88th), Bangladesh (123rd), Pakistan (131st) and Afghanistan (142nd).
    • Other Major Economies: Singapore (14th), Japan (15th), United Kingdom (18th), United States (30th), South Africa (60th), Indonesia (75th), Brazil (76th), China (92nd) and Russia (121st).
    • Largest Improvements: Latvia (+1.6%), Trinidad and Tobago (+1.2%) and Guatemala (+1.1%).
    • Largest Declines: Haiti (−5.6%), Tanzania (−3.5%) and Sudan (−2.8%). These percentages represent annual changes in index scores.

    Shown line by line as printed: in the PDF this table's text and borders do not line up, so read each line across.

    Medicine: Optogenetics Revolution

    • Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel received the Medicine Prize on 5 October.
    • Hegemann and Nagel’s work on channelrhodopsins, light-sensitive ion channels found in microorganisms, helped provide the biological basis for optogenetics.
    • Deisseroth helped develop these discoveries into a technique that allows researchers to activate or inhibit selected neurons using light.
    • Optogenetics has transformed neuroscience by allowing scientists to examine how specific neural circuits influence memory, emotion and behaviour.

    Physics: Opening a New Window on the Universe

    • Francis Halzen received the Physics Prize for his decisive role in the IceCube Neutrino Observatory.
    • IceCube uses about one cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice containing thousands of light sensors to detect extremely elusive neutrinos.
    • Its observations established the detection of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin, helping create the field of neutrino astronomy.

    Chemistry: Understanding Molecular Handedness

    • Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai jointly received the Chemistry Prize.
    • Kagan pioneered understanding of non-linear effects in asymmetric catalysis, while Soai demonstrated asymmetric autocatalysis, in which a reaction product helps produce more of the same handed molecular form.
    • Their discoveries improved understanding of chirality, an important concept in organic chemistry and pharmaceutical development.

    Literature: Anne Carson

    • Canadian poet, essayist, translator and classicist Anne Carson received the Literature Prize on 8 October.
    • She was honoured for a body of work that combines poetry, prose, criticism, translation and ancient Greek literature in innovative forms.
    • Major works include Autobiography of Red, The Beauty of the Husband, Nox and Eros the Bittersweet.

    Peace: Navi Pillay

    • South African jurist Navanethem “Navi” Pillay received the Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote peace and international law.
    • Pillay served as UN High Commissioner for Human Rights (2008–2014) and held judicial positions at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR) and the International Criminal Court (ICC).
    • Her career has focused on accountability for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity.
    • Pillay was born in Durban into a family of Indian Tamil origin, making her award especially noteworthy from an Indian current-affairs perspective.

    Economic Sciences: Stabilising Economic Fluctuations

    • Robert E. Hall of Stanford University and Michael Woodford of Columbia University received the Economic Sciences Prize on 12 October.
    • Their research connected the decisions of households and firms with economy-wide fluctuations in inflation, output and employment.
    • Their work provided theoretical foundations for modern macroeconomic stabilisation policies, including the use of fiscal policy, interest rates and central-bank communication.
    • Their models are widely used by central banks and finance ministries to analyse economic shocks.

    Global Hunger Index 2026 Must knowPDF pp. 62–63

    Global Hunger Index 2026 ranked India 100th of 122 countries (score 24.1, 'serious'); theme: 'No Security Without Food Security.'

    • Released October 2026; 21st edition; first published in 2006.
    • Publishers: Concern Worldwide, Welthungerhilfe and IFHV.
    • India: 100th of 122, score 24.1 ('serious'); South Asia average 23.5, world 18.1.
    • Four indicators: undernourishment (1/3), child stunting (1/6), child wasting (1/6), under-five mortality (1/3).
    • India: child wasting 19.0% (main concern); stunting fell from 50% (2000) to 29.3%.
    • Last: Somalia (122nd, 47.0, 'alarming'); 24 countries share ranks 1–24.

    Memory aid Weights add up to 1: undernourishment and child mortality 1/3 each; stunting and wasting 1/6 each.

    Don't confuse GHI score runs backwards: 0 is best, 100 is worst — a higher score means more hunger.

    हिंदी: Undernourishment (अल्पपोषण) · Stunting (बौनापन) · Child wasting (दुबलापन)

    From the magazine

    The Global Hunger Index (GHI) 2026, released in October 2026 under the theme “No Security Without Food Security,” ranked India 100th among 122 countries, with a score of 24.1, placing it in the “serious” hunger category. India’s score improved from 38.1 in 2000 and 37.0 in 2006, but remained worse than the South Asian average of 23.5 and the global average of 18.1.

    Key Highlights

    • About GHI: First published in 2006, the Global Hunger Index is an annual, peer-reviewed assessment jointly published by Concern Worldwide, Welthungerhilfe and the Institute for International Law of Peace and Armed Conflict (IFHV). The 2026 report is its 21st edition.
    • Four Indicators: The Index measures hunger using undernourishment (1/3 weight), child stunting (1/6), child wasting (1/6) and under-five mortality (1/3). Scores range from 0 (best) to 100 (worst).
    • Data Period: The 2026 Index combines undernourishment data (2023–2025), child wasting (2021–2025), child stunting (2024) and under-five mortality (2024), using international sources including FAO, WHO and UNICEF.
    • India’s Performance:
      • Undernourished population: 9.8%
      • Child stunting: 29.3%
      • Child wasting: 19.0%
      • Under-five mortality: 2.7%
    • Child wasting remains India’s major nutritional concern, while stunting declined significantly from 50% in 2000 to 29.3% in 2026.
      • Top Performers: Twenty-four countries, including Armenia, Belarus, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria and Chile, recorded GHI scores below 5 and were jointly placed in ranks 1–24.
      • Lowest-Ranked Countries: Somalia (122nd; 47.0) recorded the highest hunger score, followed by the Democratic Republic of the Congo (121st; 39.5), Chad (120th; 38.0), Madagascar (119th; 36.5) and Haiti (118th; 34.4). Somalia was classified in the “alarming” category.
      • Global Findings: The global GHI score increased from 17.6 in 2018 to 18.1 in 2026, indicating stalled progress against hunger. South Asia scored 23.5, remaining in the serious category. Burundi, South Sudan, Sudan and Yemen received provisional alarming designations because of incomplete data.
      • Major Challenges: Conflict, climate shocks, economic pressures and disrupted food systems continue to undermine global food security.
    • In India, inadequate dietary diversity, maternal malnutrition, poor sanitation and limited healthcare access contribute to persistent child undernutrition.

    • The report documented 382 attacks arising from 321 verified incidents involving higher-education communities across 59 countries and territories between 1 July 2025 and 30 June 2026.
    • Free to Think is an annual publication of the Scholars at Risk Academic Freedom Monitoring Project, examining threats to academic freedom, institutional autonomy and higher-education communities.

    • It is jointly implemented by Germany’s Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU) and the V-Dem Institute, using assessments from 2,357 country experts.
    • Five AFI Indicators: The Index evaluates: 1. Freedom to research and teach. 2. Freedom of academic exchange and dissemination. 3. Institutional autonomy. 4. Campus integrity. 5. Freedom of academic and cultural expression.
    • India was placed in the “severely restricted” category alongside Hong Kong, Indonesia, Pakistan, the West Bank and Ukraine.
    • SAR attributed India’s declining score partly to restrictions on research and teaching freedom.
    • It also raised concerns about university governance, leadership appointments, faculty dismissals, cancellation of academic events, student expression and changes in UGC regulations.
    • Afghanistan, China, Gaza, Iran, Russia, Türkiye, Syria, Venezuela and Zimbabwe were among the countries and territories identified as having completely restricted academic freedom.

    On September 22, 2026, the US, Denmark and Greenland signed an Arctic Defense Agreement at the UN in New York, expanding US military access.

    On September 22, 2026, the United States, Denmark and Greenland signed a new Arctic Defense Agreement at the United Nations Headquarters in New York, strengthening military cooperation and security in the Arctic and North Atlantic.

    • The agreement, signed by US President Donald Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenland’s Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen, expands US military access while recognising Denmark’s sovereignty and Greenland’s right to self-determination.
    • The agreement amends the 1951 Defense Agreement concerning Greenland and will enter into force after the necessary parliamentary procedures in Denmark and Greenland are completed.
    • The original US–Denmark Defense Agreement was signed on 27 April 1951 under the framework of the North Atlantic Treaty.
    • It was subsequently supplemented by the 1991 Memorandum of Understanding and the 2004 Igaliku Agreement.
    • The agreement permits the expansion and modernisation of US military activities at Pituffik Space Base, formerly known as Thule Air Base, in north-western Greenland.
    • The facility supports ballistic missile early warning, missile defence, satellite tracking and space surveillance.
    • The agreement also refers to the proposed US Golden Dome missile-defence system.
    • The agreement promotes greater North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) involvement in Arctic military planning, exercises, intelligence gathering, surveillance and interoperability.
    • It generally prohibits non-NATO countries from establishing military installations or maintaining a persistent military presence in Greenland without the parties’ agreement.

    FAO Food Price Index PDF p. 66

    The FAO Food Price Index averaged 131.1 points in July 2026, its highest since early 2023, driven by cereals, vegetable oils and sugar.

    • FFPI: 131.1 points in July 2026, up 0.7 points (0.6%) from June.
    • Still 29.1 points (18.2%) below the March 2022 peak.
    • Tracks five groups: cereals, vegetable oils, meat, dairy, sugar; base period 2014–2016.

    Don't confuse FFPI tracks international commodity prices, not domestic retail food prices.

    हिंदी: Food price index (खाद्य मूल्य सूचकांक) · Inflation (मुद्रास्फीति)

    From the magazine

    The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) reported that the FAO Food Price Index (FFPI) averaged 131.1 points in July 2026, increasing by 0.7 points (0.6%) from June and 1.0% from July 2025. It reached its highest level since early 2023 but remained 29.1 points (18.2%) below its March 2022 peak. The increase was driven by higher cereal, vegetable oil and sugar prices, partly offset by declines in meat and dairy prices.

    • The FFPI measures monthly changes in international prices of five globally traded commodity groups— cereals, vegetable oils, meat, dairy products and sugar—weighted by their average export shares during the 2014–2016 base period.
    • It reflects international commodity prices rather than domestic retail food prices.
    • The Cereal Price Index averaged 113.8 points, rising 3.4% monthly and 6.9% annually.
    • Wheat prices increased 5.8% due to Black Sea export disruptions, infrastructure damage and heatwaves affecting production.
    • Maize prices also rose amid hot, dry weather in parts of the United States and higher energy costs.
    • The Vegetable Oil Price Index increased 2.0%, reaching its highest level since June 2022.
    • Higher palm and soybean oil prices reflected strong biodiesel demand, rising crude-oil prices and increased consumption.
    • The Sugar Price Index rose 5.6%, driven by adverse weather in Europe and Asia and expectations of increased sugarcane diversion towards ethanol production in Brazil.
    • Meat prices declined 2.8% from their June record high, while dairy prices fell 0.7%, reflecting greater export availability and weaker demand for certain products.
    • Higher international food prices can contribute to domestic inflation and complicate the Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) monetary policy management.

    World Investment Report 2026 Must knowPDF pp. 66–67

    UNCTAD's World Investment Report 2026 (July 7, 2026) said global FDI rose 6% to about US$1.6 trillion; India's inflows rose nearly 44%.

    • Released July 7, 2026 by UNCTAD (UN Trade and Development); title 'International Investment in a Turbulent Era'.
    • Global FDI up 6% to about US$1.6 trillion in 2025, ending two years of decline.

    • India outward FDI: US$24.3 billion → US$35.7 billion; rank 20th → 18th.

    हिंदी: Foreign Direct Investment (प्रत्यक्ष विदेशी निवेश)

    From the magazine

    The World Investment Report 2026, titled International Investment in a Turbulent Era, was released on July 7, 2026. Global foreign direct investment (FDI) rose by 6% to approximately US$1.6 trillion in 2025, ending two consecutive years of decline.

    • The report is the principal annual publication of the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), published since 1991.
    • UNCTAD is now publicly known as UN Trade and Development.
    • It examines investment flows, multinational enterprises, investment policies and sustainable development.
    • FDI is cross-border investment intended to establish a lasting interest and significant managerial influence. At least 10% of voting power generally indicates this relationship.
    • Unlike portfolio investment, it normally involves long-term influence, technology and capital transfers, and productive assets.
    • India’s inward FDI rose nearly 44%, from approximately US$27.1 billion in 2024 to US$38.9 billion in 2025, improving its rank from 13th to 11th.
    • Outward FDI increased from approximately US$24.3 billion to US$35.7 billion, improving its rank from 20th to 18th.
    • At the end of 2025, inward and outward FDI stocks were approximately US$559 billion and US$296.4 billion.
    • Outward growth indicates Indian companies’ international expansion.
    • Inward inflows remained below 2021 and 2022 levels.
    • UNCTAD publishes the World Investment Report, Trade and Development Report, Digital Economy Report, Technology and Innovation Report, Least Developed Countries Report, Economic Development in Africa Report, Review of Maritime Transport, and Commodities and Development Report.

    US–Saudi Arabia Civil Nuclear Cooperation Agreement 2026 PDF p. 67

    The US and Saudi Arabia signed a Section 123 civil nuclear agreement in July 2026, valid 30 years, without Saudi renouncing enrichment.

    • Signed by US Energy Secretary Chris Wright (20 July, Washington) and Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman (22 July, Riyadh).
    • Legal basis: Section 123 of the US Atomic Energy Act, 1954.
    • Duration: 30 years after entry into force (Article 16).
    • Article 7: two-year joint study on enrichment; later enrichment needs written consent.
    • Unlike the 2009 US–UAE deal, Saudi Arabia has not renounced enrichment and reprocessing.
    • IAEA Additional Protocol not mandatory; Trump sent it to Congress on 24 August 2026.

    Don't confuse 'Gold Standard' = giving up enrichment and reprocessing. The 2009 US–UAE deal has it; the Saudi deal does not.

    हिंदी: Civil nuclear cooperation (असैन्य परमाणु सहयोग) · Uranium enrichment (यूरेनियम संवर्धन)

    From the magazine

    The United States and Saudi Arabia signed a Section 123 Civil Nuclear Cooperation Agreement in July 2026. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright signed on 20 July (Washington) and Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman on 22 July (Riyadh).

    Key Highlights

    • Legal Basis: Section 123 of the US Atomic Energy Act, 1954. Preliminary cooperation began in 2008, with negotiations concluding on 18 November 2025.
    • Duration: 30 years after entry into force, following completion of domestic procedures and exchange of diplomatic notes (Article 16).
    • Nuclear Safeguards: Restricts military use, unauthorised transfers, enrichment and reprocessing.
    • Uranium Enrichment: Article 7 provides for a two-year joint study; subsequent enrichment requires written consent and safeguards.
    • Gold Standard: Unlike the 2009 US–United Arab Emirates agreement, Saudi Arabia has not renounced enrichment and reprocessing.
    • IAEA Protocol: The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) Additional Protocol is not mandatory. A separate bilateral safeguards agreement was signed. Saudi Arabia withdrew its Small Quantities Protocol on December 31, 2024.
    • Congressional Review: Trump submitted the agreement on 24 August 2026, triggering statutory 30- and 60-day review periods. Senators Jeff Merkley and Edward Markey introduced S.J. Res. 221 on 15 October seeking disapproval.
    • Abraham Accords: Trump publicly linked the agreement to Saudi participation, but the published text contains no such condition. Two confidential side letters remain undisclosed.

    US and Iranian Initial Peace Agreement Must knowPDF p. 67

    On June 17, 2026, the US and Iran signed a 14-point MoU, an initial peace deal and ceasefire to end the four-month West Asia war.

    • June 17, 2026: Trump and Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian signed the 14-point MoU electronically; mainly a ceasefire.
    • Ends fighting on all fronts, including Lebanon; Strait of Hormuz reopens toll-free within 30 days.
    • Sanctions relief: US Treasury waivers let Iran export crude oil and petroleum products.
    • Nuclear: Iran halts enrichment and down-blends (dilutes) highly enriched uranium to 3.67% under IAEA monitoring.
    • Reconstruction fund of at least $300 billion, to be financed by Gulf Arab nations; US not directly.
    • US to unfreeze Iranian assets (Tehran seeks about $24 billion); 60-day talks for a final nuclear pact.

    Memory aid Hormuz in 30 days, final nuclear deal in 60 days: the harder job gets double the time.

    Don't confuse $300 billion is the reconstruction fund (Gulf Arab money, not US); $24 billion is Iran's frozen assets.

    हिंदी: Ceasefire (युद्धविराम) · Sanctions (प्रतिबंध) · Memorandum of Understanding (समझौता ज्ञापन)

    From the magazine

    On June 17, 2026, the United States and Iran signed a historic initial peace agreement—formalised via a 14-point Memorandum of Understanding (MoU)— aimed at ending the four-month West Asia war.

    • The agreement was signed electronically by US President Donald Trump and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian; the interim pact serves primarily as a comprehensive ceasefire to halt active military operations and stave off global economic depression.
    • However, the agreement is facing immense strain, highlighted by Iran’s declaration that it is closing the Strait of Hormuz due to ongoing Israeli strikes in Lebanon.

    Key Terms of the 14-Point MoU

    • Termination of Hostilities: An immediate and permanent end to military operations on all fronts, explicitly including the conflict in Lebanon
    • Strait of Hormuz Reopening: Free, toll-free passage through the crucial energy shipping corridor is restored to full capacity within 30 days.
    • Sanctions Relief: The US Department of the Treasury must immediately issue waivers allowing Iran to export crude oil, petroleum products, and access associated banking and transportation services.
    • Reconstruction Fund: A framework with regional partners to develop an economic development plan for Iran worth at least $300 billion. White House officials noted that Gulf Arab nations are expected to finance the fund, and the US will not contribute directly.
    • Unfreezing Assets: The US commits to unblocking restricted Iranian funds and assets abroad, with Tehran seeking the return of approximately $24 billion.
    • Nuclear Constraints: Iran is required to halt further enrichment and “down-blend” (dilute) its existing highly enriched uranium stocks to 3.67% under IAEA monitoring.
    • The 60-Day Window: The initial arrangement sets up a 60-day technical negotiation period to secure a final, legally binding nuclear pact endorsed by the UN Security Council.

    Iran–Israel Conflict Must knowPDF pp. 67–68

    Joint US–Israeli strikes on February 28, 2026 widened the Iran–Israel war and killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei; his son Mojtaba succeeded him.

    • February 28, 2026 strikes: US called it Operation Epic Fury; Israel, Operation Roaring Lion; Iran replied 'True Promise'.
    • Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei (since 1989) killed; son Mojtaba, selected by Assembly of Experts, announced March 9, 2026.
    • June 2025: Israel's 12-day Operation Rising Lion; Iran hit back with Operation True Promise 3.
    • US 'Operation Midnight Hammer': B-2 bombers struck Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan; India launched Operation Sindhu.
    • Strait of Hormuz (Iran–Oman) links Persian Gulf to Arabian Sea; Kharg Island handles ~90% of Iran's crude exports.
    • Modi: first leader honoured by both Israel (Knesset Medal, February 25, 2026) and Palestine (Grand Collar, 2018).

    Memory aid Lions are Israel's: Rising Lion (June 2025), Roaring Lion (February 2026). US names: Midnight Hammer, Epic Fury. Iran: True Promise.

    Don't confuse Rising Lion (Israel, June 2025) vs Roaring Lion (Israel, February 2026): one word apart.

    हिंदी: Strait (जलडमरूमध्य) · Supreme Leader (सर्वोच्च नेता)

    From the magazine

    • On February 28, 2026, joint U.S.-Israeli attacks pushed the conflict into a new phase.
    • The United States called it Operation Epic Fury, while Israel called it Operation Roaring Lion.
    • After these strikes, Iran presented its missile and drone attacks as successive waves of “Operation True Promise.”
    • Earlier, in June 2025, Israel had carried out a 12-day campaign called Operation Rising Lion targeting Iranian nuclear and military infrastructures including Tehran, Natanz, Tabriz, and Kermanshah.
    • The most inhuman face of the war was seen in the attack on Shajarah Tayyibeh Girls’ School in Minab, southern Iran, where a large number of girls were killed.
    • Iran targeted over 17 key U.S. sites in the Gulf region, including the 5th Fleet Headquarters in Bahrain.

    Ali Khamenei

    • Ali Khamenei, Iran’s Supreme Leader since 1989, was assassinated in Tehran on February 28, 2026, during a joint US-Israeli strike.
    • Following this, his son, Mojtaba Khamenei, was announced as the new Supreme Leader on March 9, 2026, selected by the Assembly of Experts.
    • High-level U.S.–Iran talks took place in Islamabad on April 11–12, 2026, and ended without a deal.

    Strait of Hormuz and Strait of Malacca:

    • The Strait of Hormuz, located between Iran and Oman, connects the Persian Gulf to the Arabian Sea.
    • It is the world’s most important oil transit chokepoint.
    • The Strait of Malacca, located between Malaysia, Indonesia, and Singapore, connects the Indian Ocean to the South China Sea.
      • It is the shortest sea route between the Middle East and East Asia.

    Kharg Island

    • Another important dimension is Kharg Island, Iran’s principal oil export terminal in the Persian Gulf.
      • Handles nearly 90% of Iran’s crude oil exports.
    • On 17 April 2026, the UK and France co-chaired an international meeting on the Strait of Hormuz Maritime Navigation / Freedom of Navigation Initiative, with 51 countries participating to support free navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.

    U.S. Joins the Fray

    • In June 2025, in a dramatic escalation of hostilities, Israel launched Operation Rising Lion, a series of coordinated airstrikes and drone attacks targeting Iran’s nuclear and military infrastructure.
    • Key targets included in this operation were the Natanz uranium enrichment facility, a nuclear research center in Tehran; military bases in Tabriz; and an underground missile storage site in Kermanshah.
    • This pre-emptive operation aimed to halt Iran’s progress toward acquiring nuclear weapons.
    • In response, Iran launched Operation True Promise 3, firing ballistic missiles at Israeli targets, with explosions reported in Jerusalem and Tel Aviv, marking a major regional escalation.
    • The United States formally entered the conflict with precision airstrikes on Iran’s major nuclear installations—Fordow, Natanz, and Isfahan— using B-2 stealth bombers armed with bunker-buster bombs.
    • The official U.S. name for the strike on Iranian nuclear sites was Operation Midnight Hammer.
    • In response to growing tensions, the Government of India launched Operation Sindhu.
    • India has a strong track record in such operations, as seen during the 1990–91 Gulf War, the Libya crisis, and Operation Ganga in Ukraine (2022).

    Modi Becomes First Leader Honoured by Israel and Palestine

    • PM Narendra Modi became the first leader to receive top honours from both Israel and Palestine.
    • He was awarded the Speaker of the Knesset Medal (Israel’s highest parliamentary honour) on February 25, 2026.
    • The award was presented by Amir Ohana at the Knesset in Jerusalem.
    • Earlier, in 2018, he received the Grand Collar of the State of Palestine from Mahmoud Abbas.

    हिंदी: Misinformation (भ्रामक सूचना) · Inequality (असमानता)

    From the magazine

    The Global Risks Report 2026 is the 21st edition of the World Economic Forum’s annual report and was published on January 14, 2026, warns that the world is entering an “Age of Competition”—a phase where geopolitical rivalry, economic weaponization, technology disruption and climate stress are interacting and creating cascading crises.

    • The World Economic Forum defines a global risk as an event or condition that can cause a significant negative impact on:
      • Global GDP
      • World population
      • Natural resources and ecosystems
    • Such risks are cross-border, interconnected, and capable of triggering cascading crises.
    • The report is built mainly on:
      • Global Risks Perception Survey (GRPS) for global-level risk severity and interconnections.
      • Executive Opinion Survey (EOS) for country-level “national risk perceptions”.
    • The report uses three time horizons: immediate (2026), short-to-medium term (to 2028), and long term (to 2036).

    Top 5 Global Risks ranked by severity

    • Short term (2 years):
      • Geo-economic confrontation
      • Misinformation & disinformation
      • Societal polarization
      • Extreme weather events
      • State-based armed conflict
    • Long term (10 years):
      • Extreme weather events
      • Biodiversity loss & ecosystem collapse
      • Critical change to Earth systems
      • Misinformation & disinformation
      • Adverse outcomes of AI technologies
    • Inequality is shown as the most interconnected global risk (linked strongly with economic and social risks).

    India’s Risk Outlook

    • For India, EOS 2025 identifies the following five risks, in descending order of selection frequency, over the next two years.
      • Cyber insecurity ranks first.
      • Inequality of wealth and income ranks second.
      • Insufficient public services and social protections, including education, infrastructure and pensions, rank third.
      • Economic downturn, including recession or stagnation, ranks fourth.
      • State-based armed conflict ranks fifth.

    The World Inequality Report 2026 Must knowPDF pp. 71–72

    World Inequality Report 2026 (3rd edition, December 2025) finds extreme global inequality; in India the top 10% earn 58% of income.

    • India: top 10% earn 58% of national income; bottom 50% get only 15%.
    • India: richest 10% own about 65% of wealth; top 1% about 40%.

    Memory aid India's income split '58–15': the top tenth takes 58%, the bottom half gets 15%.

    हिंदी: Inequality (असमानता) · Climate justice (जलवायु न्याय)

    From the magazine

    In December 2025, the World Inequality Report 2026 (3rd edition), published by the World Inequality Lab and edited by economists like Thomas Piketty and Lucas Chancel, revealed that global economic and environmental disparities remain at an extreme and persistent level.

    • The report highlights unprecedented concentration of wealth at the global level:
      • The top 10% of the global population controls nearly 75% of total wealth, while the bottom 50% owns only 2%.
      • The top 1% holds around 37% of global wealth, exceeding the combined wealth of the bottom half of the world.
      • The wealthiest 0.001% (about 60,000 individuals) possess three times more wealth than the poorest 50% globally.
    • The report identifies India as one of the most unequal countries globally.
      • The top 10% earns 58% of national income.
      • The bottom 50% receives only 15% of income.
      • The disparity has widened compared to earlier assessments.
      • The richest 10% owns about 65% of national wealth.
      • The top 1% alone holds around 40% of total wealth.
      • Average annual income per capita: €6,200 (PPP).
      • Average wealth per capita: €28,000 (PPP).
    • These figures highlight that while India has witnessed economic growth, wealth creation remains highly concentrated.
    • Globally, women earn 61% of men’s wages when unpaid work hours are excluded.
    • When unpaid care work is included, women earn only 32% of male income.
    • Women receive just 28.2% of global labour income, showing minimal progress over decades.
    • India’s female labour income share was 15.7% in both 2014 and 2024, reflecting structural barriers such as social norms, skill gaps, and unpaid care responsibilities.
    • The report introduces climate inequality as a major global concern:
      • The top 10% contributes 77% of emissions linked to private capital ownership.
      • The poorest 50% contributes only 3% of such emissions.
      • The wealthiest 1% is responsible for 41% of emissions, almost double that of the bottom 90%.
    • This indicates that those contributing least to climate change face the highest vulnerability, raising issues of climate justice and equity.
    • The report highlights systemic financial imbalances:
      • Approximately 1% of global GDP annually flows from poorer to richer nations through financial and investment mechanisms.
      • Developed countries benefit from lower borrowing costs and higher investment returns, reinforcing global economic hierarchy.

    EU Signs Association Agreement with Andorra and San Marino PDF p. 72

    On October 19, 2026, the EU signed an Association Agreement with Andorra and San Marino, bringing them into the EU Single Market without membership.

    • Signed October 19, 2026 in Brussels by the European Commission on behalf of the EU.
    • Mixed Agreement: free movement of goods, services, capital and persons, with conditions.
    • Talks began in 2015; Monaco's talks suspended September 2023; concluded December 2023.
    • Council of the EU authorised signing and provisional application on 16 July 2026.
    • Full implementation needs approvals, including European Parliament consent; Article 112(3) allows provisional application.
    • Andorra (2011), San Marino (2012) use the euro by monetary agreement; may issue coins, not banknotes.

    Memory aid Nickname 'EEA Plus' (Maroš Šefčovič, December 2023); the official legal name stays Association Agreement.

    Don't confuse Monaco was in the talks, but they were suspended in September 2023; only Andorra and San Marino signed.

    हिंदी: Single Market (एकल बाज़ार)

    From the magazine

    On October 19, 2026, the European Commission, on behalf of the European Union (EU), signed an Association Agreement with Andorra and San Marino in Brussels, Belgium. It aims to integrate these European microstates into the EU Single Market without granting EU membership.

    Key Highlights

    • Nature and Scope: The Mixed Agreement involves the EU, its member states, Andorra and San Marino. It provides for the free movement of goods, services, capital and persons, subject to agreed conditions.
    • Financial Services: Market access will be phased in after regulatory assessments by the European Supervisory Authorities (ESAs). Cooperation also covers research, education, environment and consumer protection.
    • Negotiation Timeline: Talks began in 2015 under December 2014 Council directives. Negotiations with Monaco were suspended in September 2023, while those with Andorra and San Marino concluded in December 2023.
    • Approval Process: The European Commission submitted proposals on 26 April 2024. The Council of the EU authorised signing and provisional application on 16 July 2026.
    • Legal Status: Under Article 112(3), provisional application may begin separately with either country after prescribed procedures. Full implementation requires necessary approvals, including European Parliament consent. Provisional application remained unconfirmed as of 21 October 2026.
    • Monetary Agreements: Andorra (2011) and San Marino (2012) use the euro through monetary agreements without euro-area membership. They may issue limited national-design euro coins but not banknotes. Updated agreements were also signed.
    • EEA Plus: European Commission Executive Vice-President Maroš Šefčovič informally described the arrangement as “EEA Plus” in December 2023. EEA means European Economic Area; its official legal designation remains Association Agreement.
