    On October 14, 2026, India approved accession to the Southern Indian Ocean Fisheries Agreement (SIOFA) to promote sustainable high-seas fishing.

    • India has been a Cooperating Non-Contracting Party (CNCP) since 2022; full membership remained pending as of October 21, 2026.
    • Under Articles 23–25, accession takes effect 30 days after depositing the instrument with the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) Director-General.
    • Signed in Rome on July 7, 2006 and effective from June 21, 2012, SIOFA is a Regional Fisheries Management Organisation (RFMO) headquartered in Le Port, Réunion (France).

    • SIOFA promotes scientific cooperation and action against Illegal, Unreported and Unregulated (IUU) fishing.
    • Its boarding-and-inspection measures became effective in October 2019. Article 8 generally requires consensus for substantive decisions.
    • India's 2025 guidelines mandate vessel-specific fishing authorisations. Unlike SIOFA, the Indian Ocean Tuna Commission (IOTC) regulates tuna.
    • India accepted its agreement on March 13, 1995, effective March 27, 1996.

    From the magazine

    The 28th Session of the Committee on Forestry (COFO) of the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) was held from 28 September to 2 October 2026 in Rome, Italy, under the theme “Forests for Food, Resilience and Prosperity.” The 10th World Forest Week was organised alongside it.

    Key Highlights

    • About COFO: Established in 1971 at the 16th FAO Conference, it is FAO’s highest intergovernmental forestry body, comprising 128 members, including the European Union. It meets biennially and reports to the FAO Council on budgetary matters and FAO Conference on policy matters.
    • State of the World’s Forests (SOFO) 2026: Released on 28 September, titled “Restoring Forests and Landscapes: The Way Forward for a Sustainable Future.” It estimated 1.56 billion hectares of degraded land globally, with potential restoration returns of up to US$30 per US$1 invested.
    • Four Restoration Pathways: Community empowerment and rights, landscape-level restoration, sustainable financing and coherent policies, institutions and laws.

    India’s Performance and Initiatives

    • Forest and Tree Cover: As per the India State of Forest Report (ISFR) 2023, India’s combined cover is 8,27,357 sq. km (25.17%), comprising forest cover of 7,15,343 sq. km (21.76%) and tree cover of 1,12,014 sq. km (3.41%).
    • Global Ranking: India ranks 9th in total forest area and 3rd in net annual forest area gain, according to FAO’s Global Forest Resources Assessment 2025.
    • Carbon Sink: India created an additional 2.29 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent during 2005– 2021, increasing to 2.44 billion tonnes during 2005–2022. Its enhanced Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) targets 3.5–4.0 billion tonnes by 2035.
    • Bonn Challenge: India targets restoration of 26 million hectares by 2030, with 21.76 million hectares brought under restoration during 2011–2020.
    • Aravalli Green Wall: Covers Gujarat, Rajasthan, Haryana and Delhi, with approximately 6.45 million hectares identified for restoration in India’s COFO statement.
    • MISHTI Initiative: The Mangrove Initiative for Shoreline Habitats and Tangible Incomes (MISHTI), launched on 5 June 2023, targets restoration of 54,000 hectares of mangroves by 2028.
    • Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam: Over 3.5 billion saplings had been planted by September 2026.
    • Ramsar Sites: India reported 101 sites during COFO 28. The addition of Sukhna Wetland (Chandigarh) and Sauj Jheel (Uttar Pradesh) on 15 October 2026 increased the total to 103.
    • UN Afforestation Decade: India reaffirmed support for the United Nations Decade for Afforestation and Reforestation (2027–2036), proclaimed under UN General Assembly Resolution 79/283 on 16 April 2025.

    हिंदी: Presidency (अध्यक्षता)

    From the magazine

    The 18th BRICS Summit was held on 12–13 September 2026 at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi, under India’s Presidency. Its theme was “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability.” Leaders unanimously adopted the New Delhi BRICS Leaders’ Declaration on 12 September, covering cooperation and the interests of the Global South.

    Key Highlights of the Summit

    • India assumed its fourth BRICS Presidency on 1 January 2026, after chairing the grouping in 2012, 2016 and 2021.
    • Its 11 full members account for approximately 49.5% of the global population, approximately 40% of global GDP and 26% of global trade.
    • The 10 Partner Countries engage through a structured framework without full membership.
    • Summit-related engagements involved 32 delegations: 11 member states, 10 partner states, four regional organisations and seven international organisations.

    New Delhi BRICS Leaders, Declaration 2026

    • It condemned the 22 April 2025 Jammu and Kashmir terrorist attack that killed 26 people.
    • China and Russia supported India’s and Brazil’s aspirations for a greater UN role, including the Security Council.
    • Prime Minister Modi proposed a BRICS Continuity and Implementation Mechanism to follow up decisions across Presidencies.
    • BRICS supported an open, transparent, fair and rules-based trading system centred on the World Trade Organization (WTO).
    • It expressed concern over unilateral tariff and non-tariff measures that could disrupt trade and supply chains, and supported restoration of a fully functioning two-tier binding WTO dispute settlement mechanism.
    • BRICS encouraged local currencies in cross-border trade, investment and financial transactions among member countries.
    • The BRICS Payment Task Force continued work on interoperability among payment and financial messaging systems. No common BRICS currency was announced.
    • It recognised fossil fuels’ continued role in emerging and developing economies while supporting renewable and nuclear energy, hydropower, hydrogen and other low-carbon technologies.
    • BRICS emphasised women-led development and women’s participation in governance, decision-making, entrepreneurship, economic development, peace-building, climate action, and food and nutrition security.
    • Key initiatives included the BRICS Centres of Excellence on Agro-Ecology and Regenerative Agriculture, BRICS Network on Digital Agriculture, BRICS Mission for Healthy Lifestyle, BRICS CONNECT for Skilling, BRICS MSME Cooperation Portal, BRICS Incubator Network and BRICS Logistics Supply-Chain Cooperation Framework.

    From the magazine

    Second BRICS Anti-Corruption Working Group Meeting

    • The Second Meeting of the BRICS Anti-Corruption Working Group (ACWG) and the Expert Network on Asset Recovery took place in Hyderabad, Telangana, from August 4–5, 2026.
    • Host: Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT), Government of India.

    Core Agenda

    • Asset Recovery: Strengthening international cooperation to trace and recover stolen assets.
    • Fugitive Offenders: Discussing the BRICS Repository on Informal Cooperation to stop the cross-border movement of corruption offenders and support extradition.
    • Side Event: A dedicated session was held on August 5, 2026, titled “Ethical Governance through Innovation and Tech-Driven Systems,” focusing on digital public procurement and transparency.

    13th BRICS Education Ministers’ Meeting in Odisha

    • The 13th BRICS Education Ministers’ Meeting and 3rd Senior Officials’ Meeting took place in Bhubaneswar, Odisha, from August 5–7, 2026, under India’s BRICS chairship.
    • Priority Discussions: Leaders focused on strengthening Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE), enhancing skill development via the BRICS TVET Cooperation Alliance, and promoting joint research, innovation, and start-ups.
    • Key Frameworks: Delegations worked on the Mutual Recognition of Qualifications (MRQ), academic leadership capacity building, and new guiding principles on Traditional and Indigenous Knowledge Systems.

    Meeting of Heads of National Statistical Offices of BRICS Countries

    • India successfully hosted the Meeting of Heads of National Statistical Offices (NSO) of BRICS Countries in Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh, from August 3–4, 2026, under its BRICS Chairship.
    • Organized by the National Statistical Office and the Ministry of Statistics & Programme Implementation (MoSPI), the high-level gathering brought together over 350 delegates, including statistical leaders, policymakers, and technical experts.
    • India’s Specific Theme: “Quality Statistics as Driver of Change,” which highlights data quality, innovation, and people-centric systems.
    • India’s 2026 BRICS chairship followed the theme “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability”.

    11th BRICS Energy Ministers Meeting

    • India hosted the meeting in Gurugram, Haryana, on June 25–26, 2026, with the energy track theme “Energy for All”.
    • Its three priorities were energy security and sustainability, energy access and equity, and technology and innovation.
    • Members adopted a Joint Communiqué supporting resilient infrastructure and capacity building and launched the BRICS Digital Centre of Excellence for Smart Grids and Energy Storage.
    • Discussions covered universal access, green cooperation and energy transitions, with participation from the International Solar Alliance and Global Biofuels Alliance.

    Guwahati Declaration on Drug Control

    • At the two-day BRICS Heads of Anti-Drug Agencies Meeting in Guwahati, Assam, members adopted the Guwahati Declaration on July 7, 2026.
    • It strengthens cooperation against illicit drug trafficking, synthetic drugs and transnational organized crime.
    • Commitments include real-time intelligence sharing, cross-border networks, AI and technology for enforcement, monitoring darknet and virtual asset transactions, and control of precursor chemicals and synthetic drug laboratories.
    • Demand reduction emphasizes rehabilitation, education and youth protection.

    16th BRICS National Security Advisers, Meeting

    • Held in New Delhi on June 22–23, 2026, under National Security Adviser Ajit Doval’s leadership, the meeting addressed energy, food and supply chain security, climate-induced instability and cybersecurity.
    • It focused on preventing terrorist use of emerging technologies and AI and reviewed BRICS working group reports on counter-terrorism and ICT security.
    • Discussions also covered West Asia, Ukraine and supply chain relief through the opening of the Strait of Hormuz.

    BRICS Agriculture Conference and Indore Declaration

    • Indore hosted the conference on June 9–13, 2026, with participants from 21 countries representing nearly half the global population.
    • The unanimously adopted Indore Declaration targets sustainable farming, digital agriculture and farmers’ welfare.
    • Discussions addressed food and nutrition security, global supply chains, AI and machine learning, eco-friendly and climate-resilient farming, and smallholders’ access to modern technology and fair markets.

    BRICS Foreign Ministers, Meeting 2026

    • India hosted the BRICS Foreign Ministers’ Meeting in New Delhi from May 14–15, 2026, under its national chairship of the bloc.
    • Chaired by External Affairs Minister Dr. S. Jaishankar, the gathering brought together foreign ministers and heads of delegations from BRICS member and partner countries.

    17th BRICS Summit, 2025

    The 17th BRICS Summit was held from July 6-7, 2025, in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil.

    • The previous 16th BRICS Summit was held in October 2024 in Kazan, Russia, while the 18th BRICS Summit will be held in India in 2026.

Intelligence: AI, quantum computing and disruptive technologies. 4. Planet: Climate change, resources and sustainability. 5. Humanity: Employment, ethics and the social impact of technology.

    The 48th UNESCO World Heritage Committee session, chaired by Mr LEE Byong Hyun, was held in Busan, Republic of Korea, from July 19 to 29, 2026, and added 25 sites.

    • The inscription of the Funerary Tradition in the Prehistory of Sardinia - Domus de Janas raised Italy’s total to 62 sites, comprising 56 cultural and 6 natural sites. Italy leads China (61), France (56), Germany (55), Spain (50) and India (45).
    • Italy’s position reflects over three thousand years of continuous civilization.

    • Italy also preserves medieval towns, religious buildings, archaeological remains and cultural landscapes.
    • Its natural heritage includes the Dolomites, Mount Etna, Aeolian Islands and ancient beech forests.
    • The 1972 World Heritage Convention protects cultural and natural heritage possessing Outstanding Universal Value as humanity’s common heritage.
    • India ranks sixth with 45 sites: 37 cultural, 7 natural and 1 mixed. Recent additions include Sarnath (2026), Maratha Military Landscapes (2025) and Moidams (2024).

    • Report out July 1, 2026; informed first UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance (Geneva, 6–7 July 2026).
    • Panel created by UNGA Resolution A/RES/79/325 (26 August 2025), after the Global Digital Compact.

    • Assesses only non-military AI; has no regulatory or enforcement powers.

    On July 1, 2026, the United Nations-established Independent International Scientific Panel on Artificial Intelligence (AI) released its first Preliminary Report: Evidence-based Assessment of Opportunities, Risks and Impacts of AI.

    • The assessment informed the inaugural UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance, held in Geneva, Switzerland, on 6–7 July 2026.
    • The report warns that AI capabilities are advancing faster than scientific understanding, independent evaluation and governance safeguards.
    • Created under UN General Assembly Resolution A/RES/79/325 of 26 August 2025, following the Global Digital Compact, the Panel comprises 40 independent experts from all five UN regional groups, appointed for three-year terms.
    • Co-Chairs: Yoshua Bengio (Canada), recipient of the 2018 Turing Award, and Maria Ressa (Philippines), recipient of the 2021 Nobel Peace Prize.
    • The Panel provides independent, non-prescriptive scientific assessments of non-military AI applications; it has no regulatory or enforcement powers.
    • In 2025, US institutions produced 59 notable AI models, China 35 and the rest of the world 13.
    • The private sector accounted for 91% of notable models.
    • Among the 500 largest known AI computing clusters, the US controlled approximately 75% of computing capacity, China 15% and other countries 10%.
    • India’s IndiaAI Mission, approved in March 2024 with an outlay of ₹10,371.92 crore, has onboarded over 38,000 GPUs to expand affordable computing access.

    हिंदी: Free Trade Agreement (मुक्त व्यापार समझौता)

    From the magazine

    The 16th India–European Union (EU) Summit was held on January 27, 2026 in New Delhi, attended by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, European Council President António Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. Its major outcomes included the conclusion of Free Trade Agreement (FTA) negotiations, the first India–EU Security and Defence Partnership, and the “Towards 2030” Strategic Agenda.

    • The FTA negotiations began in 2007, were suspended in 2013 and resumed in 2022.
    • The EU offered preferential access across 97% of tariff lines, covering 99.5% of Indian exports by value.
    • Labour-intensive sectors worth approximately US$33 billion will benefit from duty-free access.
    • India offered concessions on 92.1% of tariff lines, covering 97.5% of EU exports, while protecting sensitive agricultural products and phasing in automobile and alcohol tariff reductions.
    • The EU opened 144 services subsectors, while India offered 102, alongside provisions for professional mobility, digital trade and regulatory cooperation.
    • The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) and other non-tariff barriers remain concerns.
    • The FTA had not entered into force by October 2026, pending formal approvals.
    • The Security and Defence Partnership covers maritime security, cybersecurity, counterterrorism and defence cooperation, with opportunities under the EU's Security Action for Europe (SAFE) programme, subject to applicable conditions.
    • Other outcomes included a Comprehensive Mobility Framework, proposed EU Legal Gateway Office in India, Green Hydrogen Task Force, renewed scientific cooperation for 2025–2030, exploratory talks on Horizon Europe, and disaster-management cooperation.
    • About the EU: Established through the Maastricht Treaty (1992), it has 27 members. The eurozone expanded to 21 countries following Bulgaria's accession on January 1, 2026.

    • ACITI Partnership (Australia–Canada–India) launched 22 November for green energy, AI and minerals.
    • Next: 21st in Doral, Florida (December 14–15, 2026); 22nd in Manchester, UK (2027).

    Don't confuse 20th summit = Johannesburg (2025); 21st = Doral, US (2026); 22nd = Manchester, UK (2027).

    हिंदी: Debt relief (ऋण राहत)

    From the magazine

    The 20th Group of Twenty (G20) Summit was held on November 22-23, 2025 in Johannesburg, South Africa, the first G20 Summit on African soil, under the theme “Solidarity, Equality, Sustainability.”

    • The Johannesburg Leaders’ Declaration, reflecting the African philosophy of Ubuntu (shared humanity), emphasised debt relief, climate finance, food security, energy transition and multilateral reforms.
    • Leaders supported Mission 300, targeting electricity access for 300 million Africans by 2030.
    • Prime Minister Narendra Modi, attending his 12th G20 Summit, proposed six initiatives: Traditional Knowledge Repository, Africa Skills Multiplier, Global Healthcare Response Team, Open Satellite Data Partnership, Critical Minerals Circularity Initiative and Drug–Terror Nexus Initiative.

    • The first G20 Global Inequality Report, released in November 2025 by a committee chaired by Nobel laureate Joseph Stiglitz, found that 83% of countries, representing 90% of humanity, had high income inequality (Gini coefficient above 0.4).
    • During 2000–2024, the richest 1% captured 41% of new global wealth, against just 1% for the bottom 50%.
    • It proposed an International Panel on Inequality. In India, the richest 1%'s wealth share increased by approximately 62% during 2000–2023.
    • The 21st summit is scheduled for Doral, Florida, United States, on December 14–15, 2026.
    • The 22nd will be held in Manchester, UK, on 27–28 November, 2027. The Republic of Korea will host in 2028.

    On August 28–29, 2026, a military mutiny occurred in Niamey, Niger, targeting the government of President Abdourahamane Tiani. Niger’s Defence Ministry and the Confederation of Sahel States (AES) reported that the attempt had been suppressed.

    Key Highlights

    • Mutiny: Began around 12:20 a.m. on 29 August at Air Base 101, where dissident soldiers detained fellow personnel and attacked sensitive installations near Diori Hamani International Airport, the presidential complex and state broadcaster.
    • Response: On 30 August, Russia reported assistance from its Africa Corps. On 4 September, Niger’s government attributed the incident to elements of a special intelligence battalion.
    • Niger’s Background: A landlocked West African country, independent from France since 3 August 1960; capital Niamey. It experienced five successful coups in 1974, 1996, 1999, 2010 and 2023.
    • 2023 Coup: On 26 July, President Mohamed Bazoum was removed by the National Council for the Safeguard of the Homeland (CNSP). The 26 March 2025 Charter designated Tiani as President for a modifiable 60-month transition.
    • AES: Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso formed the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) through the Liptako-Gourma Charter (16 September 2023) and established a confederation on 6 July 2024. They formally withdrew from the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) on 29 January 2025.

    E. International Disasters

    Nepal’s Rasuwa Flash Flood 2026 Must knowPDF p. 82

    A rock–ice avalanche set off a catastrophic flash flood in Nepal's Rasuwa district on August 26, 2026; India sent rescue and forensic help.

    • August 26, 2026: flash flood in Rasuwa, near the Nepal–China border, on Lhende Khola–Bhote Koshi–Trishuli rivers.
    • ICIMOD: slope failure on Langtang Lirung caused a rock–ice avalanche — not a conventional GLOF.
    • Trishuli River rose about nine metres within 30 minutes at Galchhi.
    • India: NDRF teams in Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, tunnel-rescue staff, 19-member forensic team.
    • GLOF = flood when a glacial lake's ice or moraine dam fails.
    • The debris-laden flood damaged settlements, roads, bridges, hydropower projects and communication networks.

    Don't confuse Rasuwa flood was mainly an avalanche-induced cascading hazard, not a conventional GLOF.

    हिंदी: Flash flood (आकस्मिक बाढ़) · Avalanche (हिमस्खलन) · Glacial lake (हिमनद झील)

    From the magazine

    • On August 26, 2026, a catastrophic flash flood struck Nepal’s Rasuwa district near the Nepal–China border, sweeping through the Lhende Khola–Bhote Koshi–Trishuli river system.
    • The debris-laden flood damaged settlements, roads, bridges, hydropower projects and communication networks.
    • According to the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD), a slope failure on Langtang Lirung triggered a massive rock–ice avalanche that entered the Lhende Khola catchment.
    • The avalanche generated a debris-rich flood, potentially involving temporary river obstruction or displacement followed by sudden water release.
    • At Galchhi, the Trishuli River reportedly rose approximately nine metres within 30 minutes. Several monitoring stations were damaged or destroyed.
    • Initially considered a possible Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) or earthquake-related disaster, the event was subsequently identified primarily as a rock–ice avalanche-induced cascading hazard, rather than a conventional GLOF.
    • India deployed NDRF teams in Bihar and Uttar Pradesh and provided specialised tunnel-rescue personnel and a 19-member forensic team for DNA identification, strengthening bilateral Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief (HADR) cooperation.
    • A GLOF occurs when a glacial lake suddenly releases water following the failure of its natural ice or moraine dam.

    Colombia Declares Emergency After 7.4-Magnitude Earthquake PDF p. 82

    A 7.4-magnitude earthquake hit western Colombia on August 10, 2026 — the country's largest of the 21st century — leading to an emergency.

    • August 10, 2026; epicentre near San José del Palmar, Chocó Department; depth about 103 km.
    • Colombian Geological Service: largest-magnitude earthquake of the 21st century in Colombia.
    • Cause: the oceanic Nazca Plate subducts beneath the South American Plate.
    • Colombia lies on the Circum-Pacific Belt, about 40,000 km around the Pacific.
    • This subduction also built the Andes Mountains and feeds volcanism.

    हिंदी: Earthquake (भूकंप) · Tectonic plate (विवर्तनिक प्लेट)

    From the magazine

    On August 10, 2026, a powerful 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck western Colombia, with its epicentre near San José del Palmar in Chocó Department, at a depth of approximately 103 km.

    • The Colombian Geological Service (SGC) described it as the country’s largest-magnitude earthquake of the 21st century.
    • Colombia lies in north-western South America, bordering both the Pacific Ocean and Caribbean Sea.
    • Its seismic activity is influenced by the interaction of the Nazca, South American and Caribbean tectonic plates.
    • Along Colombia’s Pacific margin, the oceanic Nazca Plate subducts beneath the continental South American Plate.
    • This convergence generates tectonic stress, causing earthquakes, crustal deformation and volcanic activity.
    • Colombia is part of the Circum-Pacific Belt, extending approximately 40,000 km around the Pacific Ocean.
    • This tectonically active region experiences frequent earthquakes and volcanic eruptions due to convergent plate boundaries and subduction zones.
    • The subduction of the Nazca Plate beneath the South American Plate produces compression, crustal folding and uplift, contributing to the formation of the Andes Mountains.
    • Fluids released from the descending plate also promote magma formation and volcanism.

    California Bans Child Marriage

    • On September 30, 2026, California Governor Gavin Newsom signed Assembly Bill 1267 (AB 1267), establishing 18 years as the minimum age for marriage and registered domestic partnerships without exceptions.
    • The legislation, authored by Assembly member Gail Pellerin, will take effect on 1 January 2027, making California the 18th U.S. state to completely prohibit child marriage.

    Scotland Legalises Water Cremation:

    • Scotland has become the first UK nation to legalise water cremation (alkaline hydrolysis).
    • It introduces a third funeral option alongside burial and traditional cremation.
    • The process is considered a major reform since the cremation laws of 1902.
    • Alkaline hydrolysis uses water, heat, and potassium hydroxide to decompose the body.
    • It produces significantly lower carbon emissions (about 7 times less CO2) than traditional cremation.
    • The method is seen as an eco-friendly alternative with reduced pollution and energy use.

    Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, 2026

    • On September 18, 2026, US President Donald Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act (Public Law 119-111), following Senate (86–11) and House (262–159) approval.
    • The Act authorises tariffs of up to 500% on Russian imports (Section 112) and 100% on imports from major Russian-energy buyers (Section 113), alongside financial and shadow-fleet sanctions.
    • Section 201 extends the Iran Sanctions Act until 31 December 2031.

    India Chairs UNCTAD’s Ninth Consumer Protection Session

    • India chaired the Ninth Session of the Intergovernmental Group of Experts on Consumer Protection Law and Policy (IGE), organised by United Nations Trade and Development (UNCTAD), from July 6 to 8, 2026 at the Palais des Nations, Geneva, Switzerland. Nidhi Khare, Secretary, Department of Consumer Affairs, led the delegation.

    Spain Becomes First European Country to Ban Social Media for Children Under 16

    • Spain became the first European country to ban social media for children under 16.
    • It is the second country globally after Australia (December, 2025) to take such a step.
    • The announcement was made by Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez at the World Government Summit, Dubai.

    India Gifts the Maldives Its First High-Speed Ferry

    • India gifted Maldives its first high-speed ferry under the HICDP Phase III agreement.
    • The ferry launches Raajje Transport Link (RTL) services in Faafu and Dhaalu Atolls.
    • A total of 12 high-speed ferries are planned under the project.

    WTO 14th Ministerial Conference (MC-14), 2026

    • In March 2026, the 14th WTO Ministerial Conference (MC-14) was held in Yaoundé, Cameroon, where members failed to reach a broad consensus package, mainly due to differences over WTO reform and the e-commerce moratorium.

    India Hosts First BRICS Sherpas Meeting 2026

    • India hosted the first BRICS Sherpas and Sous-Sherpas meeting under its 2026 Chairship in New Delhi from February 9–10, 2026, setting the agenda for its fourth presidency.
    • The meeting, led by India’s BRICS Sherpa Sudhakar Dalela, centered on the theme “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability,” focusing on strengthening economic ties, innovation, and people-centric initiatives within the expanded BRICS bloc.

    Pakistan–Afghanistan Escalation

    • In late February 2026, Pakistan–Afghanistan tensions escalated.
    • Operation “Ghazab lil-Haq” refers to Pakistan’s military operation against targets it claimed were linked to Afghan-based militant threats.
    • Pakistan accused the Afghan Taliban of sheltering or failing to act against the Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP).
    • The conflict is linked to the disputed Durand Line, the border between Pakistan and Afghanistan.
    • The Durand Line is about 2,640 km long and was drawn in 1893.

    Cyclone Gezani Hits Madagascar

    • Cyclone Gezani hit Madagascar causing major destruction.
    • It made landfall at Toamasina (eastern port city).
    • Wind speeds exceeded 195 km/h, Gezani was an Intense Tropical Cyclone.
    • Around 75% of infrastructure in Toamasina was affected with power outages.

    Arrest of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro 2026

    • On January 3, 2026, US forces captured Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, in power since 2013, during Operation Absolute Resolve in Caracas, Venezuela.
    • Following his removal, the Supreme Court directed Vice President Delcy Rodríguez (in office since 2018) to assume the acting presidency.
    • She was sworn in on 5 January 2026 and is associated with Hugo Chávez's Bolivarian socialist movement.
    • The operation raised concerns over state sovereignty and international law, particularly Article 2(4) of the UN Charter, which prohibits the threat or use of force against another state's territorial integrity or political independence.
    • Opposition groups demanded fresh democratic elections.

    India Launches e-B-4 Business Visa

    • In January, 2026 India introduced a new e-Production Investment Business Visa (e-B-4) for Chinese nationals.
    • The new system allows eligible professionals to complete the entire visa process online — eliminating the need to visit Indian embassies or consulates.

    Operation Hawkeye Strike

    • On December 19 2025, Operation Hawkeye Strike was a joint U.S.–Jordan operation in Syria.
    • It followed an ISIS attack in Palmyra on December 13, 2025.
    • Two Iowa National Guard soldiers were killed, and three U.S. soldiers were injured.

    2,000-Year-Old Kushan Coins from King Vasudeva’s Era Found in Pakistan’s Rawalpindi

    • Archaeologists found bronze Kushan coins of King Vasudeva I at Bhir Mound (near Taxi-la, Rawalpindi, Pakistan), along with lapis lazuli fragments.
    • The coins date to the 2nd century CE, while the lapis lazuli fragments date to ~6th century BCE, pointing to long-standing trade activity.
    • Numismatic analysis notes coin imagery of the king on the obverse and a female deity on the reverse, indicating religious pluralism.
    • The find reinforces Taxila’s role as a key Kushan-era hub linked to wider Silk Route trade networks across Central and South Asia.

    Russia to establish its first naval base in Africa, in Sudan

    • Sudan has approved an agreement allowing Russia to establish its first naval base in Africa, near Port Sudan on the Red Sea, after talks between Sudan’s FM Ali Youssef Ahmed al-Sharif and Russia’s FM Sergei Lavrov in Moscow.
    • The move strengthens Russia’s presence in a crowded theatre where other major powers already operate.
    • It is also discussed as a hedge against uncertainty around Russia’s naval access in Tartus, Syria.

    Finke River: the world’s oldest surviving river system

    • Australia’s Finke River is recognised as the world’s oldest surviving river system, with studies dating it to around 300–400 million years.
    • It lies across the Northern Territory and South Australia, is about 640 km long, and is called Lhere-pirnte, meaning 'salty river' by the Arrernte people.
    • It flows through the MacDonnell Ranges and is an antecedent river, meaning it maintained its course during mountain uplift by eroding downward, cutting gorges through the ranges.

    India, Netherlands Join Hands to Promote Lothal Maritime Heritage

    • India and the Netherlands signed an MoU (December 2025) to strengthen maritime heritage cooperation for the National Maritime Heritage Complex (NMHC) at Lothal, Gujarat.
    • The NMHC is being developed under the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways.
    • The MoU was exchanged during talks between EAM S. Jaishankar and Dutch FM David van Weel.
    • The NMHC will collaborate with the National Maritime Museum, Amsterdam on museum planning/design, curation, conservation, plus joint exhibitions, research and cultural exchanges.

    India hosted the 28th Conference of Speakers and Presiding Officers of the Commonwealth

    • India hosted the 28th Conference of Speakers and Presiding Officers of the Commonwealth (CSPOC) in New Delhi (14–16 January 2026).
    • It brought 61 Speakers/Presiding Officers from 42 Commonwealth countries and 4 semi-autonomous parliaments, making it one of the largest editions.
    • CSPOC was created in 1969 on the initiative of Lucien Lamoureux (Canada) and functions as an independent body, with secretariat support provided by Canada.
    • India has hosted CSPOC in 1970–71, 1986, 2010, and 2026, and the 29th CSPOC is scheduled in London (2028).
    • Key themes in 2026 included AI/digital tools in parliamentary work, social media’s impact on legislative discourse, strengthening democratic institutions/public engagement, and security, health and wellbeing of MPs.
    • The conference was inaugurated by PM Narendra Modi at Samvidhan Sadan and chaired by Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla.

    CEC Gyanesh Kumar to Chair International IDEA Council for 2026

    • On December 3, 2025, India assumed the Chairship of the Council of Member States of International IDEA for 2026, with Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar representing India as Chair in Stockholm, Sweden.
    • International IDEA stands for the International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance.
    • It is an intergovernmental organisation working to support democracy and electoral processes.
    • India is a founding member of International IDEA.
    • Gyanesh Kumar will chair the Council of Member States for 2026.
    • Mauritius and Mexico will serve as Vice-Chairs along with India.
    • The 2026 chairship theme is “Democracy for an Inclusive, Peaceful, Resilient and Sustainable World.”
    • International IDEA’s Council has 35 Member States and two Observers.
    • Gyanesh Kumar is the 26th Chief Election Commissioner of India.

    UN Cybercrime Convention Signed

    • At Hanoi, countries signed the first-ever UN Cybercrime Convention, creating a global legal framework to combat ransomware, online fraud, and digital exploitation.
      • It defines and criminalizes hacking, online fraud, and child exploitation.
      • Enables real-time evidence sharing and 24/7 law enforcement cooperation.
      • Managed by the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC).

    China’s CR450: World’s Fastest Bullet Train Unveiled

    • China has unveiled the CR450, the world’s fastest bullet train, reaching a record speed of 453 km/h during testing.
    • With this, China surpassed all global competitors in both speed and efficiency.
    • China operates the world’s largest high-speed rail network, spanning 50,000 km, linking almost all major cities.
    • The CR450 strengthens China’s leadership in rail innovation and export, supporting global projects under the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI).

    Bulgaria Joins the Eurozone

    • Bulgaria officially joined the eurozone on January 1, 2026, replacing the Bulgarian lev and becoming the 21st member of the euro area.

    Strategic Restructuring of IDBI Bank Must knowPDF p. 87

    On 14 October 2026, CCEA approved 10955230 Canada Inc. (Fairfax group) to buy 60.72% of IDBI Bank for about ₹52,878.08 crore.

    • Buyer: 10955230 Canada Inc.; parent company Fairfax Financial Holdings Limited.
    • Stake sold: Government of India 30.48% + LIC 30.24% = 60.72%.
    • Bid ₹81 per share vs benchmark ₹75.99 (average of two independent valuations).
    • After the sale: Government about 15%, LIC about 19%.
    • Started as Industrial Development Bank of India on 1 July 1964; banking company from 1 October 2004.
    • RBI classed it a private sector bank from 21 January 2019, after LIC bought 51%.

    Memory aid 60.72 = 30.48 (Govt) + 30.24 (LIC): two near-30s add up to about 61.

    Don't confuse CCEA (Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs) approved the buyer; the deal is still subject to regulatory conditions.

    हिंदी: Strategic disinvestment (रणनीतिक विनिवेश)

    From the magazine

    On October 14, 2026, the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA), chaired by the Prime Minister, approved 10955230 Canada Inc., whose parent company is Fairfax Financial Holdings Limited, as the buyer for the strategic sale of a 60.72% stake in IDBI Bank Limited. The approved purchase consideration is approximately ₹52,878.08 crore. This decision marks an important stage in the transfer of the bank’s ownership and management control; completion of the transaction remains subject to compliance with further regulatory conditions.

    Background of the Bank

    • IDBI was originally known as the Industrial Development Bank of India. It came into existence as a development finance institution on 1 July 1964, and its undertaking was transferred to a banking company with effect from 1 October 2004.
    • IDBI Bank is a scheduled commercial bank regulated by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). Following LIC’s acquisition of 51% of its paid-up equity capital, the RBI classified it as a private sector bank for regulatory purposes with effect from 21 January 2019.
    Indicative Shareholding Based on the Approved Main Transaction

    Key Features of the Approved Transaction

    • The strategic buyer is 10955230 Canada Inc., whose parent company is Fairfax Financial Holdings Limited.
    • The total approved stake is 60.72%, and the purchase consideration is ₹52,878.08 crore.
    • The Government of India will sell a 30.48% stake, while LIC will sell a 30.24% stake. The sale proceeds will be distributed in the corresponding proportion.
    • The approved bid is ₹81 per share, compared with the benchmark of ₹75.99 per share, calculated as the average of two independent valuations.

    57th GST Council Meeting Must knowPDF p. 87

    The 57th GST Council meeting (New Delhi, 8 October 2026), chaired by Nirmala Sitharaman, recommended simpler registration, faster refunds and easier compliance.

    • 57th GST Council meeting: New Delhi, October 8, 2026; chair Nirmala Sitharaman.
    • Simpler registration form FORM GST REG-01; auto-approval of amendments except Principal Place of Business (PPoB).
    • Rule 14B: simple registration route for small e-commerce sellers.
    • Refund acknowledgement/deficiency memo time cut from 15 days to 10 days.
    • Minimum tax amount for issuing a show-cause notice: ₹10,000.
    • ITC on input services received on or after 1 November 2026 to count for inverted duty refunds.

    हिंदी: Show-cause notice (कारण बताओ नोटिस) · Input Tax Credit (इनपुट कर क्रेडिट)

    From the magazine

    The 57th meeting of the GST Council was held in New Delhi on October 8, 2026, chaired by Union Minister for Finance and Corporate Affairs Nirmala Sitharaman.

    • The Council recommended simplifying the registration application, FORM GST REG-01, issuing clear guidelines on the documents required and making the portal more user-friendly.
    • Automatic approval of amendments to registration particulars, other than the Principal Place of Business (PPoB), has been proposed.
    • A simplified registration mechanism for small e-commerce sellers has been proposed under Rule 14B.
    • Reforms have been proposed to improve the reconciliation of tax liability and Input Tax Credit (ITC) across GSTR-1, GSTR-1A, GSTR-2B and GSTR-3B.
    • The Council recommended automating refunds of excess balances in the electronic cash ledger and reducing the time limit for issuing an acknowledgement or deficiency memo for refund applications from 15 days to 10 days.
    • The inclusion of ITC on input services received on or after 1 November 2026 has been recommended for eligible inverted duty structure refunds.
    • ITC on eligible capital goods received on or after 1 April 2027 is proposed to be included in the calculation of refunds of unutilised ITC arising from.
    • A minimum tax amount of ₹10,000 has been recommended for issuing a show-cause notice.

    Registration of Births and Deaths (Amendment) Act, 2026 Must knowPDF p. 88

    The Registration of Births and Deaths (Amendment) Act, 2026, in force from 1 October 2026, names different authorities for late registration by length of delay.

    • Amends Section 13 of the Registration of Births and Deaths Act, 1969.
    • Presidential assent: August 6, 2026; in force: October 1, 2026.
    • Delay over one year but within two years: order of DM, SDM or authorised Executive Magistrate (Section 13(3)).
    • Delay over two years: order of a Judicial Magistrate of the First Class (Section 13(3A)).
    • Normal reporting time: 21 days; registration within 30 days needs a late fee.
    • Start date notified by Registrar General, India (MHA) through S.O. 5081(E), 16 September 2026.

    Don't confuse Under the 2023 amendment every delay over one year needed a DM/SDM order; the 2026 Act shifts over-two-year cases to a Judicial Magistrate.

    हिंदी: Judicial Magistrate (न्यायिक मजिस्ट्रेट) · Registration (पंजीकरण)

    From the magazine

    The Registration of Births and Deaths (Amendment) Act, 2026 amended Section 13 of the Registration of Births and Deaths Act, 1969, specifying the competent authorities for cases reported more than one year after the event. The amendment came into force on October 1, 2026.

    Key Details of the Act

    • It received presidential assent on August 6, 2026.
    • Section 2 of the Amendment Act substituted the existing Section 13(3) of the principal Act with new subsections 13(3) and 13(3A).
    • The Office of the Registrar General, India, under the Ministry of Home Affairs, appointed 1 October 2026 as the commencement date through Notification S.O. 5081(E), dated 16 September 2026. The notification was issued under Section 1(2) of the Amendment Act.

    New Framework for Delayed Registration

    • Information reported after one year but within two years: Under Section 13(3), registration may take place only on an order of the District Magistrate, Sub-Divisional Magistrate or an Executive Magistrate authorised by the District Magistrate.
    • Information reported after more than two years: Under Section 13(3A), registration requires an order of a Judicial Magistrate of the First Class.
    • Jurisdiction: The Magistrate issuing the order must have jurisdiction over the place where the birth or death occurred.

    Previous Framework and the Change

    • Following the 2023 amendment, registration of all births and deaths reported more than one year after the event required an order of the District Magistrate, Sub-Divisional Magistrate or an authorised Executive Magistrate. The 2026 amendment specifies different authorities for delays of more than one year but within two years, and more than two years.

    Other Provisions

    • Births and deaths are ordinarily required to be reported within 21 days. Registration after the ordinary reporting period but within 30 days attracts a late fee.

    PMJDY Completes 12 Years Must knowPDF pp. 88–89

    PMJDY, India's National Mission for Financial Inclusion launched on 28 August 2014, completed 12 years on 28 August 2026 with 59.09 crore accounts.

    • Launched by PM Narendra Modi on 28 August 2014.
    • Accounts: 14.72 crore (2015) to 59.09 crore (19 August 2026), about fourfold.
    • Women hold 32.92 crore accounts (about 55.7%); rural and semi-urban 45.95 crore (77.8%).
    • Deposits: ₹15,670 crore (March 2015) to ₹3,16,514 crore (August 2026); average ₹5,356 per account.
    • Accident cover ₹2 lakh for accounts opened after August 28, 2018; overdraft up to ₹10,000.
    • Guinness record (January 2015): 18,096,130 accounts opened in one week, August 23-29, 2014.

    Memory aid Same birthday: launched 28 August 2014, 12 years on 28 August 2026.

    हिंदी: Financial inclusion (वित्तीय समावेशन)

    From the magazine

    The Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY) completed 12 years on August 28, 2026, expanding access to formal banking and financial services among underserved and economically disadvantaged sections.

    Key Facts and Background

    • Prime Minister Narendra Modi launched PMJDY on 28 August 2014 as India’s National Mission for Financial Inclusion.
    • India’s Financial Inclusion Index increased from 53.9 in 2021 to 67 in March 2025.
    • In January 2015, Guinness World Records recognised 18,096,130 bank accounts opened in a single week (from August 23-29, 2014) under the Department of Financial Services campaign.

    Major Features and Benefits

    • Eligible account holders receive a RuPay debit card, accepted at ATMs and most Point-of-Sale terminals. Banks had issued 41.29 crore cards by 19 August 2026, promoting digital payments.
    • Accident insurance cover increased from ₹1 lakh to ₹2 lakh for new accounts opened after August 28, 2018.
    • An overdraft of up to ₹10,000 is available to one eligible account holder per household, ordinarily after six months of satisfactory account operation and subject to prescribed conditions.

    Progress so Far

    • Accounts increased approximately fourfold from 14.72 crore in 2015 to 59.09 crore by 19 August 2026. Rural and semi-urban areas held 45.95 crore accounts, or 77.8%, while urban and metropolitan areas held 13.14 crore.
    • Women held 32.92 crore accounts, or approximately 55.7% of the total, as of 19 August 2026, reflecting greater gender equality in formal financial access.
    • Deposits increased approximately twentyfold from ₹15,670 crore in March 2015 to ₹3,16,514 crore in August 2026. Average deposits reached ₹5,356 per account on 19 August 2026.

    CBDC-Based Food Subsidy Distribution under PMGKAY Must knowPDF p. 89

    Under PMGKAY, eligible beneficiaries now get food subsidy as programmable Digital Rupee (e₹) tokens in CBDC wallets instead of bank transfers.

    • CBDC-based DBT for PMGKAY launched in Chandigarh and Dadra & Nagar Haveli on August 14, 2026.
    • Launched by Union Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan.
    • Pilots: Gujarat by Amit Shah (February 15, 2026); Puducherry by Prahlad Joshi (February 26, 2026).
    • Digital Rupee (e₹) is a tokenised digital rupee issued by RBI as a CBDC.
    • Chandigarh was an early adopter of food-subsidy DBT in September 2015.

    Don't confuse Pilot began in Gujarat (February 2026); the PMGKAY launch was in Chandigarh and Dadra & Nagar Haveli (14 August 2026).

    हिंदी: Digital Rupee (डिजिटल रुपया) · Direct Benefit Transfer (प्रत्यक्ष लाभ अंतरण)

    From the magazine

    The Government of India has introduced a Central Bank Digital Currency-based Direct Benefit Transfer (CBDC-based DBT) system under the Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana (PMGKAY). Under this model, eligible beneficiaries receive food subsidies as programmable Digital Rupee tokens in their CBDC wallets instead of receiving the subsidy through conventional bank-account transfers.

    Background

    • The Digital Rupee, also known as the e₹ or e-rupee, is a tokenised digital form of the Indian rupee issued by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) as a Central Bank Digital Currency.
    • Chandigarh was among the early adopters of food-subsidy DBT in September 2015, when it shifted from physical distribution of subsidised foodgrains to direct subsidy transfers into beneficiaries’ Aadhaar-linked bank accounts.
    • CBDC based food subsidy was initiated on a pilot basis on February 15, 2026 by Home Minister Amit Shah in Gujarat and later on February 26, 2026 by Prahlad Joshi in Pducherry as a pilot initiative.
    • The Government launched CBDC-based DBT for PMGKAY beneficiaries in Chandigarh and Dadra & Nagar Haveli on August 14, 2026.
    • The initiative was launched by Union Minister for Agriculture and Farmers’ Welfare Shivraj Singh Chouhan.

    India’s Proposed ₹10 and ₹20 Polymer Banknotes Must knowPDF p. 89

    The Government approved RBI's proposal for field trials of ₹10 and ₹20 polymer banknotes; existing paper notes stay legal tender.

    • RBI proposed one billion notes of each: 200 crore notes, face value about ₹3,000 crore.
    • Proposal under Sections 24 (denominations) and 25 (design, form, materials) of the RBI Act, 1934.
    • BRBNMPL, an RBI subsidiary, started procuring polymer substrate.
    • Australia first issued a polymer banknote in 1988; more than 60 countries use them.
    • Currency in circulation up 12% to ₹41.23 lakh crore (end-March 2026); ₹500 notes about 86% of value.
    • Printing cost fell nearly 24% to ₹4,875 crore in 2025–26.

    Don't confuse Section 24 = denominations; Section 25 = design, form and materials.

    Check Coins in circulation printed as '₹40,814' with no unit (crore?).

    हिंदी: Legal tender (वैध मुद्रा) · Banknote (बैंक नोट)

    From the magazine

    The Government of India has approved a proposal by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) for field trials of ₹10 and ₹20 polymer banknotes.

    Key Facts

    • The RBI proposed one billion notes of each denomination, totalling 200 crore notes with a face value of approximately ₹3,000 crore. The Government informed Parliament of the approval in 2026, when procurement remained at an initial stage. Regular issuance may be considered only after successful trials.
    • The RBI submitted the proposal under Sections 24 and 25 of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, following its Central Board’s recommendation. Section 24 covers the banknote denominations whereas Section 25 covers design, form and materials. Bharatiya Reserve Bank Note Mudran Private Limited (BRBNMPL), an RBI subsidiary, initiated polymer-substrate procurement.
    • Polymer banknotes use a non-fibrous, non-porous plastic film. Existing Indian paper banknotes use long cotton fibres from cotton comber and cotton linter.
    • Polymer notes will circulate alongside existing ₹10 and ₹20 paper notes, which will remain legal tender. Trials will assess cleanliness, security, handling and suitability for India’s cash economy.

    Global Experience

    • Australia first issued a polymer banknote in 1988. More than 60 countries reportedly use polymer currency, including Canada, the United Kingdom, New Zealand and Singapore.

    Currency in Circulation

    • According to the supplied RBI figures, currency in circulation rose 12% year-on-year to ₹41.23 lakh crore (banknotes alone excluding coins) at the end of March 2026 (₹40,814 coins in circulation). ₹500 notes represented approximately 86% of banknotes’ total value. Printing expenditure reportedly fell nearly 24% to ₹4,875 crore in 2025–26, mainly because of lower printing requirements.

    Bankers’ Books Evidence Act, 2026 Must knowPDF pp. 89–90

    The Bankers' Books Evidence Act, 2026 (in force 1 October 2026) replaces the 1891 Act and accepts physical, electronic and digital bank records as evidence.

    • Replaces the Bankers' Books Evidence Act, 1891 with a technology-neutral framework.
    • Lok Sabha passed it 5 August 2026, Rajya Sabha 10 August; assent 13 August 2026.
    • Bankers' books include records at off-site, virtual, cloud, backup and disaster recovery locations.
    • 'Banks' include post office savings bank and money order offices.
    • Certified copies are prima facie (first-look), not conclusive, evidence.
    • NBFCs, payment aggregators and fintechs covered only if notified or under another law.

    हिंदी: Evidence (साक्ष्य)

    From the magazine

    The Bankers’ Books Evidence Act, 2026 came into force on October 1, 2026. The Act replaces the Bankers’ Books Evidence Act, 1891 with a technology-neutral framework recognising physical, electronic and digital banking records as evidence. The definition of bankers’ books includes records at off site, virtual, cloud, backup and disaster recovery locations. Banks and bankers also include post office savings bank and money order offices.

    Legislative Background

    • The Lok Sabha passed the Bill on 5 August 2026 and the Rajya Sabha on 10 August. Presidential assent followed on 13 August 2026.

    Major Provisions

    • The first schedule applies to copies of books maintained in written or physical form. The second schedule applies to copies of books maintained electronically, digitally or through other data storage mechanism.
    • Certification of Banking Records – Certificates must confirm accuracy and be authenticated manually, digitally or electronically by an authorised bank officer.
    • Conditions for Digital Records – Digital records are admissible if created and stored in the ordinary course of banking through regularly used, properly functioning systems.
    • Evidentiary Value – Certified copies are prima facie, not conclusive, evidence where original entries are legally admissible.
    • Extension to Financial-Sector Entities – The Central Government may extend coverage by notification. NBFCs, payment aggregators and fintech firms are covered only if notified or under another law.
    • Legal Proceedings and Production of Records – Proceedings include court cases, arbitration, investigations and inquiries.

    Indian Statistical Institute Bill 2026 PDF p. 90

    The Indian Statistical Institute Bill, 2026 (Lok Sabha, 3 August 2026) would replace the 1959 Act and make ISI a statutory body corporate.

    • Introduced in Lok Sabha on 3 August 2026; replaces the 1959 Act (in force April 1, 1960).
    • ISI stays an institution of national importance under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation.
    • President of India would be the Visitor; can order reviews and nominate the Board Chairperson.
    • An 11-member Board would replace the 33-member Council.
    • Board: Chairperson, government representatives, four external experts and four ISI representatives.
    • The Director would be the Chief Executive Officer.

    Memory aid 11 replaces 33: the new Board is one-third the size of the old Council.

    हिंदी: Institution of national importance (राष्ट्रीय महत्व का संस्थान)

    From the magazine

    Introduced in the Lok Sabha on 3 August 2026, the Indian Statistical Institute Bill, 2026 seeks to replace the 1959 Act (came into force on April 1, 1960). It would convert ISI into a statutory body corporate while retaining its status as an institution of national importance.

    Change in Legal Status

    • Body-corporate status would provide clearer legal authority and institutional continuity. ISI would remain under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation.

    Key Highlights

    • The President of India would be the Visitor, empowered to order reviews or inquiries and issue binding directions. The Visitor would nominate the Board’s Chairperson on the Centre’s recommendation.
    • Admission and Reservation – Admissions would follow transparent, merit-based criteria without discrimination.
    • An 11-member Board would replace the 33-member Council as the principal policy-making and executive body, accountable to the Centre. It would comprise the Chairperson, government representatives, four external experts and four ISI representatives.
    • The Board would approve budgets, plans, fees and regulations, reorganise academic units and award degrees on the Academic Council’s recommendation.
    • The Director-led Academic Council would include Centre-Directors, all full-time Professors, selected faculty and the Dean of Academic Affairs.
    • Director – The Director would be the Chief Executive Officer, managing daily administration and implementing institutional decisions.
    • ISI may receive government grants after parliamentary appropriation, earn revenue, accept donations and maintain funds.

    VB – G RAM G Act, 2025 Must knowPDF p. 90

    The VB-G RAM G Act, 2025 replaced MGNREGA from July 1, 2026 and raised the rural job guarantee from 100 to 125 days a year.

    • Full name: Viksit Bharat – Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, 2025.
    • In force across rural India from July 1, 2026; repealed MGNREGA, 2005.
    • Guarantee raised from 100 to 125 days per year; wage floor ₹300/day for 2026–27.
    • Funding: 90:10 for Northeastern and Himalayan States; 60:40 for other States/UTs with legislatures.
    • Shivraj Singh Chouhan released over ₹25,000 crore as first instalment, the 'Mother Sanction'.
    • FY 2026–27 Central share ₹95,692.31 crore (Budget Estimate); total outlay over ₹1.51 lakh crore.

    Memory aid VB-G RAM G = Viksit Bharat – Guarantee for Rozgar And Ajeevika Mission (Gramin). Motto: 'Rozgar Bhi, Samman Bhi'.

    Don't confuse Old MGNREGA guarantee = 100 days; new Act = 125 days. UTs without legislatures get full Central funding.

    हिंदी: Rural employment (ग्रामीण रोजगार) · Unemployment allowance (बेरोजगारी भत्ता)

    From the magazine

    The Viksit Bharat – Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, 2025, or VB-G RAM G Act, is India’s statutory framework for rural wage employment and village development. It came into force across rural India on July 1, 2026, repealing the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005 (MGNREGA).

    About the News

    • Rural Development Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan released over ₹25,000 crore as the first installment, called the Mother Sanction, to support timely wage payments. A total ₹7.5 lakh crore (as on July, 2026) will be invested in 2.86 lakh Panchayats over the next five years. Wage rates have increased by around 10 percent on average.
    • The Act guarantees wage employment, strengthens village economies and promotes sustainable livelihoods. It links employment with productive public assets, transparency, convergence, climate resilience and local economic development, following “Rozgar Bhi, Samman Bhi”, or employment with dignity.

    Key Features of the VB-G RAM G Act

    • The Act increases the employment guarantee from 100 to 125 days per financial year for rural households whose adult members volunteer for unskilled manual work.
    • The notified minimum wage floor for 2026–27 is ₹300 per day.
    • Wages should be paid weekly or within fifteen days of work and muster-roll closure measures delayed compensation.
    • Delays attract compensation of 0.05 percent of unpaid wages per day beyond the sixteenth day after closure.
    • Existing e-KYC-verified job cards remain valid until Gramin Rozgar Guarantee Cards are issued. Workers may register at Gram Panchayats, and pending e-KYC cannot justify denial of employment.
    • Work may be demanded orally, through Form-6 or digitally.
    • Failure to provide employment within the prescribed timeframe entitles workers to unemployment allowance of at least one-fourth of the notified wage for the first thirty days of the financial year and one-half for the remaining period.
    • Four Priority Areas – Water security; Rural infrastructure; Livelihood infrastructure; Climate resilience.
    • Funding Pattern – The Act operates as a Centrally Sponsored Scheme, with a 90:10 funding ratio for Northeastern and Himalayan States (like Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh and Jammu & Kashmir); and it is 60: 40 for other States and UTs with legislatures.
    • UTs without legislatures receive full Central funding. Central allocations follow objective, rule-based parameters. States bear expenditure beyond normative allocations and must distribute funds transparently according to local needs.
    • Budgetary Commitment – For FY 2026–27, the Central share is ₹95,692.31 crore, described as the largest Budget Estimate allocation for a rural employment programme. Including the estimated State share, total outlay is expected to exceed ₹1.51 lakh crore.

    The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 completed ten years in 2026, moving India from delay-based liquidation towards reviving companies.

    • IBC enacted May 28, 2016; IBBI set up October 1, 2016.
    • Till March 31, 2026: 8,987 cases admitted, 7,102 closed, 1,419 resolution plans approved.
    • 4,099 companies rescued; creditors realised more than ₹4 lakh crore.
    • Realisation about 95% of fair value and about 167% of liquidation value.

    • Banks' gross NPA ratio (domestic): 2.15% on September 30, 2025.

    From the magazine

    The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 completed ten year milestone in 2026 (It was enacted on May 28, 2016). Over the last decade, the IBC has moved India’s insolvency regime away from delay-based liquidation towards corporate revival and preservation of enterprise value. The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India was established on October 1, 2016.

    Resolution and Recovery Performance

    • As of March 31, 2026, a total of 1,419 cases had resulted in approved resolution plans under the IBC.
    • The IBC resolution process has facilitated realisation of more than ₹4 lakh crore for creditors.
    • The amount realised by creditors was around 95 percent of the fair value of the assets.
    • The amount realised was also around 167 percent of the liquidation value, showing that resolution under the IBC helped preserve enterprise value.
    • Till March 31, 2026, a total of 8,987 cases had been admitted under the IBC framework.
    • Out of these admitted cases, 7,102 cases had reached closure.
    • Among the closed cases, 4,099 companies were successfully rescued.
    • For Domestic Operations gross NPA ratio of the Scheduled Commercial Banks stood at 2.15 percent as of September 30, 2025.
    • Scheduled Commercial Banks recovered a total of ₹1.04 lakh crore through various recovery channels for FY 2024-25.
    • Out of this, nearly ₹0.54 lakh crore was realised through the IBC process.
    • This means that about 52.4 percent of total recoveries by Scheduled Commercial Banks came through the IBC route.

    Income-Tax Act, 2025 Must knowPDF pp. 92–93

    The Income-tax Act, 2025 came into force on 1 April 2026, replacing the Income-tax Act, 1961 with simpler language and a single 'Tax Year'.

    • In force from 1 April 2026; replaces the six-decade-old Income-tax Act, 1961.
    • 'Tax Year' replaces 'Assessment Year' and 'Previous Year'.
    • CBDT notified the Income-tax Rules, 2026 to implement the Act.
    • Form 130 replaces Form 16 (TDS certificate issued by employers).
    • New Act: 536 Sections, 23 Chapters, 16 Schedules; TDS/TCS in sections 392,393 and 394.
    • New regime (AY 2026-27): zero tax up to ₹12 lakh; standard deduction ₹75,000 (was ₹50,000).

    Don't confuse Form 130 is new; Form 16 is the old TDS certificate. Zero-tax limit ₹12 lakh (new) vs ₹7 lakh (old).

    Check 1961 Act shown as '819+ sections and 298 Chapters' and gross direct tax 2025–26 as ₹7.99 lakh crore; both look doubtful.

    हिंदी: Tax Year (कर वर्ष) · Assessment Year (निर्धारण वर्ष)

    From the magazine

    The Income-tax Act, 2025 has come into force from 1 April 2026, replacing the six-decade-old Income-tax Act, 1961. The reform aims to modernise India’s tax system and make it more aligned with current economic realities. It simplifies language, structure and tax compliance while improving the efficiency of tax administration.

    Key Highlights

    Operational and Structural Changes

    • The Central Board of Direct Taxes has notified the Income-tax Rules, 2026 to implement the provisions of the new Act.
    • A major procedural reform is the introduction of Form 130, which replaces the traditional Form 16 (TDS certificate issued by employers).
    • The act replaces the concepts of ‘Assessment Year (AY)’ and ‘Previous Year’ with ‘Tax Year’. The Financial Year (FY) continues to remain relevant in the Act.
    • A single unified concept called the “Tax Year” has been introduced for simplification.

    Report of the 16th Finance Commission (2026–31) Must knowPDF p. 93

    The 16th Finance Commission (chair Arvind Panagariya), covering 2026–27 to 2030–31, kept States' share of the divisible pool at 41%; UP's share is 17.62%.

    • Constitutional body under Article 280; 16th FC set up December 31, 2023 under Dr. Arvind Panagariya.
    • Report submitted 17 November 2025; tabled in Parliament 1 February 2026.
    • States' vertical share stays 41%; weights: income distance 42.5%, population (2011) 17.5%.
    • Total grants about ₹9.47 lakh crore for 2026–31; ₹7.91 lakh crore for local bodies.
    • Fiscal deficit: Centre to 3.5% of GDP by 2030–31; States' ceiling stays 3% of GSDP.
    • UP's share: 17.94% (15th FC) to 17.62% (16th FC), highest among States listed.

    Don't confuse 41% = States' vertical share (unchanged); 42.5% = weight for income distance. The 16th FC dropped revenue deficit, sector-specific and state-specific grants.

    हिंदी: Finance Commission (वित्त आयोग) · Centre–State fiscal relations (केंद्र-राज्य वित्तीय संबंध)

    From the magazine

    The Finance Commission is a constitutional body under Article 280 of the Constitution, constituted by the President every five years (or earlier) to recommend the principles governing Centre–State fiscal relations.

    • The 16th Finance Commission was constituted on December 31, 2023 under the Chairmanship of Dr. Arvind Panagariya (Article 280).

    Key Highlights

    • The 16th Finance Commission covers the period 2026–27 to 2030–31. It submitted its report on 17 November 2025, and it was tabled in Parliament on 1 February 2026.
    • The Commission has not recommended three grant categories recommended by the 15th Finance Commission, namely revenue deficit grants, sector-specific grants, and state-specific grants.
    • The Commission has recommended that the States’ vertical share remain 41% of the divisible pool of Union taxes.
      • The weights are 42.5% for per-capita income distance (GSDP), 17.5% for population (2011), 10% for demographic performance, 10% for area, 10% for forest, and 10% for contribution to GDP.
    • The Commission has recommended total grants of about ₹9.47 lakh crore for 2026–31. Of this, about ₹7.91 lakh crore is for local bodies and ₹1.56 lakh crore is the Union share for disaster management grants.
    • The Commission has recommended a Special Infrastructure Component of ₹56,100 crore for selected urban local bodies for comprehensive wastewater management in urban growth centres.
    • It has also recommended an Urbanisation Premium of ₹10,000 crore for the full award period.
    • The Commission has recommended a total disaster management corpus of ₹2,04,401 crore for SDRF and SDMF together for 2026–31.
    • The Commission has recommended that the Centre reduce its fiscal deficit to 3.5% of GDP by 2030–31.
    • It has recommended that the States’ annual fiscal deficit ceiling remain 3% of GSDP excluding loans under Special Assistane to States for Capital Investment (SASCI).
    • The Commission projects that combined debt of the Centre and States will decline from 77.3% of GDP in 2026–27 to 73.1% in 2030–31.

    On 14 October 2026, Cabinet approved NSAP for FY 2026–27 to 2030–31 (₹53,428 crore) and renamed it Pradhan Mantri Samajik Sahayata Yojana.

    National Family Health Survey-6 Must knowPDF pp. 95–96

    NFHS-6 (2023–24) fact sheets, released 29 May 2026, show more institutional births, better vaccination and women's empowerment; TFR stays 2.0.

    • Released May 29, 2026 by the Health Ministry; IIPS, Mumbai surveyed 6.79 lakh households in 715 districts.
    • 95.9% of pregnant women got antenatal care; first-trimester care 70.0% to 76.2%; at least four visits 58.5% to 65.2%.
    • TFR stayed 2.0 (urban 1.6, rural 2.1); institutional deliveries 88.6% to 90.6%.
    • Full vaccination (12–23 months) 83.8% to 87.1%; rotavirus 36.4% to 85.4%.
    • Stunting fell 35.5% to 29.3%; overweight/obese women rose 24.0% to 30.7%.
    • Women using internet 33.3% to 64.3%; spousal violence 29.2% to 22.3%.

    Memory aid Women's internet use nearly doubled: 33.3 to 64.3.

    Don't confuse NFHS-6 survey was done in 2023–24 but released in 2026; it is compared with NFHS-5 (2019–21).

    हिंदी: Total Fertility Rate (कुल प्रजनन दर) · Institutional delivery (संस्थागत प्रसव) · Stunting (बौनापन)

    From the magazine

    The fact sheets for the sixth round of the National Family Health Survey (NFHS-6) were released on May 29, 2026 by the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. Conducted during 2023–24 by the International Institute for Population Sciences (IIPS) in Mumbai, the survey covered nearly 6.79 lakh households across 715 districts in India.

    Key Highlights

    • Institutional deliveries increased from 88.6% in NFHS-5 to 90.6% in NFHS-6.
    • Births attended by skilled health personnel increased from 89.4% to 91.3%.
    • Full vaccination coverage among children aged 12– 23 months increased from 83.8% to 87.1% (based on information from vaccination cards).
    • India’s Total Fertility Rate remained at 2.0.
    • The contraceptive Prevalence Rate increased from 66.7% to 69.1%.
    • Health insurance or financing scheme coverage increased from 41.0% to 60.2% at the household level.
    • The percentage of women who had ever used the internet increased from 33.3% to 64.3%.
    • The percentage of women having a bank or savings account that they themselves use increased from 78.6% to 89.0%.
    • The percentage of women having a mobile phone that they themselves use increased from 53.9% to 63.6%.
    • Stunting among children under five declined from 35.5% to 29.3%.
    • Severe wasting among children under five declined from 7.7% to 5.2%.
    • Spousal violence among ever-married women aged 18–49 declined from 29.2% to 22.3%.

    Maternal and Child Healthcare

    • A total of 95.9% of pregnant women received antenatal care.
    • The percentage of mothers receiving antenatal care in the first trimester increased from 70.0% to 76.2%.
    • The percentage of mothers receiving at least four antenatal care visits increased from 58.5% to 65.2%.
    • Institutional deliveries increased from 88.6% to 90.6%.
    • Births attended by skilled health personnel increased from 89.4% to 91.3%.
    • Postnatal care for newborns within two days of delivery increased from 79.1% to 85.3%.

    Family Planning

    • India’s Total Fertility Rate remained at 2.0.
    • The Total Fertility Rate was 1.6 in urban areas and 2.1 in rural areas.
    • The Contraceptive Prevalence Rate increased from 66.7% to 69.1%.

    Child Immunization and Child Health

    • Full vaccination coverage among children aged 12–23 months increased from 83.8% to 87.1%.
    • A total of 95.6% of children received most vaccinations through public health facilities.
    • The share of children aged 12–23 months receiving any vaccine remained above 96%.
    • Rotavirus vaccination coverage increased sharply from 36.4% to 85.4%.

    Child Nutrition

    • A total of 95.6% of children under six months were breastfed during the survey period.
    • The percentage of children under three years breastfed within one hour of birth increased from 41.8% to 50.1%.
    • Stunting among children under five declined from 35.5% to 29.3%.
    • Severe wasting among children under five declined from 7.7% to 5.2%.
    • Underweight prevalence among children under five declined slightly from 32.1% to 31.8%.

    Population and Household Profile

    • The share of population below age 5 was 8.0% in NFHS-6.
    • The share of population below age 15 was 25.5%.
    • The share of population aged 60 years and above was 12.9%.
    • The percentage of population living in households with electricity increased from 96.8% to 98.3%.

    Marriage and Fertility

    • The percentage of women aged 20–24 years married before age 18 declined from 23.3% to 20.1%.
    • The percentage of men aged 25–29 years married before age 21 declined from 17.7% to 15.9%.
    • The percentage of women aged 15–19 years who were already mothers or pregnant declined slightly from 6.8% to 6.7%.

    Adult Nutrition

    • The percentage of women aged 15–49 years with below-normal BMI increased from 18.7% to 19.7%.
    • The percentage of men aged 15–49 years with below-normal BMI increased from 16.2% to 19.7%.
    • The percentage of women who were overweight or obese increased from 24.0% to 30.7%.
    • Health insurance or financing scheme coverage increased from 41.0% to 60.2% at the household level.

    Women’s Empowerment and Financial Inclusion

    • The percentage of women who had ever used the internet increased from 33.3% to 64.3%.
    • The percentage of women having a bank or savings account that they themselves use increased from 78.6% to 89.0%.
    • The percentage of women having a mobile phone that they themselves use increased from 53.9% to 63.6%.

    Gender-Based Violence

    • The percentage of ever-married women aged 18–49 who experienced spousal violence declined from 29.2% to 22.3%.
    • The percentage of ever-married women aged 18–49 who experienced physical violence during pregnancy declined from 3.1% to 2.7%.
