    Sample Registration System (SRS) Bulletin 2024 Must knowPDF pp. 96–97

    The SRS Bulletin 2024, released by the Registrar General of India on 20 May 2026, shows birth rate 18.3, death rate 6.4 and IMR 24.

    • Released May 20, 2026 with the Special Bulletin on Maternal Mortality (2022-24).
    • Birth rate 18.3 (2014: 21.0); highest Bihar 26.8, lowest Andaman and Nicobar 9.9.
    • Death rate 6.4; highest Chhattisgarh 8.4, lowest Chandigarh 3.9.
    • IMR 24 (2014: 39); highest Chhattisgarh 36, lowest Manipur 2.
    • MMR 87 per 100,000 live births (2022-24) vs 130 in 2014-16.
    • Natural growth rate 11.9; Bihar 20.8 (high), Kerala 3.9 (low).

    Don't confuse Chhattisgarh tops both death rate (8.4) and IMR (36). 3.9 is twice: Chandigarh's death rate and Kerala's natural growth rate.

    हिंदी: Infant Mortality Rate (शिशु मृत्यु दर) · Maternal Mortality Ratio (मातृ मृत्यु अनुपात) · Birth rate (जन्म दर)

    From the magazine

    The Sample Registration System (SRS) Bulletin for 2024 (Volume 59-I) and the Special Bulletin on Maternal Mortality (2022-24) were officially released by the Registrar General of India on May 20, 2026. The SRS Bulletin 2024 was released by the Office of the Registrar General of India.

    • SRS provides annual estimates of important demographic indicators in India.
      • It gives data on Birth Rate, Death Rate, Natural Growth Rate and Infant Mortality Rate.

    Key Highlights

    • Birth Rate means the number of live births per thousand population in a year.
    • Birth Rate is an important indicator of fertility and population growth.
    • India’s Birth Rate declined from 36.9 in 1971 to 18.3 in 2024.
    • During the last decade, India’s Birth Rate declined from 21.0 in 2014 to 18.3 in 2024.
    • This shows a decline of about 13% in the last ten years.
    • The rural Birth Rate declined from 22.7 in 2014 to 20.2 in 2024.
    • The urban Birth Rate declined from 17.4 in 2014 to 14.7 in 2024.
    • In 2024, the Birth Rate was 20.2 in rural areas and 14.7 in urban areas.
    • Bihar had the highest Birth Rate at 26.8.
    • Andaman and Nicobar Islands had the lowest Birth Rate at 9.9.
    • Death Rate means the number of deaths per thousand population in a year.
    • India’s Death Rate declined from 14.9 in 1971 to 6.4 in 2024.
    • In 2024, India’s total Death Rate was 6.4.
    • The rural Death Rate was 6.8 in 2024.
    • The urban Death Rate was 5.6 in 2024.
    • The rural Death Rate remained the same in 2023 and 2024 at 6.8.
    • The urban Death Rate declined slightly from 5.7 in 2023 to 5.6 in 2024.
    • Chhattisgarh recorded the highest Death Rate at 8.4.
    • Chandigarh recorded the lowest Death Rate at 3.9.
    • The male Death Rate was 7.1.
    • The female Death Rate was 5.6.
    • The data shows that the male Death Rate was higher than the female Death Rate.
    • Male IMR was 24 and female IMR was 25.
    • Rural IMR was 27 and urban IMR was 17.
    • In rural areas, male IMR was 27 and female IMR was 28.
    • In urban areas, male IMR was 17 and female IMR was 16.
    • Natural Growth Rate is the difference between Birth Rate and Death Rate.
    • India’s Natural Growth Rate in 2024 was 11.9.
    • The rural Natural Growth Rate was 13.5.
    • The urban Natural Growth Rate was 9.0.
    • Bihar had a high Natural Growth Rate of 20.8.
    • Kerala had a low Natural Growth Rate of 3.9.
    • Infant Mortality Rate is commonly called IMR.
    • India’s IMR in 2024 was 24 infant deaths per thousand live births.
    • India’s IMR declined from 129 in 1971 to 24 in 2024.
    • India’s IMR declined from 39 in 2014 to 24 in 2024.
    • This shows a decline of about 38% in the last decade.
    • Rural IMR declined from 43 in 2014 to 27 in 2024.
    • Urban IMR declined from 26 in 2014 to 17 in 2024.
    • In 2024, rural IMR was 27 and urban IMR was 17.
    • Chhattisgarh recorded the highest IMR at 36.
    • Manipur recorded the lowest IMR at 2 (estimate covers 2022-24).
    • At the national level, about one in every 42 infants died before completing one year of life.
    • India’s maternal mortality ratio was 87 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births in SRS 2022-24, compared with 130 in 2014-16.

    Sample Coverage

    • The SRS Bulletin 2024 covered 8,839 sample units across India.
    • Out of these, 4,960 sample units were rural and 3,879 were urban.
    • The total population covered was about 8.981 million.

    MoSPI Launches New Logo and Mascot PDF p. 97

    MoSPI unveiled a new logo and a citizen-friendly mascot on 1 January 2026 to modernise its identity and build trust in official statistics.

    • New logo and mascot unveiled by MoSPI on 1 January 2026.
    • Ashoka Chakra = truth, transparency, good governance; ₹ symbol at the centre.
    • Logo message: 'Data for Development'; colours saffron, white, green and deep blue.
    • Mascot 'सांख्यिकी' to be used in National Sample Surveys by the NSS wing of NSO.
    • Finance Ministry unveiled a common logo for Regional Rural Banks on 18 December 2025.

    Check Mascot name is printed with a broken character ('सांख्य⼿की'); likely सांख्यिकी.

    हिंदी: Statistics (सांख्यिकी) · Mascot (शुभंकर)

    From the magazine

    • The Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) unveiled its new logo and new mascot on 1 January 2026 to modernise its institutional identity, strengthen public outreach, and reinforce the role of official statistics in nation-building.
    • The Ashoka Chakra in the logo represents truth, transparency, and good governance.
    • The Rupee symbol (₹) at the centre underlines the role of statistics in economic planning, policy design, and national growth.
    • The design uses numbers and statistical symbols to indicate modern data systems and statistical science.
    • The upward growth bar conveys progress and explains how credible data supports sustainable economic growth.
    • The colour scheme–saffron, white, green, and deep blue–is used to represent national values such as growth, truth, sustainability, stability, and knowledge, strengthening the credibility of official statistics.
    • The logo carries the message “Data for Development”.

    New Mascot

    • MoSPI introduced a mascot named “सांख्य⼿की” as a citizen-centric character to make statistics simple, relatable, and engaging for the public.
    • “सांख्य⼿की” will be used across National Sample Surveys in the NSS wing of NSO (earlier called NSSO) for its outreach, awareness campaigns, educational content, digital platforms, and public events to encourage participation and trust in official data.
      • New Logo for Regional Rural Banks
    • The Ministry of Finance (Government of India) unveiled a new common logo for Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) on 18 December 2025. The main purpose is to create a single, unified brand identity for all RRBs across the country, especially after the recent restructuring of the RRB system.
    • A single unified logo has been introduced to reinforce the common identity of Regional Rural Banks nationwide.
    • The design of the new logo uses specific colours to symbolically represent the objectives of RRBs.
    • The dark blue colour in the logo represents finance, and trust.
    • The green colour in the logo symbolizes life and growth.

    Basic Animal Husbandry Statistics (BAHS) 2025 Must knowPDF pp. 99–100

    Basic Animal Husbandry Statistics 2025, released on National Milk Day (26 November 2025), shows India 1st in milk with 247.87 million tonnes.

    • Released November 26, 2025 (National Milk Day) by MoS Prof. S.P. Singh Baghel.
    • Based on the Integrated Sample Survey, March 1, 2024 to February 28, 2025.
    • Milk 2024-25: 247.87 million tonnes (+3.58%), India 1st; 485 g/day per person.
    • Eggs: 149.11 billion, India 2nd; meat: 10.50 million tonnes, India 4th.
    • Top States: milk – Uttar Pradesh (15.66%); eggs – Andhra Pradesh; wool – Rajasthan (47.85%).
    • Livestock GVA up about 195% (2014–15 to 2023–24); 31% of agricultural GVA.

    Don't confuse UP is first in milk (15.66%) but second in meat (12.20%), behind West Bengal (12.46%).

    हिंदी: Animal husbandry (पशुपालन) · Per capita availability (प्रति व्यक्ति उपलब्धता)

    From the magazine

    On November 26, 2025, in celebration of National Milk Day, the Minister of State for Fisheries, Animal Husbandry & Dairying and Panchayati Raj, Prof. S.P. Singh Baghel, ceremoniously released the Basic Animal Husbandry Statistics 2025.

    Key Highlights of the Event

    • The Basic Animal Husbandry Statistics (BAHS) 2025 is based on the results of the Integrated Sample Survey (ISS) conducted from March 1, 2024, to February 28, 2025.
      • The estimated number of animals involved in milk production, egg-laying birds, animals slaughtered, and sheep shorn.

    Key Facts and Data from BAHS 2025

    • The livestock sector’s Gross Value Added (GVA) increased by nearly 195% (at current prices) from 2014–15 to 2023–24, and it contributed 31% of total Agricultural GVA in 2023–24 and 5.5% of national GVA (current prices).
    • The total value of livestock product exports reached ₹66,249 crore in 2024–25, with exports driven largely by the meat industry (including bovine meat and edible offal). 1. Milk Production:
      • India ranks 1st globally in milk production, with an estimated 247.87 million tonnes for 2024-25, showing a 3.58% increase from the previous year (239.30 million tonnes in 2023-24). The data is based on FAO 2023 rankings.
      • Per Capita Availability: The availability has risen from 319 g/day in 2014-15 to 485 g/day in 2024-25.
      • Top 5 states together contribute 54.09% of India’s total milk production. 2. Egg Production:
      • India ranks 2nd globally in egg production, with an estimated 149.11 billion eggs for 2024-25, showing a 4.44% increase from the previous year.
      • Per Capita Availability: Eggs have increased from 62 eggs/annum in 2014-15 to 106 eggs/annum in 2024-25.
      • Commercial poultry contributes 84.49% of the total egg production. 3. Meat Production:
      • India ranks 4th globally in meat production, with an estimated 10.50 million tonnes for 2024-25, reflecting a 2.46% increase.
      • Poultry accounts for about 50% of total meat production. 4. Wool Production:
      • Total wool production in India is estimated at 34.57 million kg for 2024-25, showing a 2.63% increase.
      • These states together contribute 85.98% of the country’s wool output.

    Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development (Amendment) Act, 2026 Must knowPDF pp. 100–101

    The MSMED (Amendment) Act, 2026 amends the 2006 Act to fight delayed payments, ease registration and speed up MSME dispute resolution.

    • Introduced in Rajya Sabha on 28 July 2026 by MSME Minister Jitan Ram Manjhi.
    • Rajya Sabha passed 3 August, Lok Sabha 7 August, assent 13 August 2026; Act No. 16 of 2026.
    • CPSEs must settle MSME invoices through TReDS (RBI-regulated invoice platform).
    • Mediation within 90 days; failed mediation goes to arbitration within 30 days.
    • Buyer challenging an award deposits 75%; court releases at least 50% after six months.
    • Memorandum filing free and voluntary; TReDS discounted invoices ₹40,000 crore (2021–22) to ₹3.47 lakh crore (2025–26).

    Don't confuse Bill was introduced first in the Rajya Sabha (28 July), not the Lok Sabha.

    हिंदी: Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (सूक्ष्म, लघु एवं मध्यम उद्यम) · Mediation (मध्यस्थता)

    From the magazine

    The Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development (Amendment) Act, 2026 modernises the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Act, 2006. It seeks to address delayed payments, improve MSME liquidity, simplify digital registration, strengthen dispute-resolution institutions and rationalise compliance-related penalties.

    Legislative Background and Present Status

    • The measure was introduced in the Rajya Sabha on 28 July 2026 by Union Minister for Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Jitan Ram Manjhi.
      • Rajya Sabha passed it on 3 August 2026.
      • Lok Sabha passed it on 7 August 2026.
      • It received Presidential assent on 13 August 2026.
      • It was published as Act No. 16 of 2026 in the Gazette of India.
    • The act seeks to address delayed payments, improve MSME liquidity, accelerate dispute resolution, simplify registration and compliance, and promote the Ease of Doing Business.
    • It amends specific provisions of the MSMED Act, 2006 rather than replacing the entire principal legislation.

    Key Provisions of the MSMED (Amendment) Bill, 2026

    • Filing of the memorandum will be free and voluntary for all MSMEs.
    • CPSEs must settle MSME invoices through TReDS, while States may impose the same requirement on their public enterprises and authorities.
    • TReDS, regulated by the RBI, enables MSMEs to obtain funds against unpaid invoices.
    • Discounted invoices increased from ₹40,000 crore in 2021–22 to ₹3.47 lakh crore in 2025–26.
    • States may establish multiple MSEFCs and provide them with adequate infrastructure, digital systems and trained personnel.
    • Mediation must be completed within 90 days of the first appearance.
    • Failed mediation must be referred to arbitration within 30 days.
    • A buyer challenging an award must deposit 75% of the awarded amount.
    • If the case remains pending beyond six months, the court must release at least 50% of the award to the MSME supplier.

    The India Electric Mobility Index (IEMI) is a composite index that measures the progress of electric mobility across states and Union Territories. Developed by NITI Aayog in collaboration with WRI India, it assesses policy frameworks related to e-mobility and the outcomes of their implementation.

    Introduction and Objectives

    • IEMI 2025 is the second edition of the index. It was released on 16 September 2026, covering the assessment period from January to December 2025. The first edition, IEMI 2024, was released on 4 August 2025.
    • The index has four principal objectives:
      • To identify states and Union Territories performing well in e-mobility.
      • To identify the key success factors influencing progress in e-mobility.
      • To encourage states to adopt a more proactive and ambitious approach towards e-mobility.
      • To support evidence-based policymaking for sustainable EV growth.

    Structure of the Index

    • IEMI 2025 comprises 16 indicators, classified as Outcome Indicators and Enabler Indicators, across three principal thematic areas.

    Overall and Group-wise Performance

    • Among the large states, Maharashtra ranked first and Karnataka second. They were the only two states in this group classified as Top Performers.
    • Among the other large states, Tamil Nadu scored 61, Madhya Pradesh 59, Odisha 55, and Andhra Pradesh 52. Telangana, Haryana, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh scored 51 each. All were classified as Front Runners.
    • Among the hilly and northeastern states, Manipur led with 46 points, followed by Tripura with 36 and Assam with 35. All three were classified as Emerging Performers.
    • In the Union Territories and city-states group, Delhi, Chandigarh and Goa were classified as Top Performers.
    • Between 2024 and 2025, the country’s highest score increased from 77 to 84, while the median score rose from 36 to 40.
    • Uttar Pradesh scored 51 overall, placing it in the Front Runner category. It scored 58 in the thematic area of progress in transport electrification, also qualifying as a Front Runner in this thematic area.

    हिंदी: Multidimensional poverty (बहुआयामी गरीबी)

    From the magazine

    The Global Multidimensional Poverty Index, 2026, released on October 12, 2026, is jointly published by the UN Development Programme (UNDP) and the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative (OPHI).

    Key Highlights of the Report

    • The 2026 Global Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) report provides a statistical update of the Global Multidimensional Poverty Index, covering 108 countries.
    • The report highlights that, of the 6.3 billion people living in these countries, 1.2 billion people - or 18.9 per cent - are living in acute multidimensional poverty.
    • The number of people living in multidimensional poverty has risen for the first time since the index was launched in 2010.
    • This year’s update of the global MPI database includes new surveys from 13 countries.
    • The report identifies 33 countries that halved their MPI over the observed periods, including India.
    • China achieved the fastest halving in the available data–in four years, between 2010 and 2014.
    • The publication of the 2026 Multidimensional Poverty Index Report was supported by a financial contribution from the Republic of Korea.
    • Severe poverty: 534 million people, representing 44.6% of multidimensionally poor people, experience severe multidimensional poverty. Another 952 million people are vulnerable to multidimensional poverty.
    • A total of 617 million children under 18 years of age constitute 51.5% of all multidimensionally poor people. Approximately one in three children is poor, compared with one in seven adults.
    • 83.3% of poor people (998 million) live in rural areas, compared with 16.7% (200 million) in urban areas. Poverty incidence is 28.7% in rural areas, against 7.0% in urban areas.
    • Sub-Saharan Africa has both the highest poverty incidence (51.4%) and the largest poor population (616 million). South Asia follows with approximately 393 million poor people, with poverty incidence of 19.9%.
    • Approximately 65.1% of multidimensionally poor people–779 million–live in middle-income countries.
    • In 21 countries, more than half the population is multidimensionally poor; 18 of these countries are in Sub-Saharan Africa.

    Countries at the top and bottom

    • Lowest poverty: Serbia, with a reported MPI of 0.000 and poverty incidence of 0.1%. The rounded MPI value does not mean poverty is entirely absent.
    • Highest poverty: Chad, with an MPI of 0.517 and a poverty incidence of 84.2%.
    • The five countries with the highest MPI values, arranged from highest to lowest, are:
    CountryMPI valuePoverty incidence
    Chad0.51784.2%
    Niger0.47079.9%
    Central African Republic0.46180.4%
    Burundi0.40975.1%
    Madagascar0.38668.4%

    India Specific Highlights

    • Based on its 2019–2021 survey, India’s MPI is 0.069, poverty incidence 16.4%, and deprivation intensity 42.0%; 4.2% of the population is severely poor and 18.7% vulnerable.
    • Between 2005–2006 and 2019–2021, its MPI declined from 0.283 to 0.069, while poverty incidence fell from 55.1% to 16.4%.
    • The report estimates that 237.849 million people (approximately 23.78 crore) as multidimensionally poor based on the 2024 population, the largest absolute number among the countries covered.
    • This is a population-based projection using the older survey poverty rate, not a new 2024 or 2026 poverty survey.
    About Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI)
    AspectDescription
    AboutThe MPI is a comprehensive measure that goes beyond income to capture the multiple and overlapping deprivations faced by individuals. It complements income-based poverty measures (like the USD 3.00/day threshold) by including non-monetary dimensions of poverty for better policy targeting.
    Structure3 Dimensions → 10 Indicators (covering health, education, and living standards).
    Weighting System- Each dimension has equal weight (1/3 each). - Health (2 indicators) → 1/6 weight each. - Education (2 indicators) → 1/6 weight each. - Standard of Living (6 indicators) → 1/18 weight each.
    RangeMPI values range from 0 to 1. Higher values indicate greater poverty.
    Identification of the PoorA person is considered multidimensionally poor if their deprivation scores ≥ 33.3% (1/3).

    Index of Services Production (ISP) Must knowPDF p. 105

    On 14 July 2026, NSO (MoSPI) released India's first Trial Index of Services Production, for April 2026, with base year 2024–25.

    • ISP: India's first high-frequency measure of short-term changes in formal services output.
    • Fills a gap: the Index of Industrial Production does not cover services.
    • Trial covered 19 sub-sectors (about 60% of services); no single overall ISP yet.
    • April 2026 leader: accommodation and food services, 37.2% year-on-year growth.
    • Fourteen sub-sectors had double-digit growth in April 2026.
    • Base year 2024–25, broadly aligned with the new CPI series (reference year 2024).

    Don't confuse IIP measures industry; ISP measures services. ISP base year 2024–25; CPI reference year 2024.

    Check Released July 14, 2026, but coverage is stated 'as of July 24, 2026'.

    हिंदी: Services sector (सेवा क्षेत्र) · Base year (आधार वर्ष)

    From the magazine

    On July 14, 2026, the National Statistics Office under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) released India’s first Trial Index of Services Production for April 2026.

    Introduction

    • The ISP is India’s first high-frequency macroeconomic indicator measuring short-term changes in the volume of formal services output relative to a base year. It fills a statistical gap because the Index of Industrial Production does not capture changes in services activity.

    First Trial Release

    • As of July 24, 2026, the trial covered 19 sub-sectors representing about 60% of the services economy, without a single overall ISP.
    • Fourteen sub-sectors recorded double-digit year-on-year growth in April 2026 compared with April 2025.

    Top-Performing Sub-sectors in April 2026

    • Accommodation and food services led year-on-year growth at 37.2%, followed by retail trade (30.8%), administrative and support services (28.7%), real estate (27.7%) and telecommunications (22.8%).

    Top-Performing Sub-sectors in 2025–26

    • During 2025–26, annual growth was 35.6% in accommodation and food services, 30.5% in retail trade, 25.1% in repair services, 23.6% in wholesale trade and 22.6% in road transport.

    Base Year

    • The base year is 2024–25, aligning the ISP with revised economic indicators and broadly with the new Consumer Price Index series, whose reference year is 2024.

    Women Towards Better Livelihoods Through Work and Enterprise PDF p. 110

    Government data (15 October 2026) show rising women's work: female labour force participation rose from 23.3% (2017–18) to 40.0% (2025).

    • Female LFPR (age 15+, usual status): 23.3% in 2017–18 to 40.0% in 2025.
    • Female WPR: 22.0% to 38.8% over the same period.
    • About 20 crore women aged 15+ were employed on average in 2025.
    • About 3.69 crore women-owned MSMEs (about 38%) as of October 2026.
    • Over 1.07 lakh recognised startups (about 48%) have at least one woman director or partner.
    • Women: about 70% of mobile manufacturing workforce; 15% of pilots; 29% of STEM researchers (2023–24).

    Don't confuse 2025 LFPR = 40.0%; 2025 WPR = 38.8%. Don't swap them.

    हिंदी: Labour Force Participation Rate (श्रम बल भागीदारी दर) · Worker Population Ratio (कामगार जनसंख्या अनुपात)

    From the magazine

    The expansion of women’s economic participation in India is evident across employment, entrepreneurship, manufacturing and research. The government presented key figures on women’s employment and entrepreneurship on October 15, 2026.

    Women’s Employment

    • For women aged 15 years and above, LFPR based on usual status—principal and subsidiary activities—was 23.3% in 2017–18. It stood at 40.0% in 2025. The corresponding female WPR figures for the same age group were 22.0% and 38.8%, respectively.
    • During 2025, an average of approximately 20 crore women aged 15 years and above were employed.

    Women’s Role in Entrepreneurship

    • Approximately 3.69 crore registered women-owned MSMEs as of October 2026, representing a share of approximately 38% (October 15, 2026).
    • The MSME dashboard dated 17 October 2026 recorded 3,71,97,598 registrations in the women’s category, including those under Udyam Registration and the Udyam Assist Platform. Their calculated share of the total 9,89,02,198 registrations was approximately 37.61%.
    • As of 31 March 2026, more than 1.07 lakh recognised startups had at least one woman director or partner, accounting for approximately 48% of all recognised startups.

    Participation in Technical and Highly Skilled Fields

    • As of July 2026, women accounted for approximately 70% of the direct workforce in mobile phone manufacturing.
    • In civil aviation, women were reported to constitute approximately 15% of India’s pilots, one of the highest proportions globally. According to figures reported in June 2025, women accounted for 15% of air traffic controllers, 11% of flight dispatchers and 33% of the Directorate General of Civil Aviation’s (DGCA) Flight Operations Inspectors.
    • According to Research and Development Statistics 2025–26, women’s share in research careers in Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) was 13% in 2000–01, 18.6% in 2020–21 and 29% in 2023–24. These figures relate to the research workforce.

    On 10 August 2026, NITI Aayog Vice-Chairman Ashok Kumar Lahiri launched a report on regulation of professional services, third in its Services Thematic Series.

    • Title: India's Services Sector: Insights on Regulatory Regime in Professional Services.
    • Launched August 10, 2026 by NITI Vice-Chairman Ashok Kumar Lahiri; PIB release August 14, 2026.
    • Third report under the Services Thematic Series.
    • Four-pronged strategy: professional development, best practices, moving up the value chain, emerging trends.

    हिंदी: Professional services (व्यावसायिक सेवाएँ)

    From the magazine

    On August 10, 2026, NITI Aayog Vice-Chairman Ashok Kumar Lahiri launched India’s Services Sector: Insights on Regulatory Regime in Professional Services. It is the third report under the Services Thematic Series; the related PIB release was published on August 14, 2026. It identifies reforms that could improve regulatory clarity, professional mobility, recognition of qualifications and international competitiveness.

    Four-Pronged Strategy

    1. Continuous Professional Development for Professionals: Structured CPD and lifelong learning can maintain professional competence as technology and industry practices change. 2. Adoption of Best Practices in Professional Services: Regulators should publish clear eligibility rules, contact details, processing timelines, decisions and review mechanisms and should hold regular consultations. 3. Elevate Professional Services within the Services Value Chain: India should move from routine, cost-based delivery towards research, engineering design, legal analytics, advanced financial modelling and strategic consulting. 4. Advance Emerging Trends in Professional Services: Professionals should build capabilities in artificial intelligence, automation, ESG reporting, carbon accounting, climate-risk assessment, sustainable finance and supply-chain advisory. The report cautions that adopting best practices does not mean mechanically copying foreign laws.

    Income Mobility in India (2014–2025) PDF p. 111

    A study of CMIE household data (2014–2025) finds more families slipping down the income ladder: downward mobility rose from 14% to 26.8%.

    • Based on CMIE Consumer Pyramids Household Survey; same households tracked 2014 to 2025.
    • Groups by 2014 income: Top 10%, Next 40%, Bottom 50%.
    • Downward mobility: 14% (2015) to 26.8% (2025).
    • Upward mobility: 14.1% to 23.5%.
    • Households with no change fell from over 70% to below 50%.
    • Rural stress: nearly 29% of rural households worse off in 2025 than in 2014.

    Don't confuse Downward mobility rose more (14% to 26.8%) than upward (14.1% to 23.5%).

    हिंदी: Income mobility (आय गतिशीलता)

    From the magazine

    • The study is based on real per capita income data from the CMIE Consumer Pyramids Household Survey, using a balanced panel of households observed from 2014 to 2025.
    • The analysis classifies households according to their 2014 per capita income rank, into three groups: Top 10%; Next 40%; and Bottom 50%.
    • A household is considered:
      • Upwardly mobile if it moves to a higher group,
      • Downwardly mobile if it moves to a lower group,
      • Stable if it remains in the same group.
    • The share of households facing downward mobility rose from 14% in 2015 to 26.8% in 2025.
    • The share of households with no change fell sharply from over 70% to below 50%.
    • Upward mobility also increased, from 14.1% to 23.5%, but this improvement is gradual and trail in rise in downward movement.
    • Rural India shows the sharpest stress. By 2025, nearly 29% of rural households were worse off than in 2014.
    • By 2025, around one-fourth or more of households in these groups were worse off than in 2014.

    India's FDI Inflow in FY 2024–25 Must knowPDF p. 111

    India's FDI inflows rose 14% to USD 81.04 billion (provisional) in FY 2024–25; services drew the most, and Singapore was the top source.

    • FDI: USD 36.05 billion (FY 2013–14) to USD 81.04 billion (FY 2024–25, provisional).
    • Up 14% from USD 71.28 billion in FY 2023–24.
    • Top sectors: services 19%, computer software and hardware 16%, trading 8%.
    • Top States: Maharashtra 39%, Karnataka 13%, Delhi 12%.

    Memory aid Source order S-M-U: Singapore 30, Mauritius 17, US 11.

    हिंदी: Foreign Direct Investment (प्रत्यक्ष विदेशी निवेश)

    From the magazine

    • According to government estimates, FDI inflows have seen a steady rise from USD 36.05 billion in FY 2013–14 to USD 81.04 billion (provisional) in FY 2024–25, marking a 14% increase from USD 71.28 billion in FY 2023–24.
    • The services sector emerged as the top recipient of FDI equity in FY 2024–25, attracting 19% of total inflows, followed by computer software and hardware (16%) and trading (8%).
      • FDI into the services sector rose by 40.77% to USD 9.35 billion from USD 6.64 billion in the previous year.
    • India is also becoming a hub for manufacturing FDI, which grew by 18% in FY 2024–25, reaching USD 19.04 billion compared with USD 16.12 billion in FY 2023–24.
    • Maharashtra accounted for the highest share (39%) of total FDI equity inflows in FY 2024–25, followed by Karnataka (13%) and Delhi (12%).
    • Among source countries, Singapore led with a 30% share, followed by Mauritius (17%) and the United States (11%).
    • Over the last eleven financial years (2014–25), India attracted FDI worth USD 748.78 billion, reflecting a 143% increase over the previous eleven years (2003– 14), which saw USD 308.38 billion in inflows.

    News in Shorts Must knowPDF pp. 111–112

    Short economic news: first soil carbon payments to farmers, sugar export ban, first mega greenfield shipyard, IST rules, gig-worker grievance system and more.

    • Sugar exports moved from 'Restricted' to 'Prohibited' till September 30, 2026 (DGFT, May 13, 2026).

    • IST Rules, 2026 notified August 27, 2026; IST = UTC+5:30, meridian 82°30′E passes through UP.
    • SARTHAK-PDS: ₹25,530 crore central outlay, approved May 27, 2026, till 31 March 2031.

    From the magazine

    First Soil Carbon Payments to Farmers in India

    • An initiative in India has linked soil carbon sequestration and reductions in greenhouse gas emissions with additional income for farmers. Payments based on verified carbon credits have begun for farmers in Punjab and Haryana.
    • A payment event was held at Punjab Agricultural University, Ludhiana, on 14 September 2026. Dr M. L. Jat, Secretary, Department of Agricultural Research and Education (DARE), and Director General, Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR), initiated the Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT). Arrangements for digital payments totalling more than ₹2.9 crore to 2,550 farmers in Punjab and Haryana were announced.
    • Grow Indigo launched the ‘Aadi’ farmer carbon programme in 2019 under ICAR’s technical guidance. During 2019–2022, participating farmers adopted practices such as direct-seeded rice, reduced tillage and crop residue management.

    India Bans Sugar Exports

    • India has prohibited the export of sugar with immediate effect until September 30, 2026, or until further orders, whichever was earlier. The Directorate General of Foreign Trade’s officially notified an “Amendment in Export Policy of Sugar” on May 13, 2026.
    • The decision changed sugar exports from the “Restricted” category to the “Prohibited” category.
    • The latest order remained effective till September 30, 2026, or until the government issued further directions.

    India’s First Mega Greenfield Shipyard

    • India has taken an important step towards becoming a major global shipbuilding nation with the proposed development of India’s first mega Greenfield shipyard at Thoothukudi, Tamil Nadu. A tripartite Memorandum of Understanding was signed on 20 April 2026 for this project among HD Korea Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering Co. Ltd., National Shipbuilding & Heavy Industries Park, Tamil Nadu Limited, and Sagarmala Finance Corporation Limited under the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways.

    India Adopts “One Nation, One Time” Framework

    • The Department of Consumer Affairs notified the Legal Metrology (Indian Standard Time) Rules, 2026 on August 27, 2026.
    • IST will become the standard time reference for official documents, commercial operations, legal contracts, transport and financial activities.

    Basic Facts About Indian Standard Time

    • IST is 5 hours and 30 minutes ahead of Coordinated Universal Time, or UTC+5:30.
    • Its conventional geographical basis is the 82°30′ east longitude, also written as 82.5° E.
    • The Standard Meridian passes through Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Odisha and Andhra Pradesh.

    NABL Accreditation Scheme for Mobile Food Testing Laboratories

    • On August 10, 2026, the National Accreditation Board for Testing and Calibration Laboratories (NABL) launched what the government described as India’s first accreditation scheme specifically for Mobile Food Testing Laboratories.
    • It was launched under the Integrated Assessment Programme at the “Gunvatta Samanvaya” event in New Delhi.

    India’s First Digital Grievance Redressal System for Gig Workers

    • Karnataka has become the first State in India to launch a government-backed digital grievance redressal system for gig workers (Karnataka Platform Based Gig Workers Welfare Board).
    • Gig workers can now lodge complaints through the Integrated Public Grievance Redressal System portal.

    Cabinet Approves Technology-Driven SARTHAK-PDS Scheme

    • The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, approved the continuation and integration of the SARTHAK-PDS Scheme on May 27, 2026. The scheme has a central outlay of ₹25,530 crore and will be implemented during the 16th Finance Commission award cycle, up to 31 March 2031.

    Government Notifies Two New SEZs in Puducherry

    • The Government of India has notified two new Special Economic Zones in the Union Territory of Puducherry. The notification was issued by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry on May 27, 2026, after the proposals were approved by the Board of Approval for SEZs under the Department of Commerce in its 137th meeting held on February 27, 2026. These two SEZs are aimed at accelerating investment, manufacturing activity and job creation in Puducherry.

    M S Sahoo Committee for NPS Reforms

    • On 13 January 2026, the Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA) has constituted a high-level committee to formulate guidelines and regulations to enable a framework for assured payouts under the National Pension System (NPS).
    • The committee will be chaired by Dr. M. S. Sahoo, founder of Dr. Sahoo Regulatory Chambers and former Chairperson of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI).
    • The 15-member panel includes a diverse group of experts.

    Kerala: Declared an ‘Extreme Poverty–Free’ State

    • Kerala Chief Minister Pinarayi Vijayan, on 1 November 2025, on the occasion of ‘Kerala Piravi’, declared the state ‘extreme poverty–free’ in a special session of the Legislative Assembly. With this declaration, Kerala became the first state in India to achieve this status. Pinarayi Vijayan described this year’s Kerala Piravi as “the birth of a new era” for Kerala.

    Union Budget 2026–27 Must knowPDF pp. 113–117

    Nirmala Sitharaman presented Union Budget 2026–27 on 1 February 2026 around '3 Kartavyas'; fiscal deficit 4.3% of GDP and public capex ₹12.2 lakh crore.

    • Total expenditure ₹53.47 lakh crore (+7.7%); fiscal deficit 4.3% of GDP (2025–26 RE: 4.4%).
    • Debt-to-GDP 55.6%; target about 50% by March 2031; revenue deficit 1.5%.
    • Public capex ₹12.2 lakh crore (2025–26: ₹11.2 lakh crore).
    • Defence has the highest ministry allocation: ₹7.85 lakh crore (15% of spending).
    • VB-G RAM G gets the highest scheme allocation, ₹95,692 crore; MGNREGS still ₹30,000 crore.
    • New: Biopharma SHAKTI ₹10,000 crore; CCUS ₹20,000 crore; seven HSR corridors incl. Delhi–Varanasi.

    Don't confuse Interest is 26% of total expenditure but 20% in the 'Rupee Goes To' chart; the two use different bases.

    Check Finance Commission grants for 2026–27 are given as ₹1.4 lakh crore in one place and ₹1.29 lakh crore in another.

    हिंदी: Fiscal deficit (राजकोषीय घाटा) · Capital expenditure (पूंजीगत व्यय) · Revenue deficit (राजस्व घाटा)

    From the magazine

    Union Minister for Finance and Corporate Affairs, Smt. Nirmala Sitharaman, tabled the Union Budget 2026-27 in the Parliament on February 01, 2026. The highlights of the budget are as follows:

    Core Theme: 3 Kartavyas

    • The Budget targets faster and more resilient growth by raising productivity and competitiveness amid global volatility.
    • The Budget aims to build people’s capacities so citizens become partners in prosperity.
    • The Budget seeks inclusive access to resources and opportunities for every region and section under Sabka Saath, Sabka Vikas.

    Macro & Fiscal Snapshot (BE 2026–27)

    • Non-debt receipts are estimated at ₹36.5 lakh crore, and total expenditure is estimated at ₹53.5 lakh crore.
    • Centre’s net tax receipts are estimated at ₹28.7 lakh crore.
    • Gross market borrowings are estimated at ₹17.2 lakh crore, and net borrowings (dated securities) are estimated at ₹11.7 lakh crore.
    • Fiscal deficit is estimated at 4.3% of GDP, while RE 2025–26 keeps fiscal deficit at 4.4% of GDP.
    • Debt-to-GDP is estimated at 55.6% (BE 2026–27) versus 56.1% (RE 2025–26).

    PART-A: Interventions

    Kartavya 1: Growth Push (6 Interventions)

    (1) Scale manufacturing in 7 strategic/frontier sectors

    • The Budget launches Biopharma SHAKTI with ₹10,000 crore (5 years) to build India as a global biopharma hub.
    • The Budget expands biopharma capacity via 3 new NIPERs, upgrading 7 NIPERs, and 1,000+ accredited clinical trial sites.
    • The Budget announces India Semiconductor Mission 2.0 for equipment/materials, full-stack IP, and supply-chain strengthening with industry-led R&D and training.
    • The Budget raises Electronics Components Manufacturing Scheme outlay to ₹40,000 crore.
    • The Budget proposes Rare Earth Corridors in Odisha, Kerala, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu for activities ranging from mining to manufacturing.
    • The Budget supports 3 Chemical Parks through a challenge-mode, cluster-based plug-and-play model.
    • The Budget strengthens capital goods manufacturing through Hi-Tech Tool Rooms, CIE equipment scheme, and a Container Manufacturing scheme with ₹10,000+ crore (5 years).
    • The Budget announces an Integrated Textile Programme, including the National Fibre Scheme, cluster modernisation, challenge-mode Mega Textile Parks, and Mahatma Gandhi Gram Swaraj for khadi/handloom/handicrafts. (2) Rejuvenate legacy industrial sectors
    • The Budget announces a scheme to revive 200 legacy industrial clusters through tech and infrastructure upgrades. (3) Create “Champion SMEs”
    • The Budget introduces an SME Growth Fund of ₹10,000 crore to build future champion firms.
    • The Budget tops up the Self-Reliant India Fund by ₹2,000 crore for micro-enterprise risk capital.
    • The Budget proposes training ‘Corporate Mitras’ through professional institutes to provide support in Tier-II/III areas. (4) Infrastructure push
    • Public capex is raised to ₹12.2 lakh crore in FY 2026–27.
    • An Infrastructure Risk Guarantee Fund is proposed to improve private developer confidence.
    • CPSE real-estate recycling is proposed through dedicated REITs.
    • A new Dedicated Freight Corridor is proposed from Dankuni to Surat.
    • 20 new National Waterways are to be operationalised in 5 years, starting with NW-5 (Odisha).
    • Regional training centres and ship repair ecosystems at Varanasi and Patna are proposed.
    • A Coastal Cargo Promotion Scheme targets raising waterways/coastal shipping share from 6% to 12% by 2047.
    • A Seaplane VGF Scheme is proposed for tourism and remote connectivity. (5) Energy security
    • ₹20,000 crore (5 years) is allocated for Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage (CCUS) technologies. (6) City Economic Regions (CERs)
    • ₹5,000 crore per CER (5 years) is announced through challenge-mode, reform-cum-results based financing.
    • Seven High-Speed Rail corridors are proposed: Mumbai–Pune, Pune–Hyderabad, Hyderabad– Bengaluru, Hyderabad–Chennai, Chennai– Bengaluru, Delhi–Varanasi and Varanasi–Siliguri.

    Banking & Investment Ecosystem

    • A High-Level Committee on Banking for Viksit Bharat is proposed.
    • The restructuring PFC and REC is proposed to improve scale and efficiency.
    • A review of FEMA (Non-debt Instruments) Rules is proposed for a user-friendly FDI framework.
    • An incentive of ₹100 crore is announced for a single municipal bond issuance above ₹1,000 crore.

    Kartavya 2: Aspirations and Capacity

    • A high-powered Education to Employment and Enterprise Standing Committee is proposed with a services-sector focus.
    • Allied health capacity is expanded through new/ upgraded institutions and 1,00,000 Allied Health Professionals (AHP) in 5 years.
    • Five Regional Medical Hubs are proposed for medical tourism.
    • Three All India Institutes of Ayurveda are proposed.
    • Veterinary capacity is expanded by over 20,000 professionals, and a loan-linked subsidy supports private veterinary colleges/hospitals/labs.
    • AVGC labs are planned through IICT Mumbai in 15,000 schools and 500 colleges.
    • Five University Townships are proposed near industrial/logistics corridors.
    • A girls’ hostel in every district is proposed through VGF and capital support.
    • Tourism measures include upgrading NCHMCT, training 10,000 guides, and establishing a National Destination Digital Knowledge Grid.
    • 15 archaeological sites are proposed for experiential cultural tourism, and the Khelo India Mission is proposed for sports transformation.

    Kartavya 3: Sabka Saath, Sabka Vikas (Targeted Areas)

    • The budget aims to enhance farmer’s through 500 reservoirs/Amrit Sarovars and support for high-value crops including coconut, sandalwood, cocoa and cashew, along with a Coconut Promotion Scheme.
    • Bharat-VISTAAR is proposed as a multilingual AI tool integrating AgriStack and ICAR practice packages.
    • Divyangjan Kaushal Yojana is proposed for job-ready roles in IT, AVGC, hospitality, and Food & Beverage services.
    • NIMHANS-2 is proposed in North India, and mental health institutes in Ranchi and Tezpur are to be upgraded.
    • The Purvodaya/NER focus includes an East Coast Industrial Corridor, 5 tourism destinations, 4,000 e-buses, and a Buddhist Circuit Scheme in NE states.
    • ₹1.4 lakh crore is provided as Finance Commission grants for states in FY 2026–27 (as per 16th FC).

    PART –B: Overall Fiscal Framework

    • The Union Government is estimated to spend ₹53.47 lakh crore in 2026–27, representing a 7.7% increase over the Revised Estimates (RE) of 2025– 26.
    • Interest payments constitute about 26% of total expenditure and absorb nearly 40% of revenue receipts, highlighting persistent debt-servicing pressures.
    • Total receipts (excluding borrowings) are estimated at ₹36.51 lakh crore, marking a 7.2% increase over the RE of 2025–26, with tax revenue expected to grow by 8%.
    • The government has projected nominal GDP growth at 10% for 2026–27, reflecting expectations of sustained real growth and moderate inflation.

    Deficit and Debt Targets

    • The revenue deficit is targeted at 1.5% of GDP, unchanged from the revised estimate of 2025–26, indicating continued emphasis on fiscal consolidation.
    • The fiscal deficit is targeted at 4.3% of GDP, marginally lower than 4.4% of GDP in 2025–26 (RE).
    • The Centre has reiterated its commitment to reducing outstanding liabilities to around 50% of GDP by March 2031, with liabilities estimated at 55.6% of GDP in 2026–27.

    Taxation Proposals

    • Income tax slabs remain unchanged for Assessment Year 2026–27, maintaining stability in the personal tax regime.
    • A tax holiday until 2047 has been granted to foreign companies providing global cloud services using Indian data centres, subject to routing services to Indian customers through Indian resellers.
    • The tax holiday for IFSC units and Offshore Banking Units has been extended from 10 years to 20 years, with income taxed at 15% thereafter.
    • All share buybacks are proposed to be taxed as capital gains, with an additional buyback tax on promoters, raising the effective tax rate to 22% for corporate promoters and 30% for non-corporate promoters.

    • Securities Transaction Tax (STT) rates have been increased for options and futures, signalling a calibrated tightening in capital market taxation.
    • Interest expenditure deductions against dividend income or mutual fund income have been withdrawn.
    • Minimum Alternate Tax (MAT) rate has been reduced from 15% to 14%, while MAT credit accumulation is discontinued from April 2026.
    • A Foreign Assets Disclosure Scheme, 2026 has been introduced for small taxpayers, offering graded relief and immunity subject to compliance.
    • TCS rates on education and medical remittances, and overseas tour packages have been reduced to 2%, easing the burden on households.

    Finance and Financial Sector Reforms

    • A High-Level Committee on Banking for Viksit Bharat will be constituted to review the banking sector.
    • The FEMA Non-Debt Instruments Rules will be simplified to facilitate foreign investment.
    • Persons Resident Outside India (PROI) will be allowed to invest up to 10% in listed Indian companies under the Portfolio Investment Scheme.
    • A market-making framework for corporate bonds and incentives for municipal bond issuance have been announced to deepen debt markets.

    Industry, MSMEs, and Commerce

    • A scheme will be launched to revive 200 legacy industrial clusters through modern technology and infrastructure.
    • To create Champion SMEs, the government announced a ₹10,000 crore SME Growth Fund, top-up of the Self-Reliant India Fund, and liquidity support.

    Infrastructure and Connectivity

    • Public capital expenditure has been increased to ₹12.2 lakh crore, up from ₹11.2 lakh crore in 2025–26.
    • An Infrastructure Risk Guarantee Fund will be established to crowd in private investment.
    • New initiatives include five tourism destinations in Purvodaya States, 4,000 electric buses, 20 new National Waterways, and a Surat–Dankuni freight corridor.
    • Seven high-speed rail corridors and City Economic Regions (CERs) will be developed to support urban-industrial growth.

    Education, Labour, and Human Capital

    • Five university townships will be created along industrial and logistics corridors.
    • A Standing Committee on Education to Employment and Enterprise will assess skill gaps and the impact of artificial intelligence on jobs.
    • Support will be extended to creative technologies through AVGC labs in 15,000 schools and 500 colleges.

    Energy, Technology, and Strategic Sectors

    • The Electronics Components Manufacturing Scheme outlay has been increased to ₹40,000 crore.
    • Rare Earth Corridors will be established in Odisha, Kerala, Andhra Pradesh, and Tamil Nadu.
    • ₹20,000 crore has been allocated over five years for carbon capture, utilisation, and storage, and Semiconductor Mission 2.0 will be launched.

    Health, Pharmaceuticals, and Agriculture

    • New Allied Health Professional institutions, five medical tourism hubs, and three All India Institutes of Ayurveda will be established.
    • The Biopharma SHAKTI Scheme, with an outlay of ₹10,000 crore will promote domestic production of biologics and biosimilars.
    • Agricultural measures include incentives for cooperative members, support for animal husbandry, and a Coconut Promotion Scheme.

    Federal Transfers and Expenditure Composition

    • Transfers to States will increase to ₹26.21 lakh crore, including ₹15.26 lakh crore as tax devolution and ₹10.94 lakh crore as grants and loans.
    • Capital expenditure loans to States amount to ₹1.85 lakh crore.

    Overall Assessment

    • The Union Budget 2026–27 reflects a continuation of fiscal consolidation, capex-led growth, and structural reforms, while aligning macroeconomic stability with the long-term vision of Viksit Bharat.

    Expenditure Pattern: Revenue vs Capital

    • Capital expenditure, which creates government assets or reduces liabilities, is projected to grow by 11.5% in 2026–27 over the Revised Estimates (RE) of 2025–26, reinforcing the capex-led growth strategy.
    • Revenue expenditure, which includes salaries, subsidies, and interest payments, is expected to rise by 6.6%, indicating relatively tighter control over consumption-oriented spending.
    • Interest payments alone account for 26% of total expenditure, underlining the structural challenge of high debt servicing costs.
    Growth in Expenditure Components (2026–27)

    Interest Payments~10%

    Receipts Structure for 2026–27

    • Total receipts, excluding borrowings, are estimated at ₹36.51 lakh crore, reflecting a 7.2% increase over 2025–26 (RE), mainly driven by higher net tax revenue.
    • Gross tax revenue is budgeted to grow by 8%, which is lower than the nominal GDP growth estimate of 10%, suggesting conservative tax buoyancy assumptions.

    Tax Revenue Trends

    • Corporation tax collections are expected to grow by 11%, reflecting stable corporate profitability.
    • Income tax collections are projected to grow by 11.7%, despite a revenue shortfall in 2025–26, following tax rate rationalisation.
    • CGST revenue is expected to grow by 6.3%, lower than overall tax growth, indicating moderate consumption expansion.

    Expenditure Composition for 2026–27

    • Total expenditure is estimated at ₹53.47 lakh crore, an increase of 7.7% over 2025–26 (RE).
    • Central Sector Schemes account for ₹17.72 lakh crore, while Centrally Sponsored Schemes (CSS) account for ₹9.90 lakh crore, with CSS showing a higher growth rate of 17.1%.

    Committed Expenditure and Transfers

    • Pension expenditure in 2026–27 is estimated at ₹2.96 lakh crore, rising modestly by 3%.
    • Interest payments are projected at ₹14.04 lakh crore, consuming over one-fourth of total expenditure.
    • Special loans to States for capital expenditure amount to ₹1.85 lakh crore, supporting state-level capex.
    • Finance Commission grants for 2026–27 are estimated at ₹1.29 lakh crore, about 15% lower than 2025–26 (RE), as per 16th Finance Commission recommendations.

    Expenditure by Major Ministries

    • The top 13 ministries account for 54% of total Union expenditure in 2026–27.
    • The Ministry of Defence has the highest allocation at ₹7.85 lakh crore, constituting 15% of total expenditure.
    • Other major allocations include Road Transport and Highways, Railways, and Home Affairs, reflecting emphasis on infrastructure, logistics, and internal security.

    Ministry-wise Expenditure Priorities

    • The Ministry of Defence allocation increases by ₹52,166 crore (7%) in 2026–27 over 2025–26 (RE), reflecting a sustained focus on national security.
    • Capital outlay for defence services rises sharply to ₹2,19,306 crore, marking a 17.6% increase, reinforcing indigenisation and modernisation of the armed forces.

    Subsidy Expenditure

    • Total subsidy expenditure in 2026–27 is estimated at ₹4,54,773 crore, representing a 3.1% decline from 2025–26 (RE).
    • Food subsidy (₹2,27,629 crore) and fertiliser subsidy (₹1,70,799 crore) together constitute 87% of the total subsidy bill.

    Flagship Schemes and Sectoral Allocations

    • VB-G RAM G receives the highest allocation of ₹95,692 crore in 2026–27, following the replacement of MGNREGA by the VB-G RAM G Act in December 2025.
    • Despite replacement, MGNREGS is also allocated ₹30,000 crore in 2026–27, indicating a transition phase.

    Loans to States for Capital Expenditure

    • ₹1,85,000 crore has been budgeted as interest-free loans to States for capital expenditure in 2026– 27, up from ₹1,44,000 crore (RE) in 2025–26.

    Deficits and Public Debt

    • The fiscal deficit for 2026–27 is estimated at 4.3% of GDP, marginally lower than 4.4% in 2025–26, signalling continued fiscal consolidation.
    • The revenue deficit remains unchanged at 1.5% of GDP, indicating continued borrowing for recurring expenditure.
    • Outstanding liabilities of the Centre are estimated at 55.6% of GDP, down from the pandemic peak of 61% in 2020–21.
    • The government aims to reduce liabilities to around 50% ±1% of GDP by March 2031.

    Economic Survey 2025–26 Must knowPDF pp. 117–120

    Economic Survey 2025–26 urges 'entrepreneurial policymaking under uncertainty' and projects FY27 real GDP growth of 6.8%–7.2%, with potential growth near 7%.

    • First Advance Estimates: FY26 real GDP growth 7.4%, GVA 7.3%; fastest-growing major economy for the fourth year.
    • Reorganised into 17 chapters; special essays on AI and quality of life in cities.
    • Average CPI inflation 1.7% (April–December 2025), lowest since the CPI series began.
    • Forex reserves USD 701.4 billion (16 January 2026), about 11 months of import cover.
    • Global Innovation Index rank 38th in 2025 (66th in 2019).
    • Extreme poverty fell to 5.3% in 2022–23 (revised World Bank line).

    Don't confuse FY26 growth 7.4% (First Advance Estimates) vs FY27 projection 6.8%–7.2% vs potential growth about 7%.

    हिंदी: Economic Survey (आर्थिक सर्वेक्षण) · Potential growth (संभावित वृद्धि)

    From the magazine

    • The Economic Survey 2025–26 urges a shift to entrepreneurial policymaking under uncertainty, where the State acts early, structures risk, learns through experimentation, and adapts without paralysis.
    • The Survey says governance is moving from compliance-driven regulation to capability-driven state capacity, signalling an emerging entrepreneurial State.
    • Despite post-COVID shocks, including global trade disruption and US tariffs in April 2025, the Indian economy has shown strong macroeconomic resilience.
    • The Survey anticipates real GDP growth above 7% in FY 2025–26 and expects growth to stay near this level in the following year.
    • It highlights a paradox in which India’s best macro performance in decades comes amid a global system that no longer reliably rewards discipline with currency stability, capital inflows, or insulation.
    • The Survey argues that India’s scale population of 145 crore, and democracy make it unrealistic to copy external development templates in a geopolitically uncertain world.
    • It states that global headwinds can become tailwinds if the State, private sector, and households align and sustain a national effort.
    • The Survey outlines three global scenarios for 2026: managed disorder, disorderly multipolar breakdown, and a low-probability, high-impact shock cascade worse that of 2008.
    • Across scenarios, it says India is relatively better placed due to a large domestic market, a less financialised growth model, strong reserves, and credible strategic autonomy, though insulation is not complete.
    • It warns of a common risk of disrupted capital flows and sustained rupee pressure that could last beyond one year.
    • The Survey says India must strengthen foreign currency earnings through exports and investor confidence to finance a rising import bill with rising incomes.
    • It recommends supply stability, strategic buffers, diversified trade routes, and alternative payment systems, calling for strategic sobriety over defensive pessimism.
    • It stresses that India must balance long-term growth with short-term shock absorption, captured in its “marathon and sprint” framing.
    • The Survey emphasises process reforms alongside policy reforms because administrative processes shape citizen-state interaction and reform outcomes.
    • It notes that recent deregulation and smart regulation by States show the State can shift from controller to enabler of growth.
    • It links State capacity, society, and deregulation as key pillars for Viksit Bharat and greater global influence.
    • It urges the State to upskill and mentally prepare for a harsher global environment where rules are changing.
    • It concludes that long-term success requires resilience, innovation, and delayed gratification rather than quick fixes.
    • The Survey has been reorganised into 17 chapters based on depth and time-relevance, making it broader and longer than earlier editions.
    • It includes special essays on AI, quality of life in Indian cities, and how State capacity and the private sector can build strategic resilience and indispensability.

    Key Highlights of Economic Survey 2025–26

    State of the Economy

    • The global economic environment remains fragile, with elevated risks from geopolitical tensions, trade fragmentation, and financial vulnerabilities, and some shocks may appear with a time lag.
    • The First Advance Estimates project real GDP growth at 7.4% and GVA growth at 7.3% for FY26, sustaining India’s position as the fastest-growing major economy for the fourth consecutive year.
    • Potential growth for India is assessed at around 7%, while FY27 real GDP growth is projected at 6.8%–7.2%.
    • Private Final Consumption Expenditure rises by 7.0% in FY26 and reaches 61.5% of GDP, the highest share since 2012 (also seen in FY23), supported by low inflation, stable employment, and rising real purchasing power.
    • Gross Fixed Capital Formation grows by 7.8% in FY26, with investment’s share steady at about 30% of GDP, aided by sustained public capex and revival in private investment signals.
    • The services sector remains the main growth engine, with services GVA rising 9.3% in H1 FY26 and estimated at 9.1% for the full year.

    Fiscal Developments

    • The Survey states that credible fiscal consolidation has reinforced macro-fiscal confidence and is linked with three sovereign credit rating upgrades in 2025 by Morningstar DBRS, S&P Global Ratings, and R&I.
    • The Centre’s revenue receipts strengthen to 9.2% of GDP in FY25 (PA), up from an average of about 8.5% of GDP during FY16–FY20.
    • Non-corporate tax collections have risen structurally, from about 2.4% of GDP in the pre-pandemic period to around 3.3% in the post-pandemic period.
    • The direct tax base expands, with income tax returns filed increasing from 6.9 crore (FY22) to 9.2 crore (FY25), reflecting higher compliance and technology-enabled administration.
    • Gross GST collections during April–December 2025 stand at ₹17.4 lakh crore, recording 6.7% YoY growth, while e-way bill volumes grow 21% YoY in the same period, indicating robust transactions.
    • The Centre’s effective capital expenditure increases to about 4.0% of GDP in FY25, up from a pre-pandemic average of 2.7% and post-pandemic level of about 3.9%.
    • Through Special Assistance to States for Capital Expenditure (SASCI), states are incentivised to maintain capital spending at around 2.4% of GDP in FY25.
    • The combined State fiscal deficit edges up to 3.2% of GDP in FY25, from about 2.8% in the post-pandemic period, reflecting emerging pressures.
    • India reduces its general government debt-to-GDP ratio by about 7.1 percentage points since 2020, while maintaining high public investment.

    Monetary Management and Financial Intermediation

    • The Survey reports robust monetary-financial performance in FY26 (April–December 2025), supported by policy actions and structural resilience.
    • Scheduled commercial banks’ asset quality has improved sharply, with GNPA at 2.2% (September 2025) and net NPA at 0.5% (September 2025), both at multi-decadal/record-low levels.
    • Outstanding credit growth of SCBs rises to 14.5% YoY (as of 31 December 2025) compared with 11.2% (December 2024).

    Financial Inclusion and Market Deepening

    • Under PMJDY, 55.02 crore bank accounts are opened as of March 2025, including 36.63 crore in rural and semi-urban areas.
    • Financial participation broadened as unique investors crossed 12 crore in September 2025, with nearly 25% being women.
    • During FY26 (till December 2025), 235 lakh demat accounts are added, taking total demat accounts beyond 21.6 crore.
    • The mutual fund investor base expanded to 5.9 crore unique investors (December 2025), with significant participation from non-Tier I and Tier II locations.
    • The Survey highlights the role of GIFT City as an enabling ecosystem to attract and channel global capital.
    • The Survey notes international validation of regulatory quality through the IMF–World Bank FSAP (2025), which found the system resilient and diversified, with adequate buffers under stress scenarios.

    External Sector

    • India’s share of global merchandise exports nearly 1.0% (2005) to 1.8% (2024), while doubled from its share of global commercial services exports rose from 2.0% to 4.3% over the same period.
    • India’s total exports reached a record USD 825.3 billion in FY25, growing by 6.1% YoY, driven mainly by services.
    • Services exports touched an all-time high of USD 387.6 billion in FY25, growing by 13.6%, reinforcing India’s strength in technology and business services.
    • India remained the world’s largest recipient of remittances, with inflows of USD 135.4 billion in FY25, helping offset the merchandise trade deficit.
    • The current account deficit remained moderate, with CAD at around 1.3% of GDP in Q2 FY26, supported by services and remittances.
    • Forex reserves rose to USD 701.4 billion (as of 16 January 2026), providing about 11 months of import cover and covering over 94% of external debt.
    • Gross FDI inflows reached USD 64.7 billion (April–November 2025) despite subdued global investment conditions.
    • India rank 4th globally in Greenfield investment announcements (2024) and emerges as the largest destination for Greenfield digital investments (2020–24).

    Inflation: Tamed and Anchored

    • India recorded the lowest headline CPI inflation since the inception of the CPI series, with average inflation at 1.7% during April–December 2025.
    • The moderation in inflation was primarily driven by declining food and fuel prices, which together constitute 52.7% of the CPI basket.
    • Among major Emerging Markets and Developing Economies, India achieved one of the sharpest disinflations, with headline inflation declining by 1.8 percentage points in 2025 over 2024.

    Agriculture and Food Management

    • The livestock sector recorded strong structural growth, with its GVA rising by nearly 195% between FY15 and FY24, while fish production, increased by over 140% during 2014–2024.
    • Benefiting from a good monsoon, India’s foodgrain production was estimated at 3,577.3 LMT in AY 2024–25, an increase of 254.3 LMT over the previous year, led by rice, wheat, maize, and coarse cereals.
    • Horticulture, contributing about 33% of agricultural GVA, emerged as a major growth driver, with production reaching 362.08 MT in 2024–25, surpassing foodgrain output.
    • Agricultural marketing efficiency improved through AMI under ISAM and the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund, while e-NAM enhanced price discovery by onboarding 1.79 crore farmers, 2.72 crore traders, and 4,698 FPOs across 1,522 mandis by December 31, 2025.
    • Farmers’ incomes were supported through assured MSP, PM-KISAN, and PM-Kisan Maandhan Yojana, with ₹4.09 lakh crore disbursed under PM-KISAN and 24.92 lakh farmers enrolled in PMKMY.

    Services Sector: From Stability to New Frontiers

    • The services sector’s share rose to 53.6% of GDP in H1 FY26, while its share in GVA reached a record 56.4%, reflecting the rising role of modern and digitally delivered services.
    • India became the world’s seventh-largest services exporter, with its share in global services trade rising from 2% in 2005 to 4.3% in 2024.
    • Services accounted for over 80% of total FDI inflows during FY23–FY25, reinforcing India’s attractiveness in globally tradable services.

    Industry: Structural Transformation and Global Integration

    • Industrial GVA grew by 7.0% in H1 FY26, despite persistent global headwinds.
    • Manufacturing GVA growth accelerated to 7.72% in Q1 and 9.13% in Q2 FY26, indicating a structural recovery.
    • PLI Schemes across 14 sectors attracted over ₹2.0 lakh crore investment, generated ₹18.7 lakh crore of incremental production, and created over 12.6 lakh jobs.
    • India’s Global Innovation Index rank improved to 38th in 2025, up from 66th in 2019.
    • The India Semiconductor Mission advanced domestic capabilities with 10 approved projects involving ₹1.60 lakh crore investment across 6 States.

    Investment and Infrastructure

    • Central government capital expenditure increased 4.2 times, from ₹2.63 lakh crore in FY18 to ₹11.21 lakh crore in FY26 (BE), with effective capex at ₹15.48 lakh crore.
    • The national highway network expanded by about 60%, while high-speed corridors increased nearly ten-fold since FY14.
    • The rail network reached 69,439 route km, achieved 99.1% electrification, and targeted 3,500 km addition in FY26.
    • India emerged as the world’s third-largest domestic aviation market, with airports increasing from 74 (2014) to 164 (2025).
    • Power sector reforms delivered a historic turnaround, with DISCOMs posting a positive PAT of ₹2,701 crore in FY25, while renewable energy accounts for nearly 50% of installed capacity.
    • 5G services now cover 99.9% of districts, tele-density reached 86.76%, and over 81% of rural households have tap water under Jal Jeevan Mission.
    • India became the fourth nation to achieve autonomous satellite docking (SpaDeX), strengthening space infrastructure.

    Environment and Climate Action

    • During FY26 (till December 2025), India added 38.61 GW of renewable energy capacity, led by 30.16 GW of solar power, reinforcing climate-aligned growth.

    Education and Health

    • India operates one of the world’s largest school systems, serving 24.69 crore students across 14.71 lakh schools.
    • Gross Enrolment Ratios improved across stages, with 90.9% at primary, 90.3% at upper primary, and 78.7% at secondary level.
    • Higher education expanded to 70,018 institutions, including 23 IITs, 21 IIMs, and 20 AIIMS, with international IIT campuses in Zanzibar and Abu Dhabi.
    • Under NEP, reforms such as NCrF, Academic Bank of Credit, and flexible entry-exit systems were widely adopted.
    • India achieved an 86% reduction in maternal mortality (since 1990), a 78% decline in under-five mortality (since 1990), and a 37% fall in infant mortality over the past decade (40 deaths per thousands live birth in 2013 to 25 in 2023).

    Employment and Skill Development

    • Total employment reached 56.2 crore in Q2 FY26, with net job creation continuing.
    • Organised manufacturing employment increased by 6% in FY24, adding over 10 lakh jobs.
    • Gig and platform workers were formally recognised under Labour Codes, while e-Shram registered over 31 crore workers, 54% of them women.
    • The National Career Service platform mobilised around 80 million vacancies, strengthening labour market matching.
    • The government proposed upgrading 1,000 ITIs to align skilling with industry needs.

    Rural Development and Social Progress

    • As per the revised World Bank poverty line, India’s extreme poverty declined to 5.3% in 2022–23.
    • Social services expenditure rose to 7.9% of GDP in FY26 (BE).
    • SVAMITVA completed drone surveys in 3.28 lakh villages, and Drone Didis strengthened rural livelihoods.
