    A. Recent Astronomical Activities

    JAXA Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission PDF p. 121

    Japan's JAXA launched the MMX mission on 20 October 2026 to achieve the world's first sample return from the Martian system.

    • Launched 20 October 2026 on H3 Flight No. 10 from Tanegashima Space Center, Japan.
    • Studies Mars's two moons, Phobos and Deimos; will return at least 10 grams from Phobos.
    • Arrival at Mars expected 2027; samples reach Earth in 2031; planned duration about five years.
    • Key question: are the moons captured asteroids or debris from a giant impact on Mars?
    • Carries 13 instruments; rover IDEFIX built jointly by France's CNES and Germany's DLR.
    • NASA gives MEGANE spectrometer, P-Sampler and Deep Space Network; NASA gets about 15% of samples.

    Memory aid Timeline 27 → 31: reach Mars 2027, back home 2031.

    Don't confuse Samples come from Phobos, not Deimos. JAXA's C-Sampler takes subsurface material; NASA's P-Sampler takes surface particles.

    हिंदी: Asteroid (क्षुद्रग्रह)

    From the magazine

    The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) launched the Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission on 20 October 2026 aboard H3 Flight No. 10 from Tanegashima Space Center, Japan. It aims to achieve the world’s first sample return from the Martian system. Its planned duration is approximately five years.

    Key Highlights

    • Mission objectives: Study Phobos and Deimos, Mars’s two moons, and return at least 10 grams of material from Phobos.
    • Timeline: Arrival at Mars is expected in 2027, and sample delivery to Earth in 2031.
    • Scientific significance: Determine whether the moons are captured asteroids or debris from a giant impact on Mars, improving understanding of planetary formation and the delivery of water and organic compounds.

    Technical Features

    • Spacecraft: Three modules—propulsion, exploration and return—use solar panels for electricity and chemical propulsion for manoeuvres.
    • Orbit: A quasi-satellite orbit around Mars near Phobos supports surface mapping and landing-site selection.
    • Instruments: The spacecraft carries 13 mission instruments. TENGOO provides approximately 40 cm imaging resolution; OROCHI captures images at multiple wavelengths; LIDAR measures surface distance using laser pulses.
    • Spectrometers: NASA’s MEGANE (Mars-moon Exploration with Gamma rays and Neutrons) measures gamma rays and neutrons to determine elemental composition. MIRS (MMX InfraRed Spectrometer) operates at 0.9–3.6 micrometres, investigating minerals, water-related substances and organic matter.
    • Rover: IDEFIX, jointly developed by France’s CNES and Germany’s DLR, will assess surface conditions before the spacecraft lands.
    • Sampling: JAXA’s C-Sampler collects subsurface material, while NASA’s P-Sampler uses high-pressure nitrogen gas to gather surface particles.
    • Communication and return: NASA’s Deep Space Network supports communication and navigation. A Sample Return Capsule will bring samples through Earth’s atmosphere; NASA will receive about 15% for research and curation.

    First GAGAN-Based Satellite Must knowPDF pp. 121–122

    In late June 2026, an IndiGo Airbus A321 made India's first satellite-based landing approach by a commercial jet, using the indigenous GAGAN system.

    • DGCA supervised India's first Satellite-Based Landing System (SLS) approach in late June 2026.
    • Aircraft: IndiGo Airbus A321; used satellite guidance instead of an Instrument Landing System (ILS).
    • GAGAN = GPS Aided GEO Augmented Navigation; built by ISRO and Airports Authority of India.
    • Ground network: 15 reference stations (INRES), 2 master control centres (INMCC), 3 uplink stations (INLUS).
    • 3 geostationary satellites carry GAGAN payloads; 4 communication networks link the stations.
    • NavIC gives positioning and timing; GAGAN corrects GPS for precise aircraft landing.

    Memory aid GAGAN ground count 15-2-3: 15 stations watch, 2 centres compute, 3 stations send up.

    Don't confuse GAGAN only improves (augments) GPS signals; NavIC is India's own regional navigation satellite system.

    हिंदी: Satellite navigation (उपग्रह नौवहन)

    From the magazine

    In late June 2026, the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) supervised India’s first Satellite-Based Landing System (SLS) approach by a commercial jet using the indigenous GAGAN system. An IndiGo Airbus A321 conducted the demonstration using satellite-derived guidance instead of relying on a conventional Instrument Landing System (ILS).

    Key Highlights

    • GAGAN (GPS Aided GEO Augmented Navigation) is India’s indigenous Satellite-Based Augmentation System developed by the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) and the Airports Authority of India.
    • It enhances GPS accuracy and provides integrity information for safer aircraft navigation. Certified to international standards, GAGAN supports satellite-based landing and serves sectors beyond aviation.

    Key Elements of GAGAN

    • GAGAN operates through an integrated network of ground stations, communication systems, and geostationary satellites. These elements monitor GPS signals in real-time, calculate corrections, and broadcast enhanced navigation information to aircraft.
    Key ElementsNo. of Elements DeployedRole
    Indian Reference Stations (INRES)15Continuously monitor GPS signals across the country and detect any errors.
    Indian Master Control Centres (INMCC)2Process data received from all reference stations, calculate signal corrections, and generate integrity information.
    Indian Land Uplink Stations (INLUS)3Transmit correction and integrity information from the ground to GAGAN satellites.
    Communication Networks4Connect all GAGAN stations and enable secure, real-time transmission of navigation data.
    Geostationary Satellites with GAGAN Payloads3Broadcast corrected navigation signals across the service area.
    • By enhancing navigation accuracy and seamless operations across the region, it continues to reinforce India’s leadership in satellite-enabled aviation services.

    India’s Indigenous Navigation Ecosystem

    • The integrated architecture of GAGAN forms an important part of India’s broader satellite navigation programme.
    • Alongside GAGAN, India has developed the Navigation with Indian Constellation (NavIC), its indigenous regional navigation satellite system. While NavIC provides positioning, navigation and timing services, GAGAN enhances GPS signals to support precise aircraft navigation and landing.

    SOLAR-1 PDF p. 122

    The US made SOLAR-1 operational on June 10, 2026; it is the first US satellite built only for continuous space-weather observation.

    • Operational on June 10, 2026; operated by NOAA (National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration).
    • Its data goes to NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center (SWPC) for forecasts and alerts.
    • SOLAR-1 = Space Weather Observations at L1 to Advance Readiness–1; earlier name SWFO-L1.
    • It orbits the Sun–Earth Lagrange Point 1 (L1).
    • Launched September 24, 2025 on a SpaceX Falcon 9 from Kennedy Space Center, Florida.
    • Final engine burn on January 23, 2026, after about four months and nearly one million miles.

    Memory aid SOLAR-1 sits at L1: both carry a '1'.

    Don't confuse Launched in 2025 (September 24) but made operational in 2026 (June 10).

    हिंदी: Space weather (अंतरिक्ष मौसम)

    From the magazine

    Space weather refers to changes in the space environment caused mainly by activity on the Sun. Powerful solar events can affect technological infrastructure and space missions. To strengthen its forecasting and early-warning system, the United States made SOLAR-1 operational on June 10, 2026. It is the first U.S. satellite designed exclusively for continuous and operational space-weather observations. The satellite is operated by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). Its observations are transmitted to NOAA’s Space Weather Prediction Center (SWPC), which uses them to issue forecasts, watches, warnings and alerts.

    Key Highlights

    • SOLAR-1 stands for Space Weather Observations at L1 to Advance Readiness–1. It was previously known as Space Weather Follow On–Lagrange 1, or SWFO-L1.
    • It was renamed SOLAR-1 after reaching its intended orbit around the Sun–Earth Lagrange Point 1.

    Launch and Journey to Deep Space

    • The spacecraft was launched on September 24, 2025, at 7:30 a.m. EDT from Launch Complex 39A at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida.
    • It travelled aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket. NASA’s Launch Services Program managed the launch.
    • After travelling for about four months and covering nearly one million miles, the spacecraft performed its final engine burn on January 23, 2026.
    • It then entered its planned orbit around L1 and was formally renamed SOLAR-1.

    Chandrayaan-3 Hop Experiment Must knowPDF p. 122

    On May 18, 2026, ISRO scientists reported ChaSTE data after the Vikram lander's 'hop', showing layered moon soil near the south pole.

    • Report shared May 18, 2026 on Chandrayaan-3's Vikram lander 'hop' experiment.
    • Vikram reignited its engines and landed nearly 50 cm away, testing ascent for future sample return.
    • ChaSTE (Chandra's Surface Thermophysical Experiment) is a lunar thermometer, re-inserted into the regolith (moon soil).
    • Found a two-layer structure in the top 6.5 cm of soil at the post-hop site.
    • Soil gets denser and stickier with depth; craters made temperatures drop faster (shadowing effect).
    • The engine firing blew away the top 3 cm of regolith.

    Memory aid Hop 50 cm, blew off 3 cm, found layers in 6.5 cm.

    हिंदी: Experiment (प्रयोग)

    From the magazine

    A team of scientists from the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) on May 18, 2026 shared a report of the findings of the ‘Hop’ experiment conducted by the Vikram Lander of Chandrayaan-3 and the Chandra’s Surface Thermophysical Experiment (ChaSTE) on the Moon.

    • A new study conducted during the final phase of the Chandrayaan-3 missions when the Vikram lander performed a successful hop experiment, has offered fresh insights into the Moon surface.
    • During the final phase of its mission, Chandrayaan-3’s Vikram lander reignited its engines to perform a controlled “hop” experiment (primarily to test ascent capabilities for future sample-return missions) and landed nearby, nearly 50 cm away from its initial position.
    • ChaSTE (Chandra’s Surface Thermophysical Experiment), a lunar thermometer was re-penetrated into the lunar regolith (soil) at the new location.
    • By analysing the ChaSTE data following this historic “hop” monoeuvre by the Vikram lander, scientists have discovered that the post-hop location at the Moon’s southern polar region possesses a complex, layered soil structure that was significantly altered by the lander’s brief flight.

    Key findings from the study have emerged, which include:

    • Layered Stratigraphy: analysis revealed a distinct two-layer structure within the top 6.5 cm of the post-hop site which means that the top few centimetres of the Moon’s surface aren’t just a uniform pile of dust; they are made of distinct layers with different properties,
    • Geotechnical Variability: the soil’s cohesion and density were found to increase significantly with depth which means that the Moon’s soil at the surface becomes more packed and sticky as we go deeper and Twilight Thermal Profiles: the data highlighted a “shadowing effect” where local craters and depressions caused temperatures to plunge faster than global models predicted.
    • Surface Erosion and Compaction: The engine firing blew away the top 3 cm of regolith, exposing and slightly compacting the material underneath.

    India’s First Orbital Data Centre Satellite Pathfinder Must knowPDF pp. 122–123

    On 4 May 2026, Pixxel and Sarvam partnered to build Pathfinder, India's first orbital data centre satellite, which will run AI in space.

    • Announced 4 May 2026: Pixxel–Sarvam strategic partnership for Pathfinder.
    • Pixxel will design, build, launch and operate it, and give the hyperspectral imaging payload.
    • Sarvam gives the AI backbone: India-built language models running on the satellite's GPUs.
    • Orbital data centre = satellites with data-centre-class GPUs that run AI in orbit (like edge computing).
    • Pathfinder is a single-satellite demonstrator, built at Pixxel's Gigapixxel facility (up to 100 units).

    Memory aid Pixxel = pictures and the satellite body; Sarvam = the AI brain.

    हिंदी: Artificial Intelligence (कृत्रिम बुद्धिमत्ता)

    From the magazine

    Recently on 4 May 2026, Pixxel announced a strategic partnership with Sarvam to develop and build Pathfinder, described as India’s first orbital data centre satellite. Pixxel will design, build, launch and operate the satellite, while Sarvam will provide the AI backbone for running full-stack language models, training and inference directly in orbit. The mission is important because it brings together remote sensing, high-performance computing and India-built AI on a single satellite platform.

    Orbital Data Centre

    • An orbital data centre is a space-based computing system in which satellites carry high-performance processors such as data-centre-class GPUs.
    • These processors can run AI models in orbit, rather than depending entirely on ground-based data centres.
    • In ordinary satellite missions, satellites collect images or signals and send large volumes of raw data to Earth.
    • In an orbital data centre model, computation happens closer to where the data is generated. This is similar to edge computing, where data is processed near its source instead of being sent to a distant cloud server.
    • Pathfinder is a single-satellite demonstrator. Its purpose is to test whether powerful computing hardware, similar to that used in ground data centres, can work reliably in the space environment.

    Role of Pixxel and Sarvam

    • Pixxel’s role:
      • Pixxel will design, build, launch and operate Pathfinder. It will also provide the hyperspectral imaging payload.
      • The satellite will be developed at Gigapixxel, Pixxel’s upcoming facility designed to scale satellite production to up to 100 units.
    • Sarvam’s role:
      • Sarvam will provide the AI backbone. Its full-stack sovereign AI platform, including models and inference infrastructure developed and governed in India, will run directly on the satellite’s GPU layer.

    Artemis II Mission PDF p. 123

    NASA's Artemis II, launched April 1, 2026, was a crewed lunar flyby, not a landing: first humans near the Moon since 1972.

    • Lifted off from Kennedy Space Center on April 1, 2026; first crewed Artemis flight.
    • Crewed lunar flyby: humans near the Moon for the first time in 53 years.
    • Tested NASA's Space Launch System and Orion spacecraft; the crew named Orion 'Integrity'.
    • Orion's heat shield worked as expected; char loss much lower than in Artemis I.
    • The last crewed Moon mission before this was Apollo 17 in 1972, which landed.
    • Artemis III: listed for 2027 as a low-Earth-orbit test of SpaceX and Blue Origin landers.

    Don't confuse Artemis II = flyby only (no landing); Apollo 17 (1972) = landing.

    हिंदी: Heat shield (ऊष्मा कवच)

    From the magazine

    Artemis II was not a Moon-landing mission; it was a crewed lunar flyby mission meant to prove that NASA’s Space Launch System, Orion spacecraft, ground systems, recovery teams and mission procedures can safely carry humans beyond low Earth orbit and bring them back. NASA describes it as the first crewed Artemis flight and a key step toward long-term human return to the Moon and future crewed missions to Mars.

    • Artemis II lifted off from the Kennedy Space Center on April 1, 2026, sending the first humans to the Moon since 1972. (Note: The Apollo 17 mission in 1972 sent humans to land on the Moon, whereas Artemis II sent humans toward the Moon.)
    • During the mission, the crew completed a lunar flyby, returning humans to the Moon’s vicinity for the first time in 53 years after the final Apollo Mission to the Moon.

    Engineering Focus of the Mission

    • The Artemis II Orion heat shield is the critical thermal protection system on the base of Orion Spacecraft. Orion heat shield protect the Capsule and Astronauts from searing temperatures and Extreme friction during high speed atmospheric re-entry.
    • During the flight, the astronauts tested Orion’s life-support, communications, control, navigation and manual operation systems in a deep-space environment.
    • The mission also tested how well astronauts could live and work inside Orion during a lunar-return flight.
    • This is important because Artemis is not only about reaching the Moon; it is about building the systems needed for repeated journeys, lunar surface work, and eventually Mars missions.
    • The Orion Spacecraft used in Artemis II was named Integrity by the crew.

    Orion’s Heat Shield and Re-entry Lesson

    • One of the most important engineering lessons came from Orion’s heat shield. During Artemis I, NASA found unexpected cracking and shedding of heat-shield material.
    • NASA later explained that heat and gases had accumulated inside the Avcoat material, creating internal pressure and uneven shedding during re-entry, although the spacecraft would still have kept a crew safe.
    • For Artemis II, NASA closely monitored re-entry and the thermal protection system.
    • The spacecraft returned at extremely high lunar-return speed, and NASA’s initial inspection found that the heat shield performed as expected and that heat-shield char loss was significantly reduced compared with Artemis I.
    • This result is important for astronaut safety in future Moon-landing missions.
    • Artemis III is now listed by NASA as a 2027 low-Earth orbit demonstration, mission to test one or both commerical landers from SpaceX and Blue Origin.

    New Telescopes in Ladakh Must knowPDF p. 124

    Union Budget 2026-27 backs four astronomy facilities: NLST and NLOT in Ladakh, an upgraded Himalayan Chandra Telescope, and COSMOS-2 planetarium at Amaravati.

    • NLST (National Large Solar Telescope): Merak near Pangong Lake, Ladakh; 2-metre class; studies the Sun.

    Memory aid Merak = Sun (Solar telescope by Pangong Lake); Hanle = night sky (NLOT + HCT).

    Don't confuse NLST (Solar) is at Merak; NLOT (Optical–Infrared) is at Hanle. One letter apart.

    हिंदी: Telescope (दूरबीन) · Planetarium (तारामंडल)

    From the magazine

    The Union Budget 2026-27 has given a major push to India’s astronomy programme. As per Budget 2026-27 four Telescope infrastructure facilities would be setup or upgraded. 1. National Large Solar Telescope (NLST)

    • The NLST will be built at Merak near Pangong Lake Ladakh. It is a 2-metre-class ground-based telescope that will observe the Sun in optical and near-infrared wavelengths.
    • It is designed to study the origin and behaviour of solar magnetic fields at very high resolution. 2. National Large Optical–Infrared Telescope (NLOT)
    • NLOT will come up at Hanle (Ladakh) and is officially described as India’s next-generation flagship ground-based optical–infrared telescope.
    • It will have a 13.7-metre segmented primary mirror, advanced adaptive optics for sharper infrared imaging, and instruments such as spectrographs and imagers. 3. Upgrade of the Himalayan Chandra Telescope (HCT)
    • The Indian Astronomical Observatory at Hanle is a high-altitude observatory in Ladakh. The Himalayan Chandra Telescope is the 2-M optical-infrared Telescope installed there.
    • It obtained first light on 26 September 2000, began regular science observations in May 2003, and is a 2-metre optical–infrared telescope remotely operated from CREST near Bengaluru through a dedicated satellite link.
    • The upgraded HCT is planned as a 3.7-metre segmented optical–infrared telescope, which would make it more useful for transient and multi-messenger astronomy. 4. COSMOS-2 Planetarium
    • It will be constructed at Amaravati and it will be implemented by Indian Institute of Astrophysics.

Initially focused on India, these models now support applications in farming, agricultural credit, water management and policy beyond the country.

    Key Highlights

    How the models work

    • ALU: Maps agricultural landscapes, including individual field boundaries, trees, woodlands and small irrigation structures such as farm wells and dug ponds.

    • It will demonstrate the feasibility of clean rail transportation in India.

    Inside India’s First Hydrogen Train

    • The hydrogen train project has been developed in accordance with design approval and technical specifications prepared by the Research, Designs & Standards Organisation (RDSO). Designed and developed entirely in India, the project demonstrates the vision of Atmanirbhar Bharat.

    Key Features of the Hydrogen Powered Train on the Jind- Sonipat Section-

    • The Train has two 1200 kW power cars, totalling 2400 kW hydrogen fuel cell propulsion system.
    • Approved to operate at a maximum speed of 75 kmph with a design speed of 110 kmph.
    • Capacity of Around 2,600 Passengers.
    • Developed from the design stage through prototype manufacturing.
    • It will connect Jind Junction, Gohana Junction and Sonipat while serving intermediate stations.

    Technology Behind the Train

    • Hydrogen fuel cell technology produces electricity through a chemical reaction using hydrogen.
    • The primary energy source is a Proton Exchange Membrane Fuel Cell (PEMFC). This is a fuel cell that generates electricity by reacting hydrogen and oxygen across a proton-conducting Perfluorosulfonic Acid (PFSA) polymer membrane.
    • The process produces only water vapour and heat as byproducts. Hydrogen is a high-energy fuel, 120 MJ/Kg (megajoules per kilogram) in comparison to diesel, which is 43 MJ/Kg.

    Hydrogen Infrastructure

    • The country’s largest railway hydrogen storage and refuelling facility has been established at Jind, Haryana.
    • The indigenous facility stores nearly 3,000 kg of hydrogen at a time. It will support hydrogen-powered train operations.
    • The train consists of two Hydrogen Driving Power Cars (DPCs) and eight Trailer Coaches (TCs).
    • Each DPC houses fuel cells, lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries and hydrogen storage cylinders.

    JAMA Blood Group in Humans PDF p. 130

    The International Society of Blood Transfusion recognised JAMA as the 49th human blood group system (ISBT 049), announced on September 14, 2026.

    • JAMA = 49th human blood group system, numbered ISBT 049.
    • Ratified at the ISBT Kuala Lumpur Congress 2026; announced September 14, 2026.
    • Found by UK and Israel researchers studying an Israeli woman and her brother.
    • Her antibody reacted with most people's red blood cells, but not with hers or her brother's.
    • JAMA is a separate antigen-based system, not a new type beside A, B, AB and O.

    Don't confuse JAMA is a blood group system (the 49th), not a fifth blood type next to A, B, AB and O.

    हिंदी: Blood group (रक्त समूह) · Antibody (प्रतिपिंड) · Antigen (प्रतिजन)

    From the magazine

    The International Society of Blood Transfusion (ISBT) has recognised JAMA as the 49th human blood group system, numbered ISBT 049. The discovery followed a joint investigation by researchers in the United Kingdom and Israel into unusual blood samples from a woman and her brother. ISBT ratified the system at its Kuala Lumpur Congress in 2026 and announced it on September 14, 2026. The finding adds to the understanding of rare blood characteristics and their possible importance in transfusion medicine.

    Key Highlights

    • Blood plays a vital role in the human body, carrying oxygen and essential nutrients to cells. For years, A, B, AB and O have been the blood groups most familiar to people.
    • Now, scientists have identified a new blood group system called JAMA, taking the total number of recognised blood group systems to 49.
    • The International Society of Blood Transfusion (ISBT) has officially recognised JAMA as the 49th blood group system.
    • The discovery came from a joint investigation by researchers from the UK and Israel. It began when scientists examined the blood of an Israeli woman and her brother.
    • The woman was found to have an antibody that reacted with the red blood cells of most people.
    • However, the same reaction did not occur with her own red blood cells or those of her brother.
    • This unusual result caught researchers’ attention because the antibody did not correspond to any previously identified blood group antigen.
    • JAMA should not be viewed as another category alongside A, B, AB and O. Instead, it is a separate blood group system involving a specific antigen.
    • This antigen is found on the red blood cells of most people. In the woman and her brother, however, it was absent.
    • Their blood also contained a corresponding antibody, helping scientists identify the unusual blood group characteristics.

    Rabies: Important Scientific Facts

    • Rabies is a viral disease that is almost always fatal after clinical symptoms appear, but deaths can be prevented through timely treatment.
    • Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) involves thorough wound washing, human rabies vaccination and rabies immunoglobulins (RIG), when indicated.
    • Infected dogs account for up to 99% of human rabies transmissions globally.
    • The Global Strategic Plan to End Human Deaths from Dog-Mediated Rabies by 2030.

    WHO Global Tuberculosis (TB) Report 2025 Must knowPDF p. 133

    WHO's Global TB Report 2025 (November 12, 2025) shows India carries 25% of the world's TB burden but cut incidence by 21% since 2015.

    • Released November 12, 2025; data from 184 countries and areas.
    • 2024: 10.7 million people got TB worldwide (131 new cases per 100,000).
    • India's share 25%, the highest; then Indonesia (10%) and Philippines (6.8%).
    • India's incidence fell 21%: 237 per lakh (2015) to 187 per lakh (2024); global fall only 12%.
    • India's TB mortality fell from 28 to 21 per lakh (2015 to 2024).
    • Treatment coverage rose from 53% (2015) to over 92% (2024); 26.18 lakh patients diagnosed in 2024.

    Memory aid '21' twice for India: incidence fell 21%, and deaths are now 21 per lakh.

    Don't confuse 21% = India's fall in incidence; 12% = global fall. India's share of burden = 25%.

    हिंदी: Tuberculosis (क्षय रोग)

    From the magazine

    Recently, WHO released the Global Tuberculosis Report 2025 on November 12, 2025, giving an updated assessment of the TB epidemic and response at global, regional and country levels based mainly on data up to 2024. Data from 184 countries and areas cover more than 99% of the world’s population and TB cases, giving the report very strong global representativeness.

    • Tuberculosis (TB) is described as the world’s leading cause of death from a single infectious agent, and remains among the top 10 causes of death worldwide.
    • TB is an airborne, contagious disease; since 2000, global efforts to combat TB have saved an estimated 83 million lives.

    Global TB Burden

    • In 2024, an estimated 10.7 million people developed TB, corresponding to 131 new cases per 100,000 population worldwide.
    • Top eight countries (≈ two-thirds of global TB burden):
      • India (25%), Indonesia (10%), Philippines (6.8%), China (6.5%), Pakistan (6.3%), Nigeria (4.8%), Democratic Republic of the Congo (3.9%), Bangladesh (3.6%).

    TB Incidence in India

    • TB incidence in India has fallen by 21%, from 237 per lakh population in 2015 to 187 per lakh population in 2024, almost double the global decline of 12%; this is described as one of the highest declines globally among high-burden countries.
    • TB mortality in India (TB deaths in HIV-negative people) has reduced from 28 per lakh population in 2015 to 21 per lakh population in 2024, with India achieving a higher reduction than the global reduction.
    • India’s treatment coverage rose from 53% in 2015 to over 92% in 2024, ahead of global universal health coverage and other high-burden countries.
    • In 2024, 26.18 lakh TB patients were diagnosed in India, out of an estimated 27 lakh incident cases, reducing the “missing cases” from 15 lakh in 2015 to less than one lakh in 2024, with no significant increase in MDR-TB cases.

    Malaria Vaccine: AdFalciVax Must knowPDF p. 134

    ICMR's Regional Medical Research Centre, Bhubaneswar, has developed AdFalciVax, a low-cost recombinant multi-stage malaria vaccine candidate stable at room temperature.

    हिंदी: Malaria vaccine (मलेरिया टीका)

    From the magazine

    • The Regional Medical Research Centre (RMRC), Bhubaneswar, of the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), has developed a recombinant multi-stage malaria vaccine candidate named AdFalciVax.
      • Its objective is to prevent individual infection against Plasmodium falciparum and to reduce community-level transmission.
      • As of June 17, 2026, this technology has been licensed to five Indian companies, while it is still in the preclinical stage (TRL 4) and is not approved for clinical use.
      • This vaccine candidate has not yet been approved for clinical use; hence, the timeline assessment will depend on regulatory progress.
    • Currently, WHO-recommended vaccines— RTS,S/AS01 (Mosquirix) and R21/Matrix-M— are available for widespread use in children; both have received WHO prequalification.
    • AdFalciVax has very high stability. It remains effective for up to 12 months at normal room temperature.
      • This eliminates the need for expensive cold chain logistics, which is a major challenge for vaccination campaigns in remote and resource-limited areas.
    • The estimated production cost of this vaccine is only ₹20 per dose, compared to existing vaccines that cost between ₹250 and ₹830 per dose.
      • This makes it extremely cost-effective for large-scale immunization programs.
    • India aims to achieve zero indigenous malaria cases by 2027 and full elimination by 2030.

    DRDO develops indigenous GaN technology PDF pp. 134–135

    On May 13, 2026, SAMEER and ISRO's ISTRAC agreed to build deep-space X-band amplifiers using indigenous GaN chips from DRDO's GAETEC.

    • Agreement May 13, 2026: SAMEER and ISRO's ISTRAC; GaN chips from GAETEC, DRDO.
    • GaN (Gallium Nitride): semiconductor for high-frequency, high-power uses.
    • One 3.5 × 3 mm GaN chip can deliver up to 30 watts.
    • DRDO's SSPL makes 4-inch Silicon Carbide (SiC) wafers and GaN HEMTs up to 150 watts.

    From the magazine

    On May 13, 2026, SAMEER and ISRO’s ISTRAC agreed to develop X-band deep-space communication amplifiers using indigenous GaN chips from GAETEC, DRDO.

    • Gallium Nitride (GaN) is a semiconductor technology suitable for high-frequency and high-power applications.
    • A single indigenous GaN chip measuring 3.5 × 3 mm can deliver up to 30 watts of power and reportedly operate at speeds 300 times faster than silicon.
    • The Solid State Physics Laboratory (SSPL) of DRDO has developed indigenous processes for manufacturing 4-inch Silicon Carbide (SiC) wafers.
    • SSPL has fabricated GaN HEMTs with power capabilities up to 150 watts and MMICs up to 40 watts for applications up to X-band frequencies.
    • Limited production capability for indigenous GaN-on-SiC MMICs has been established at GAETEC, Hyderabad.
    • Under the Innovations for Defence Excellence (iDEX) initiative, a contract was signed with Agnit Semiconductors Private Limited to develop advanced GaN semiconductors for next-generation defence wireless transmitters.

    Applications and Strategic Significance

    • GaN technology is used in radars, electronic warfare systems, communications, intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance (ISR) and unmanned systems.
    • Its high power, high frequency and compact size make it suitable for radar transmitters and electronic warfare jammers.
    • GaN-on-SiC technology offers higher efficiency, reduced size and weight, and improved performance.
    • Multifunctional MMICs have applications in strategic systems, space, aerospace, 5G and satellite communications.

    India’s first privately built FFSC rocket engine PDF p. 136

    Bengaluru's Astrobase Space Technologies unveiled EVEREST on August 7, 2026, described as India's first privately built Full-Flow Staged Combustion rocket engine.

    • Unveiled August 7, 2026 by Astrobase Space Technologies, Bengaluru.
    • FFSC = Full-Flow Staged Combustion: fuel and oxidiser go through separate pre-burners.
    • India's first LOX-methane high-thrust engine; fourth commercial FFSC globally (after SpaceX, Stoke Space, LandSpace).
    • Could support reusable launches of up to 30 tonnes to low Earth orbit.
    • As of August 22, 2026, full hot-fire testing was pending; figures are design targets.

    Don't confuse Performance figures are company design targets; the engine was not yet fully hot-fire tested.

    हिंदी: Combustion (दहन)

    From the magazine

    On August 7, 2026, Bengaluru-based Astrobase Space Technologies unveiled EVEREST, which it describes as India’s first fully integrated, privately developed Full-Flow Staged Combustion (FFSC) rocket engine. As of August 22, 2026, full-scale integrated hot-fire testing remained pending, so reported performance figures were company-stated design targets.

    Key Highlights

    • High Thrust FFSC Rocket Engines – FFSC engines route fuel and oxidiser through separate pre-burners before the main combustion chamber. Gases produced drive turbines connected to pumps and then enter the chamber, ensuring that propellants contribute to thrust instead of being released into the atmosphere.
    • Efficiency and Reusability – Unlike conventional engines, which use only part of the propellants to drive turbopumps, FFSC engines improve turbopump and propulsion efficiency. They support precise throttle control and reusable launch systems. LOX-methane propellants provide cleaner combustion, which can simplify refurbishment and support faster turnaround. However, the cycle is complex to design, develop and execute.
    • Significance of EVEREST – EVEREST is presented as India’s first LOX-methane high-thrust engine and the fourth commercial FFSC development globally, after SpaceX, Stoke Space and LandSpace. It could support reusable launches carrying up to 30 tonnes to low Earth orbit and provide a medium-lift platform for commercial and strategic missions. Advanced manufacturing includes India’s largest industrial 3D printer.

    • Dhvani is a Hypersonic Glide Vehicle (HGV) capable of high-speed changes in direction while traveling at hypersonic speeds at high altitudes.
      • The missile’s potential operational range is 6,000 to 10,000 kilometers, which could nearly double the reach of India’s Agni-V Intercontinental Ballistic Missile (ICBM).

    Indian Telecom Services Performance Indicator Report 2026 Must knowPDF p. 141

    On October 12, 2026, TRAI released its telecom performance report for the April–June 2026 quarter; internet subscriptions reached 1,114.17 million.

    • Released by TRAI on October 12, 2026; covers 1st April 2026 to 30th June 2026.
    • Internet subscriptions: 1,092.79 million (March) to 1,114.17 million (June 2026), up 1.96%.
    • Total telephone subscriptions 1,348.08 million; tele-density 94.31 per 100 people.
    • Private operators hold 92.50% of telephone subscriptions; public sector 7.50%.

    Memory aid Tele-density 94.31: about 94 connections per 100 people.

    Don't confuse Tele-density 94.31 includes machine-to-machine (M2M) links; without M2M it is 84.88.

    Check The source itself notes that rounded totals imply about 1.83% growth in mobile data subscriptions, while the official summary says 1.86%.

    हिंदी: Tele-density (दूरसंचार घनत्व)

    From the magazine

    The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) on October 12, 2026 has released the “Indian Telecom Services Performance Indicator Report” for the quarter ending 30th June 2026 details of services in India for the period covering 1st April 2026 to 30th June 2026 compiled mainly on the basis of information furnished by the Service Providers.

    Internet Access and Data Use

    • Internet subscriptions rose from 1,092.79 million in March 2026 to 1,114.17 million in June 2026, an increase of 1.96%.
    • Broadband subscriptions increased by 2.03% to 1,087.50 million, while narrowband subscriptions fell by 0.89% to 26.67 million.
    • The internet base included 47.73 million wired connections and 1,066.43 million wireless connections. Mobile wireless access accounted for 94.07% of all internet subscriptions.
    • Mobile data use rose by 8.30% to 84,424 petabytes (PB) during the quarter. Average monthly use per mobile data subscriber increased by 6.32% to 28.39 gigabytes (GB).
    • Mobile data subscriptions reached 1,045.55 million, compared with 1,026.75 million in March.
    • These rounded totals imply growth of about 1.83%, although the official summary states 1.86%.

    Telephone Connections

    • Total telephone subscriptions increased by 1.31% to 1,348.08 million. They were 10.65% higher than in June 2025.
    • Overall tele-density rose from 93.26 to 94.31 connections per 100 people. The headline totals include Machine-to-Machine (M2M) cellular connections, which allow devices to communicate. Tele-density excluding M2M was 84.88.
    • Wireless mobile and Fixed Wireless Access (FWA) connections together reached 1,300.25 million, up by 1.40%. Wireline subscriptions declined by 0.88% to 47.82 million. FWA uses a wireless link to serve a fixed location.
    • Private operators held 92.50% of all telephone subscriptions, while public sector operators held 7.50%.

    The Urban and Rural Gap

    • Rural telephone subscriptions increased to 556.01 million, but their share of the national total fell from 41.47% to 41.24%.
    • Urban subscriptions grew faster. The comparison below shows that the gap remained wide.

    Revenue and Usage

    • Monthly wireless Average Revenue per User (ARPU) rose by 1.19% to ₹187.12. Monthly Minutes of Usage (MOU) per subscriber fell by 2.65% to 933 minutes.
    • Average revenue earned per GB of mobile data fell by 5.07% to ₹7.13. This is an operator revenue indicator, not a universal retail price for one GB.
    • Access services contributed 83.85% of sector AGR. Licence fees increased by 2.41% to ₹7,103 crore.

    Indigenous Micro Graphics Processing Unit at IIT Delhi PDF p. 141

    On September 24, 2026, IIT Delhi announced an indigenous micro-GPU for embedded devices, shown on an FPGA, with a chip (ASIC) version planned.

    • Announced September 24, 2026 by IIT Delhi.
    • Led by M.Tech students Nammi Akash and M. Ravi Teja under Prof. Jayadeva and Prof. Kaushik Saha.
    • Custom floating-point GPU engine, built fully in Register Transfer Language (RTL).
    • Shown on a Spartan-7 FPGA (chip programmable after manufacture); ASIC (task-specific chip) planned.
    • Targets embedded devices: computers made for specific jobs.

    Don't confuse Demonstrated on an FPGA; the ASIC version is only planned.

    From the magazine

    On September 24, 2026, IIT Delhi announced an indigenous micro-GPU for embedded devices. As of 13 October 2026, it has demonstrated the FPGA design, while ASIC development remains planned. A Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) is a specialised processor that renders images and handles many calculations in parallel. A micro-GPU is a compact graphics processor. This project targets embedded devices, which contain computers designed for specific functions.

    Key Highlights

    Development and key features

    • M.Tech students Nammi Akash and M. Ravi Teja led the project under Prof. Jayadeva and Prof. Kaushik Saha of IIT Delhi’s Department of Electrical Engineering.
    • The team demonstrated programmable graphics rendering using a custom floating-point GPU engine, implemented entirely in Register Transfer Language (RTL).
    • The design was mapped to a Spartan-7 Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) and demonstrated on a standard development board. An FPGA is a chip whose logic can be programmed after manufacture.
    • The processor is a scalable, programmable intellectual property (IP) design that can be adapted for different devices. It can run on an FPGA or be made as an Application-Specific Integrated Circuit (ASIC), a chip designed for a particular task.

    Bharat Electricity Summit 2026 Must knowPDF pp. 142–143

    Bharat Electricity Summit 2026 was held at Yashobhoomi, New Delhi, on 19-22 March 2026; it released resource adequacy and transmission plans.

    • Held 19 to 22 March 2026 at Yashobhoomi, New Delhi.
    • Theme: 'Electrifying Growth. Empowering Sustainability. Connecting Globally.'
    • Released: National Resource Adequacy Plan; Transmission Plan for over 900 GW non-fossil capacity by 2035–36.
    • FY 2025–26: record non-fossil addition of 55.29 GW (solar 44.61 GW, wind 6.05 GW).
    • As of 31 March 2026: total capacity 5,32,740 MW; non-fossil share 53.2%.

    Memory aid 'One Nation – One Grid – One Frequency': the world's largest synchronous national grid.

    Don't confuse 52,537 MW is capacity added only up to 31 January 2026; the full-year non-fossil addition is 55.29 GW.

    हिंदी: Transmission (पारेषण) · Renewable energy (नवीकरणीय ऊर्जा)

    From the magazine

    Over the past decade, India’s power sector has undergone a period of major structural change, transitioning to a system defined by adequacy, expanded capacity, and improved reliability.

    • Bharat Electricity Summit 2026 was held from 19 to 22 March 2026 at Yashobhoomi, New Delhi.
    • The Summit was a global conference-cum-exhibition for the power and electricity sector.
    • It was held under the theme “Electrifying Growth. Empowering Sustainability. Connecting Globally.”

    The Summit was important for India’s long-term power-sector planning.

    • Two important reports were released at the Summit: the National Resource Adequacy Plan and the Transmission Plan for Integration of over 900 GW Non-Fossil Fuel Capacity by 2035–36.
    • Transmission planning is necessary because renewable energy projects are often located far from major demand centres.

    India recorded major capacity expansion during FY 2025–26.

    • The figure of 52,537 MW capacity addition belongs to the period up to 31 January 2026.
    • For the completed FY 2025–26, official MNRE data state that non-fossil capacity addition was 55.29 GW, the highest increase in any year.
    • In FY 2025–26, solar capacity addition reached 44.61 GW, while wind capacity addition reached 6.05 GW.
    • As of 31 March 2026, India’s total installed power generation capacity was 5,32,740 MW, or about 532.740 GW.
    • As of March 31, 2026, India’s total non-fossil capacity was 2,83,468 MW, or about 283.468 GW, forming 53.2% of total installed capacity.

    The latest official renewable energy data show further growth after March 2026.

    • As of 31 May 2026, India’s total renewable energy capacity, including large hydro, was 282,745.08 MW.
    • As of 31 May 2026, India’s total non-fossil capacity was 291,525.08 MW.
    • Solar power remained the largest renewable segment, with cumulative solar capacity of 157.05 GW as on May 31, 2026.
    • Wind power capacity stood at 56,807.04 MW as of 31 May 2026.
    • The National Power Portal dashboard for June 2026 showed India’s total installed capacity at 548,848.48 MW.
    • In that classification, thermal capacity was 251,489.13 MW, hydro capacity was 52,064.66 MW, RES capacity excluding large hydro was 236,514.69 MW, and nuclear capacity was 8,780 MW.

    India’s transmission network has also expanded significantly

    • In January 2026, India’s national power transmission network crossed 5 lakh circuit kilometres of transmission lines of 220 kV and above.
    • At that milestone, transformation capacity reached 1,407 GVA.
    • The Ministry of Power described India’s grid as the world’s largest synchronous national grid.
    • The milestone was linked to the vision of “One Nation – One Grid – One Frequency.”
    • As per the National Power Portal data available for June 2026, India’s transmission network reached 509,603 ckm, and transformation capacity reached 14,77,951 MVA, or about 1,477.951 GVA.
    • Transmission expansion is important because India needs to evacuate and integrate large quantities of solar, wind, hydro and other non-fossil electricity into the national grid.

    India has moved close to power sufficiency.

    • In FY 2025–26, the country’s energy requirement was 17,07,493 MU, while energy availability was 17,06,985 MU.
    • The energy deficit was only 0.03% in FY 2025–26.
    • The peak demand was 2,45,444 MW, while maximum demand met was 2,45,416 MW.
    • The peak deficit was only 0.01%, showing a very small gap between demand and supply.

    UNEP’s Emissions Gap Report 2026 Must knowPDF p. 144

    UNEP's 17th Emissions Gap Report, 'The Point of Return' (October 21, 2026), says crossing 1.5°C is now unavoidable; India is the third-largest emitter.

    • Global emissions: 58.4 GtCO2e in 2025 vs a revised 58.5 GtCO2e in 2024; no confirmed peak.
    • Cuts needed from 2025 levels: 18% by 2030, 45% by 2035, 69% by 2040.
    • Full NDC implementation gives only 5–8% cuts by 2030 and 11–15% by 2035.
    • India: 4.5 billion tonnes CO2e in 2025, third after China and the United States (excluding LULUCF).
    • India per person: 3.1 tonnes vs global average 6.4 tonnes; lowest among six largest emitters.
    • India and China together hold 95% of coal-power capacity under construction worldwide.

    Memory aid India: third in total (4.5 billion tonnes) but lowest per person (3.1 tonnes): big country, small footprint per head.

    Don't confuse 58.4 Gt = 2025 global emissions; 58.5 Gt = revised 2024 figure. 76% appears twice: G20 share of emissions and share covered by 124 Parties' updated NDCs.

    हिंदी: Emissions gap (उत्सर्जन अंतराल) · Greenhouse gas (ग्रीनहाउस गैस)

    From the magazine

    UNEP’s Emissions Gap Report 2026: 17th edition of the Emissions Gap Report 2026 (titled The Point of Return) was released by the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) on October 21, 2026.

    • Global emissions: Greenhouse gas emissions reached 58.4 gigatonnes of CO2 equivalent (GtCO2 e) in 2025, against a revised 58.5 GtCO2 e in 2024; uncertainty prevents confirming a decline or peak.
    • G20: Excluding the Afrizcan Union, members contributed 76% of global emissions; their emissions excluding land use, land-use change and forestry rose 0.7% in 2025.
    • National commitments: By 1 September 2026, 124 Parties, representing 76% of global emissions, had submitted updated nationally determined contributions (NDCs).
    • Warming threshold: Exceeding 1.5°C above preindustrial levels is unavoidable; stronger mitigation can reduce its magnitude and duration.
    • Lowest overshoot pathway: Peak warming can be limited to 1.7–1.8°C with 66% probability, with around 50% probability of returning to 1.5°C by 2100.
    • Required reductions: Against 2025 levels, emissions must fall 18% by 2030, 45% by 2035, and 69% by 2040.
    • Commitment shortfall: Full NDC implementation delivers only 5–8% reductions by 2030 and 11–15% by 2035.
    • Emissions gap: Even with conditional commitments implemented, the gap against the lowest overshoot pathway remains 5 GtCO2 e in 2030 and 16 GtCO2 e in 2035.

    Emissions Gap Report 2026: India-specific facts

    • Third-largest emitter: India’s greenhouse gas emissions were 4.5 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent in 2025, placing it third after China and the United States. This estimate excludes land use, land-use change and forestry (LULUCF).
    • Low per capita emissions: India emitted 3.1 tonnes of CO2 equivalent per person in 2025, compared with the global average of 6.4 tonnes— the lowest among the six largest emitters assessed. These figures also exclude LULUCF.
    • Decadal emissions trend: During 2016–2025, India’s total greenhouse gas emissions increased by an annual average of 3.5%, while per capita emissions increased by 2.6% annually.
    • 2035 emissions-intensity target: India’s updated nationally determined contribution (NDC) seeks to reduce greenhouse gas emissions per unit of GDP by 47% from 2005 levels by 2035.
    • 2035 non-fossil electricity target: India aims for about 60% of cumulative installed electricity capacity from non-fossil sources by 2035, conditional on technology transfer and international finance.
    • 2035 carbon-sink target: India aims for a cumulative increase of 3.5–4 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent in carbon sinks through forest and tree cover, relative to 2005 levels. Emissions-Gap-Report-2026
    • Progress towards 2030 commitments: India is among six G20 members likely to achieve their unconditional 2030 targets under existing policies, alongside China, Indonesia, Russia, South Africa and Türkiye. The report also projects India to achieve its conditional 2030 target.
    • Projected emissions under NDCs: Under full implementation of its NDC targets, India’s annual emissions in 2035 are projected to be 1,254 million tonnes of CO2 equivalent higher than in 2030, with per capita emissions of 3.6 tonnes. Emissions-Gap-Report-2026
    • Coal-power construction: India and China together account for 95% of coal-power capacity currently under construction worldwide. This figure concerns construction, rather than existing installed capacity. Emissions-Gap-Report-2026

    On October 15, 2026, Sauj Lake (Uttar Pradesh) and Sukhna Wetland (Chandigarh) became Ramsar Sites, taking India's total to 103.

    • 103rd: Sauj Lake, Mainpuri district, UP; Ganga floodplain, near Saman Bird Sanctuary.
    • 102nd: Sukhna Wetland, edge of Chandigarh, at the base of the Outer Himalayas.
    • 101st: Glaw Lake (Glaw Tuwi), Lohit district; Arunachal Pradesh's first Ramsar Site (3 August 2026).
    • 100th: Jai Prakash Narayan Bird Sanctuary (Surha Tal), Ballia, UP (5 June 2026).
    • Grew from 26 sites (2014) to 103 (2026); India third globally after UK (176) and Mexico (144).
    • Most sites: Tamil Nadu (20); largest: Sundarbans; smallest: Vembannur; first: Chilika and Keoladeo (1981).

    Memory aid UP bookends: 100th (Surha Tal, Ballia) and 103rd (Sauj Lake, Mainpuri) are both in Uttar Pradesh.

    Don't confuse Order: Glaw Lake = 101st (Arunachal) → Sukhna = 102nd (Chandigarh) → Sauj Lake = 103rd (UP).

    Check Heading dates Sukhna Wetland 'March 16, 2026', but the text says it was added on October 15, 2026.

    हिंदी: Wetland (आर्द्रभूमि) · Floodplain (बाढ़ का मैदान)

    From the magazine

    On October 15, 2026, India added Sauj Lake and Sukhna Wetland to the List of Wetlands of International Importance, taking the country’s total number of Ramsar Sites to 103. India’s Ramsar network has expanded significantly from 26 sites in 2014 to 103 sites in 2026.

    Major Ramsar Sites in India 1. Sukhna Wetland (March 16, 2026)

      • Interesting Facts

    Total Ramsar sites in India at Present: 103

    • State having the most number of Ramsar sites: Tamil Nadu (20)
    • Largest wetland under the Ramsar convention (in India): Sundarbans, West Bengal.
    • Smallest wetland under the Ramsar convention (in India): Vembannur Wetland Complex Tamil Nadu
    • First wetland under the Ramsar convention (in India): Chilika Lake and Keoladeo National Park (Rajasthan) (1981)

    Key Highlights

    103rd Ramsar Site: Sauj Lake

    • Sauj Lake, located in Mainpuri district of Uttar Pradesh, is a shallow lake surrounded by farmland in the floodplain of the Ganga River.
    • It forms part of a larger network of wetlands, contributing to ecological connectivity in the wider landscape, and is close to Saman Bird Sanctuary.

    102nd Ramsar Site: Sukhna Wetland

    • Located at the edge of the city of Chandigarh and at the base of the Outer Himalayas, Sukhna Wetland is a peri-urban reservoir that plays an important role in regulating sediment and water flows from the surrounding catchment.

    101st Ramsar Site: Glaw Lake

    • Glaw Lake in Arunachal Pradesh was announced as India’s 101st Ramsar Site on 3 August 2026.
    • It became the first wetland from Arunachal Pradesh to be included in the List of Wetlands of International Importance.
    • Glaw Lake, locally known as Glaw Tuwi, is a natural freshwater wetland in Lohit district.
    • As of August 2026, India ranked third globally by number of Ramsar Sites, behind the United Kingdom with 176 sites and Mexico with 144 sites.

    100th Ramsar Site: Jai Prakash Narayan Bird Sanctuary (Surha Tal)

    • On 5 June 2026, the Jai Prakash Narayan Bird Sanctuary, also known as Surha Tal, located in Ballia district of Uttar Pradesh, was recognised as India’s 100th Ramsar Site.

    The Kigali Amendment marked its 10th anniversary Must knowPDF p. 146

    The Kigali Amendment to the Montreal Protocol, which phases down climate-warming HFCs used in cooling, marked its 10th anniversary on October 15, 2026.

    • Adopted at Kigali on October 15, 2016; entered into force in January 2019.
    • Aim: phase down HFCs; could avoid about 0.3–0.5°C of warming by 2100.
    • HFCs don't harm the ozone layer but warm hundreds or thousands of times more than CO2.
    • Called 'phase-down', not phase-out, because limited HFC use can continue.
    • India ratified in 2021: freeze by 2028, 10% cut by 2032, 85% cut by 2047.
    • Montreal Protocol (1987) phased out CFCs; nearly 99% of controlled ozone-depleting substances eliminated.

    Memory aid India's Kigali ladder: 2028 freeze → 2032 cut 10% → 2047 cut 85%.

    Don't confuse Montreal Protocol (1987) = ozone-depleting substances like CFCs (phase-out); Kigali Amendment (2016) = HFCs (phase-down).

    हिंदी: Ozone layer (ओजोन परत) · Phase-down (चरणबद्ध कमी)

    From the magazine

    The Kigali Amendment to the Montreal Protocol marked its 10th anniversary on October 15, 2026. Adopted in Kigali, Rawanda on October 15, 2016. It seeks to phase down HFCs, which are used in cooling. Full implementation could avoid about 0.3 – 0.5°C global warming by 2100.

    Key Highlights

    Background

    • The Montreal Protocol (1987) was adopted to phase out CFCs and other ozone-depleting substances.
    • Countries have since eliminated nearly 99% of controlled ozone-depleting substances, helping the ozone layer recover.
    • HFCs became widely used in refrigeration and air-conditioning because they do not damage the ozone layer.
    • However, many HFCs have hundreds or thousands of times the warming impact of CO2 over 100 years.
    • As HFC use expanded, the Federated States of Micronesia and Mauritius proposed bringing them under the Montreal Protocol in 2009.
    • The Kigali Amendment entered into force in January 2019. It establishes binding schedules to reduce HFC production and consumption, while developing countries receive longer compliance periods.
    • Since limited HFC use can continue after reductions, it is called a phase-down rather than a phase-out.

    India’s Kigali Commitments

    • India ratified the Kigali Amendment in 2021.
      • 2028: Freeze HFC production and consumption at the agreed baseline.
      • 2032: Reduce HFCs by 10% below the baseline.
      • 2047: Achieve an 85% reduction.
    • The limits are calculated according to the gases’ warming impact.
    • Equipment purchased before the first reductions may remain in use well into the 2030s.

    Cabinet approves Green Energy Corridor Phase-III scheme Must knowPDF pp. 146–147

    On 30 September 2026, the Union Cabinet approved Green Energy Corridor Phase III to strengthen state transmission networks and add battery storage for renewable power.

    • Approved by the Union Cabinet on 30 September 2026; target completion FY 2032–33.
    • Strengthens the Intra-State Transmission System (InSTS) within States and Union Territories.
    • Supports evacuation of up to 135 GW renewable energy and 50 GWh battery storage (BESS).
    • Total outlay ₹1,86,405 crore: InSTS ₹1,36,378 crore; battery storage ₹50,000 crore.
    • Central Financial Support ₹54,082 crore, to lower intra-state transmission charges.
    • Supports India's target of 900 GW non-fossil installed capacity by 2035.

    Memory aid Green Energy Corridor = a highway of power lines carrying green electricity from plants to the grid.

    Don't confuse 135 GW = renewable power to be evacuated; 50 GWh = battery storage to be deployed.

    Check Components ₹1,36,378 crore + ₹50,000 crore = ₹1,86,378 crore, not the stated total ₹1,86,405 crore.

    हिंदी: Transmission (पारेषण) · Battery storage (बैटरी भंडारण)

    From the magazine

    On 30 September 2026, the Union Cabinet approved Green Energy Corridor Phase III to strengthen renewable electricity transmission and add battery storage.

    Key Highlights

    Green Energy Corridor

    • A Green Energy Corridor is a network of transmission lines and substations that carries electricity from renewable energy plants to the power grid.
    • Power evacuation means moving the electricity generated at a plant into this network.
    • Phase III will strengthen the Intra-State Transmission System (InSTS) within States and Union Territories.

    Objectives and Key Features

    • It aims to support evacuation of up to 135 gigawatts (GW) of renewable energy and deployment of 50 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) by FY 2032–33.
    • The scheme will strengthen transmission networks so that more renewable electricity can reach consumers.

    Financial Outlay and Implementation

    • Target Completion: FY 2032–33.
    • Total Project Outlay: ₹1,86,405 crore.
      • Intra-State Transmission System development under GEC-III: ₹1,36,378 crore.
      • Deployment of 50 GWh of battery storage: ₹50,000 crore.
    • Total Central Financial Support: ₹54,082 crore.
      • Central Financial Assistance (CFA) will reduce intra-state transmission charges and help keep electricity costs affordable.

    Expected Benefits and Significance

    • Support India’s target of 900 GW installed non-fossil fuel capacity by 2035.
    • Enhance national energy security and promote environmentally sustainable development by reducing carbon emissions.
    • Generate direct and indirect employment in the power, manufacturing, construction and energy storage sectors.
    • Create long-term skilled jobs in grid management, operation and maintenance.
    • Improve renewable energy utilisation and ensure reliable, affordable electricity for consumers.

    India’s Net Zero Portal and the NAPCC Dashboard Must knowPDF p. 147

    On World Ozone Day (16 September 2026), MoS Kirti Vardhan Singh launched India's Net Zero Portal and NAPCC Dashboard in Mumbai for transparent climate action.

    • Launched 16 September 2026 in Mumbai by MoS Environment Kirti Vardhan Singh, on World Ozone Day.
    • Net Zero Portal: voluntary registration and disclosure of Net Zero commitments by Indian entities.
    • NAPCC Dashboard: single view of progress of National Missions under the National Action Plan on Climate Change.
    • NDC for 2031–2035 (submitted 24 April 2026): 47% intensity cut, about 60% non-fossil capacity by 2035.
    • Early wins: 40% non-fossil target met in 2021, nine years early; 50% met June 2025.
    • Emissions intensity fell 37.38% by 2022 vs 2005; non-fossil about 55% of capacity (30 September 2026).

    Memory aid Target ladders for 2015 → 2022 → 2026: non-fossil share 40 → 50 → 60%; intensity cut 33–35 → 45 → 47%.

    Don't confuse The 2015 INDC and 2022 update targets are 'by 2030'; the 2026 NDC targets are 'by 2035'.

    हिंदी: Net Zero (शुद्ध शून्य) · Climate action (जलवायु कार्रवाई)

    From the magazine

    Union Minister of State for Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Shri Kirti Vardhan Singh, on 16 September, 2026 launched India’s Net Zero Portal and the National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC) Dashboard on the occasion of World Ozone Day 2026 in Mumbai. The two digital initiatives mark an important step towards strengthening transparency, coordination and evidence-based climate action.

    Key Highlights

    • Net Zero emissions refer to a state where anthropogenic greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions by an entity (organization / industry / government) over a period of one year are compensated by GHG removals through anthropogenic interventions over the same period of time.

    The Net Zero Portal

    • The Net Zero Portal is a centralised digital platform for voluntary registration and disclosure of Net Zero commitments by Indian entities across sectors.
    • Participating entities can disclose their greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, declare Net Zero targets and provide annual progress updates.

    The NAPCC Dashboard

    • The NAPCC Dashboard provides a consolidated digital view of implementation and progress across the National Missions under the NAPCC.
    • It brings together mission-related information and identified indicators on a common platform, facilitating systematic monitoring by concerned Ministries and Departments.

    Indian climate goals in 2015

    • India’s 2015 Intended Nationally Determined Contribution (INDC) contained eight goals. Three were quantitative targets, shown in the comparison below.
    • The remaining five concerned sustainable lifestyles, cleaner development, adaptation, finance and technology.

    NDC updates in 2022 and 2026

    • A Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) is a country’s climate action plan under the Paris Agreement.
    • The 2022 Updated First NDC strengthened India’s targets for 2030 and explicitly supported Lifestyle for Environment (LiFE). India submitted its NDC for 2031–2035 on 24 April 2026, raising all three quantitative targets.
    Quantitative goal2015 INDC By 20302022 update By 20302026 NDC By 2035
    Reduction in GDP emissions intensity from the 2005 level33–35%45%47%
    Share of cumulative installed electric power capacity from non-fossil sourcesAbout 40%About 50%About 60%
    Forest and tree carbon sink in billion tonnes of CO2 equivalentAdditional 2.5–3.0Additional 2.5–3.03.5–4.0 relative to 2005

    Progress and future milestones

    • 2019: The original GDP emissions-intensity goal reached a 33% reduction from 2005, eleven years before the 2030 deadline.
    • 2021: The original 40% non-fossil installed-capacity target was achieved nine years early.
    • June 2025: The revised 50% non-fossil installed-capacity target was achieved five years early.
    • India’s Progress on Climate Commitments
      • India reduced the emissions intensity of GDP by 37.38% in 2022 compared with the 2005 level.
      • During 2005–2022, India created an additional carbon sink of 2.44 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent through increased forest and tree cover.
      • This reflects India’s continued progress towards achieving its Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) targets.
    • Expansion of Non-Fossil Electricity Capacity
      • As of 30 September 2026, non-fossil fuel sources accounted for about 55% of India’s total installed electricity capacity.
      • India’s total installed electricity capacity stood at 558.8 GW, of which 308 GW came from non-fossil sources.
      • The growing share of non-fossil capacity highlights India’s transition towards a cleaner and low-carbon energy system.

    हिंदी: Floating solar plant (तैरता सौर संयंत्र) · Energy storage (ऊर्जा भंडारण)

    From the magazine

    The Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, approved the Pradhan Mantri Surya Sarovar Yojana (PM-SSY) to accelerate floating solar development. It combines Floating Solar Photovoltaic (FSPV) projects with co-located Energy Storage Systems (ESS) to support land-efficient generation, grid flexibility and peak-demand management.

    Background and Need

    • The National Institute of Solar Energy estimates floating-solar potential at approximately 102.18 GWp across reservoirs and suitable inland water bodies. With only around 700 MW operational when PM-SSY was approved, the scheme seeks to expand generation without increasing competition for scarce land.

    Key Highlights

    • PM-SSY covers all States and Union Territories and seeks to add 5,000 MW of floating-solar capacity. Eligible projects will receive Central Financial Assistance of ₹1 crore per MW after successful commissioning. Feasibility studies, including bathymetry, hydrography and environmental studies, may receive up to ₹50 lakh per project.
    • The scheme is expected to reduce annual carbon dioxide emissions by approximately 10 million tonnes, create 16,000–17,000 full-time-equivalent employment opportunities and promote domestic flotation-system, solar-PV and storage manufacturing.

    Solar Growth in India

    • Installed solar capacity increased more than 58 times, from 2.82 GW in March 2014 to 164.59 GW on 31 July 2026, making solar the largest individual component of renewable capacity. This included 122.57 GW ground-mounted, 30.74 GW grid-connected rooftop, 4.77 GW in hybrid projects and 6.51 GW off-grid solar.

    Record Growth in FY 2025 to 2026

    • India added 44.61 GW of solar capacity in FY 2025–26, compared with 23.83 GW in FY 2024–25. Total non-fossil capacity reached 283.46 GW, including 274.68 GW renewable capacity, following a record annual non-fossil addition of 55.29 GW. Solar-module manufacturing capacity rose from about 2.3 GW in 2014 to around 172 GW by 31 March 2026. On 29 July 2025, renewables met a record 51.5% of electricity demand of 203 GW.

    Enabling Infrastructure

    Solar Parks Scheme and Bhadla Solar Park

    • The Solar Parks Scheme provides land, transmission connectivity and common infrastructure. Its initial 20 GW target expanded to 40 GW in 2017. By February 2026, 54 parks with 39,188 MW sanctioned capacity had been approved, including an inter-state floating solar park spanning Jharkhand and West Bengal. Rajasthan’s Bhadla Solar Park, developed during 2015–2020, covers nearly 5,700 hectares and has approximately 2,245 MW installed capacity.

    Production Linked Incentive Scheme

    • The PLI Scheme for High-Efficiency Solar PV Modules began in 2021 with an initial outlay of ₹4,500 crore, followed by a ₹19,500 crore second tranche. By March 2026, reported cumulative investment was approximately ₹64,873 crore and direct employment 14,794. By 10 June 2026, domestic module and cell manufacturing capacities reached about 192 GW and 30 GW respectively. Module capacity enlisted under the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM) crossed 200 GW in August 2026; this category differs from total manufacturing capacity.

    Current Solar and Non Fossil Capacity Snapshot

    • On 31 July 2026, renewable capacity including large hydro was 291.73 GW. Total non-fossil capacity was 300.50 GW, comprising solar 164.59 GW, wind 58.14 GW, large and small hydro 57.24 GW, bio-power 11.75 GW and nuclear 8.78 GW. The nuclear figure excludes 100 MW under prolonged outage, temporarily removed from installed-capacity calculations from 31 May 2025. Non-fossil sources exceeded 54% of approximately 552 GW total capacity. A rounded 27 August update placed non-fossil capacity at 302–303 GW and solar at around 165 GW. The detailed 31 July break-up remains the source-wise statistical reference available up to 30 August 2026.

    Ethanol Blending in India Must knowPDF p. 150

    India's Ethanol Blended Petrol Programme reached 20% blending in 2025, cutting crude dependence, supporting farmers and lowering road transport emissions.

    • E20 = 20% ethanol + 80% petrol; India first achieved 20% blending in 2025.
    • Ethanol Supply Year (ESY) runs 1 November to 31 October, since November 2023.
    • EBP launched 2003; 2018 Biofuels Policy aimed E20 by 2030; 2022 amendment advanced it to ESY 2025–26.
    • E10 achieved in June 2022; phased E20 rollout began 6 February 2023.
    • Capacity grew from 421 crore litres (2014) to about 2,000 crore litres (2026).
    • Gains since ESY 2014–15: forex savings over ₹1.97 lakh crore; farmer payments over ₹1.66 lakh crore.

    Memory aid E-number = ethanol %: E5 = 5%, E10 = 10%, E20 = 20%.

    Don't confuse E85 is not 85% ethanol: in the US it contains about 51–83%, for flex-fuel vehicles.

    हिंदी: Ethanol blending (इथेनॉल मिश्रण) · Crude oil (कच्चा तेल) · Biofuel (जैव ईंधन)

    From the magazine

    Ethanol is a renewable alcohol fuel. India’s Ethanol Blended Petrol (EBP) Programme mixes domestic ethanol with petrol to reduce crude-oil dependence, support farmers and rural industry, and lower road transport’s environmental impact.

    Meaning and Present Status

    • E5, E10 and E20 contain about 5%, 10% and 20% ethanol by volume. E20 combines anhydrous ethanol with 80% petrol. Since November 2023, the Ethanol Supply Year (ESY) runs from 1 November to 31 October. India first achieved 20% blending in 2025; the November 2025 – August 2026 average was 20%. Public-sector outlets normally supply E20; premium grades XP100, poWer100 and Speed100 remain ethanol-free. From 1 April 2026, notified blended petrol requires a minimum Research Octane Number of 95.

    Evolution of the Programme

    • Pilots began in 2001, and the EBP Programme launched in 2003 in nine States and four Union Territories. The 2018 National Policy on Biofuels targeted E20 by 2030; the 2022 amendment advanced it to ESY 2025–26. E10 was achieved in June 2022, and phased E20 rollout began on 6 February 2023.

    Scale and Measurable Outcomes

    • Capacity grew from 421 crore litres in 2014 to about 2,000 crore litres in 2026. Procurement was about 38 crore litres in ESY 2013–14 and was projected to exceed 1,200 crore litres in ESY 2025–26. The 10 July 2026 update reported cumulative gains since ESY 2014–15: foreign-exchange savings exceeding ₹1.97 lakh crore, nearly 316 lakh tonnes of crude substitution, around 952 lakh tonnes of CO2 reduction and farmer payments exceeding ₹1.66 lakh crore.
    • Why Ethanol Blending Matters
      • Energy Security
      • Farm and Rural Economy
      • Environment and Fuel Quality
      • Major Government Measures
      • Vehicle Compatibility and Mileage

    International Perspective

    • E10 predominates in the United States; E85 contains about 51–83% ethanol and is intended for flex-fuel vehicles. Brazil mandated E30 from 1 August 2025. Brazil temporarily introduced E32 in ordinary and additivated petrol from August 1, 2026 for 180 days with one possible equal extension. Japan targets direct E10 by FY 2030 and E20 by FY 2040. India helped launch the Global Biofuels Alliance in September 2023 to promote sustainable biofuels, standards and best practices.

    Don't confuse Startup Tvasta is Chennai-based; the partner CMFRI centre is in Visakhapatnam.

    हिंदी: Artificial reef (कृत्रिम भित्ति) · Fisheries (मत्स्य पालन)

The pilot forms part of Phase II of Tamil Nadu’s artificial-reef programme supported under the Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana (PMMSY). It combines digital manufacturing with marine habitat restoration, fisheries development and coastal-community resilience.

    • Each module weighs about 1 tonne and has been developed by Chennai-based startup Tvasta, an IIT Madras-incubated company, in collaboration with the Visakhapatnam Regional Centre of the ICAR-Central Marine Fisheries Research Institute.

    • The initiative aims to restore fish habitats and strengthen the resilience of coastal communities.

    Sustainable Development Report 2026 and SDG Progress in India Must knowPDF p. 151

    SDSN's Sustainable Development Report 2026 ranks India 94th of 169 countries (score 68.3), up 18 places since 2015, but still off track for 2030.

    • Released by SDSN on June 23, 2026; India 94th of 169, score 68.3 out of 100.
    • India rose 18 places, from 112th (2015) to 94th (2026); China improved 14 places.
    • Of 75 indicators: 25 on track, eight moderately improving, 33 stagnating, nine decreasing.
    • SDG 2: only cereal yield (3.6 t/ha, 2023) on track; stunting fell 37.9% → 35.5%.
    • Child wasting rose 16.9% (2017) → 18.7% (2020); adult obesity 4.91% → 7.27%.
    • Globally none of 17 SDGs is fully on course; 2025 was 1.43°C above pre-industrial.

    Memory aid 112 − 18 = 94: India climbed 18 places since 2015.

    Don't confuse 169 appears twice: countries ranked and total SDG targets. India's trend shares use 75 indicators, not 169 targets.

    हिंदी: Stunting (बौनापन) · Malnutrition (कुपोषण)

    From the magazine

    The Sustainable Development Report, 2026, released by the Sustainable Development Solutions Network (SDSN) on June 23, 2026, places India 94th among 169 ranked countries with a score of 68.3 out of 100. On the SDSN scale, a score of 100 would indicate achievement of all the SDGs. India has climbed 18 places, from 112th in 2015 to 94th in 2026, making it one of the largest movers since the SDGs were adopted. East and South Asia have recorded the strongest regional progress since 2015. Among major economies, India improved by 18 places, while China improved by 14 places.

    Key Highlights

    • India’s higher score has not yet placed the country on course to meet the 2030 Agenda. According to the 2026 assessment.
    • A calculation from the official 2026 data set finds trends for 75 available indicators for India:
      • Of these 25 are on track or maintaining achievement (33.3%).
      • Eight are moderately improving (10.7%), 33 are stagnating (44.0%) and Nine are decreasing (12.0%)
      • Thus moderate improvement and stagnation together account for 54.7%.
      • These are indicator shares, not shares of all 169 targets.

    Zero Hunger and India’s Double Burden of Malnutrition

    • SDG 2: Zero Hunger remains one of India’s most serious development challenges. India’s overall performance under this goal is largely stagnating.
    • Of the 9 indicators assessed under SDG 2, 4 remain in the “significant challenges” or “major challenges” categories.
    • The only SDG 2 indicator presently on track is cereal yield, which reached 3.6 tonnes per hectare of harvested land in 2023. Progress on nutrition-related indicators has been much slower.

    Child stunting

    • Stunting, which refers to low height for age and usually reflects long-term undernutrition, declined from 37.9 per cent in 2015 to 35.5 per cent in 2020 in the series used by the SDG report.

    Child wasting

    • Wasting, or low weight for height, indicates acute undernutrition.
    • The series used in the Sustainable Development Report shows that child wasting increased from 16.9 per cent in 2017 to 18.7 per cent in 2020.

    Undernourishment and obesity

    • India is also off track in reducing undernourishment. The proportion of undernourished people declined from 12.1 per cent in 2015 to 10.5 per cent in 2018, but subsequently increased to 12 per cent in 2023. The trend is classified as stagnating.
    • At the same time, adult obesity increased from 4.91 per cent in 2015 to 7.27 per cent in 2022.

    Health, Climate and Governance Pressures

    • India faces major difficulties under SDG 3: Good Health and Well-being. Half of the 14 monitored health indicators are either stagnating or deteriorating.
    • The death rate associated with air pollution increased marginally from 131.72 deaths per 100,000 population in 2019 to 132 deaths per 100,000 in 2023.
    • Similarly, the probability of death from heart disease, cancer, diabetes and chronic lung disease among adults aged 30–70 increased from 22.6 per cent in 2015 to 23.6 per cent in 2021.
    • India’s carbon dioxide emissions from fossil-fuel combustion and cement production also continued to increase. Per capita emissions rose from 1.69 tonnes in 2015 to 2.21 tonnes in 2024.

    Global SDG Outlook and Why India Matters

    • The global outlook remains difficult. In SDSN’s goal-level assessment, none of the 17 Sustainable Development Goals is fully on course for achievement by 2030.
    • Progress has been especially weak in sustainable cities, environmental protection, food systems and peaceful institutions. SDG 11, SDG 14, SDG 15 and SDG 16 are among the goals furthest off track, while some of the most poorly performing indicators are connected with SDG 2 and SDG 16.
    • Disaster-related deaths fell by 65 per cent when comparing 2015-2024 with 2005-2014 (excluding COVID-19).
    • In 2025, global temperatures reached 1.43°C above pre-industrial levels, while atmospheric carbon dioxide reached its highest concentration in 2 million years.

    E85 Fuel Rollout in India Must knowPDF p. 152

    Hardeep Singh Puri launched E85 fuel at an IndianOil outlet in New Delhi on June 5, 2026, moving India toward flex-fuel vehicles.

    • Launched by Petroleum Minister Hardeep Singh Puri on June 5, 2026 (World Environment Day), New Delhi.
    • E85 = 80–85% ethanol + 14–19% petrol, made for flex-fuel vehicles.
    • Flex-fuel vehicles (FFVs) run on E20 to E100; engine detects ethanol content automatically.
    • E85 is priced nearly ₹20 per litre lower than petrol.
    • FFVs on E85 can cut lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions by around 61% vs petrol vehicles.
    • Blending rose from 1.53% (2014) to 20% (June 5, 2026), five years ahead of schedule.

    Memory aid E85 launch day = World Environment Day (June 5).

    Don't confuse E85 is a high-ethanol fuel (80–85% ethanol); E20 is the normal 20% blend.

    हिंदी: Energy security (ऊर्जा सुरक्षा)

    From the magazine

    India’s launch of E85 fuel marks a shift from ordinary ethanol blending in petrol to a wider flex-fuel mobility ecosystem. The policy is important for energy security, import reduction, farmer income, cleaner mobility and India’s long-term climate commitments.

    Key Highlights

    • Union Minister for Petroleum and Natural Gas Shri Hardeep Singh Puri launched E85 fuel at an IndianOil retail outlet in New Delhi on the occasion of World Environment Day 2026 (June 5, 2026).
    • E85 is a high-ethanol blended fuel comprising 80–85 per cent ethanol and 14–19 per cent petrol, specifically designed for use in flex-fuel vehicles.
    • The initiative aims to facilitate the adoption of Flex-Fuel Vehicles(FFVs), which are capable of operating on ethanol blends from E20 to E100, without restricting consumers to a single blend.
    • Ethanol blending has increased from 1.53 per cent in 2014 to 20 per cent as of June 5, 2026, with the target achieved five years ahead of schedule.

    Benefits of E85:

    • E85 is priced nearly ₹20 per litre lower than conventional petrol to ensure that the economic benefits of domestically produced ethanol are passed on to consumers.
    • Flex-fuel vehicles operating on E85 can reduce lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions by around 61 per cent compared to conventional petrol vehicles.

    Flex-fuel vehicles

    • A flex-fuel vehicle is typically understood as the one which holds the capability to run on different variants of fuel.
    • In the present context, the FFVs should be able to run on E20, E85, and E100 types of fuel.
    • The vehicle’s engine and fuel system automatically detect the ethanol content and adjust fuel injection and ignition timing accordingly.
