    India ranks third worldwide in installed renewable capacity (250.50 GW at end-2025, per IRENA), behind China and the United States and ahead of Brazil.

    From the magazine

    India ranks third in renewable electricity installed capacity in IRENA’s end-2025 international comparison, ahead of Brazil and behind China and the United States. The figures below incorporate the July 2026 IRENA revision, the latest verified MNRE capacity snapshot and CEA’s later generation data, checked on 18 October 2026.

    • IRENA’s Renewable Capacity Statistics 2026 originally placed India at 250.52 GW. Its July 2026 Renewable Energy Statistics revised this estimate to 250.50 GW without changing India’s third position.
    • The revised end-2025 country comparison places China first with 2,258.02 GW and the United States second with 466.45 GW.
    • Brazil follows India with 228.20 GW, followed by Germany with 200.90 GW, Japan with 134.95 GW and Canada with 110.39 GW.
    • The revised world renewable capacity total is 5,155.01 GW, compared with 5,149.28 GW in the March edition.
    • MNRE’s latest verified capacity figures are for 30 September 2026. Renewable capacity stood at 299.247 GW, and nuclear capacity of 8.780 GW raised total non-fossil capacity to 308.027 GW.
    • Renewable capacity comprised 171.051 GW of solar, 59.201 GW of wind, 11.748 GW of bio-power, 5.182 GW of small hydro and 52.065 GW of large hydro.
    • At the earlier 31 March 2026 milestone, India had 283.46 GW of non-fossil capacity, comprising 274.68 GW of renewable capacity and 8.78 GW of nuclear capacity.
    • The renewable component comprised 150.26 GW of solar, 56.09 GW of wind, 11.75 GW of bioenergy, 5.17 GW of small hydro and 51.41 GW of large hydro.
    • India achieved its 2030 NDC target of about 50% non-fossil share in cumulative installed electric power capacity in June 2025, five years ahead of schedule. This share reached 54.18% on 30 June 2026.
    • India’s NDC for 2031–2035 raises the capacity-share target to about 60% by 2035, with technology transfer and low-cost international finance. India also targets 500 GW of non-fossil installed capacity by 2030 and net-zero emissions by 2070.
    • CEA’s March 2026 Executive Summary gives an actual FY 2025–26 generation aggregate of 1,847.941 BU, including 7.831 BU imported from Bhutan. Total generation grew by 1.04%.
    • Fossil or thermal generation was 1,307.131 BU, accounting for a calculated 70.73% of this aggregate and declining by 4.10% from the preceding year.
    • Calculated non-fossil generation, including imports, was 540.811 BU or 29.27%; renewable generation including large hydro and imports was 485.620 BU or 26.28%.
    • Using the previous-year baseline published with the earlier provisional series, these updated totals imply growth of about 16.1% for non-fossil sources and 18.7% for renewables including hydro and imports.
    • CEA’s renewable generation report records 310.585 BU from renewables excluding large hydro in FY 2025–26, an increase of 21.79%.
    • Wind generation reached 106.700 BU, growing by 28.02%, while solar generation reached 174.757 BU, growing by 21.23%.
    • Together, wind and solar generated a calculated 281.456 BU, equivalent to 15.23% of the Executive Summary aggregate including Bhutan imports.
    • The 8 April 2026 provisional release reported coal generation of 1,250.189 BU, a 67.7% share and a decline of 3.69%. These coal figures belong to that earlier provisional series and should retain that qualification.
    • CEA’s domestic generation series excludes Bhutan imports. On this basis, FY 2025–26 generation was 1,840.110 BU, including 532.980 BU from non-fossil sources and 477.789 BU from renewables.
    • Installed capacity and electricity generation measure different things. Renewable capacity is part of non-fossil capacity, which also includes nuclear power. Reaching a 50% capacity share therefore does not mean that non-fossil sources generate 50% of annual electricity.

    COP 15 of the Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species Must knowPDF pp. 153–154

    CMS COP15 in Campo Grande, Brazil (March 23–29, 2026), gave new or upgraded protection to 40 migratory species, subspecies and populations.

    • CMS = Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals, also called the Bonn Convention.
    • COP15: Campo Grande, Brazil, March 23–29, 2026; theme 'Connecting Nature to Sustain Life'.
    • 40 species, subspecies and populations added or upgraded in Appendices I and II.
    • CMS now covers over 1,200 unique species.
    • Brazil holds the CMS COP Presidency for the next three years.
    • COP16: Bonn, Germany, in 2029, marking CMS's 50th anniversary (signed at Bonn, 1979).

    Memory aid Signed at Bonn in 1979 → back to Bonn in 2029 for its 50th birthday.

    Don't confuse CMS COP15 (Campo Grande) is a wildlife treaty meeting, not the UN climate COP.

    हिंदी: Migratory species (प्रवासी प्रजातियां) · Biodiversity (जैव विविधता)

    From the magazine

    Migratory species are animals that move across countries, continents, oceans, rivers and skies for food, breeding, climate suitability or survival. Their protection cannot be done by one country alone because their routes cut across political boundaries. This is why the Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals (CMS), also known as the Bonn Convention, is important for global biodiversity governance.

    • The 15th Meeting of the Conference of the Parties to CMS (CMS COP15) was held in Campo Grande, Brazil, from March 23 to March 29, 2026, under the theme “Connecting Nature to Sustain Life.”

    Major Outcome

    • The biggest outcome of COP15 was the decision to provide new or upgraded treaty protection to 40 species, subspecies and populations of birds, aquatic wildlife and terrestrial animals.
    • These were added to or upgraded within CMS Appendices I and II. With this, the Convention now covers over 1,200 unique species.

    Brazil’s Role and Next COP

    • With the conclusion of COP15, Brazil holds the CMS COP Presidency for the next three years. The focus during this period will be on implementing the decisions taken in Campo Grande.
    • The next CMS COP, COP16, will be held in Bonn, Germany, in 2029. It will coincide with the 50th anniversary of CMS, making it symbolically important because Bonn is the city where the treaty was signed in 1979.

The project focuses on scientific snow harvesting, conservation of snowmelt and glacial melt, and creation of small water bodies so that seasonal water, which usually flows away, can be stored and used during lean periods.

    State of India’s Environment (SOE) 2026 Report Must knowPDF p. 155

    CSE's State of India's Environment 2026 (February 25, 2026) says 2025 saw the sharpest rise in extreme weather in four years, on 99% of days.

    • Released by CSE and Down to Earth, February 25, 2026, at Anil Agarwal Dialogue, Nimli, near Alwar.
    • Jan 1–Nov 30, 2025: extreme weather on 99% of days; 4,419 deaths; 17.41 million hectares crops hit.
    • 2024: 88% of days, 3,393 deaths; 2023: 89% of days, 3,208 deaths.
    • Worst-hit states: Himachal Pradesh (267 days), Kerala (173), Madhya Pradesh (162).
    • Only 15% of Indians (about 200 million) live within 10 km of a continuous air monitor.
    • Ocean acidity has risen 30–40% since the industrial era.

    Memory aid Extreme-weather days: 89% (2023) → 88% (2024) → 99% (2025), almost every day of 2025.

    Don't confuse The SOE series began in 2014; CSE's Citizen's First Report dates to 1982.

    हिंदी: Extreme weather (चरम मौसम) · Heatwave (लू)

    From the magazine

    The State of India’s Environment 2026 report was released by the Centre for Science and Environment (CSE) and Down to Earth Magazine on February 25, 2026 at the Anil Agarwal Dialogue 2026 in Nimli near Alwar Rajasthan. The annual SOE series began in 2014, though CSE’s longer environmental reporting tradition goes back to the 1982 Citizen’s First Report.

    Key Highlights

    • The report states that 2025 recorded the highest rise in the frequency and impact of extreme weather events in India during the last four years.
    • These events included heatwaves, cold waves, heavy rainfall, and floods.
    • From January 1 to November 30, 2025, extreme weather events occurred on 99% of the days in India, causing 4,419 deaths and affecting at least 17.41 million hectares of crop area.
    • In comparison, 2024 saw such events on 88% of the days, with 3,393 deaths and 3.61 million hectares of crop damage, while 2023 recorded them on 89% of the days, causing 3,208 deaths and affecting 2.09 million hectares.
    • Among the States, Himachal Pradesh was the worst affected with extreme weather on 267 days, followed by Kerala with 173 days and Madhya Pradesh with 162 days.

    Air Pollution, Freshwater Stress, and Novel Entities

    • On air pollution, CSE’s analysis shows that only 15% of India’s population, about 200 million people, lives within 10 km of a continuous air quality monitor.
    • This means that 85% of the population, or over 1.2 billion people, lives beyond 10 km of a continuous monitor in CSE’s February 2026 analysis.
    • The report notes that ocean acidity has increased by 30–40% since the industrial era, threatening marine ecosystems, including corals and shell-forming organisms, and weakening the ocean’s ability to absorb carbon.

    30th Conference of the Parties to the UNFCCC: COP30 Must knowPDF p. 156

    COP30 in Belém (November 10-22, 2025) shifted climate talks to implementation, producing the Belém Package of about 29 decisions built on the Global Mutirão decision.

    • Held in Belém, Amazon region, November 10-22, 2025; an 'implementation-first' COP.
    • Belém Package: around 29 decisions as an implementation toolkit, based on the Global Mutirão decision.
    • Two-year Climate Finance Work Programme launched; Paris Agreement Article 9.1 reading strengthened.
    • Tropical Forest Forever Facility: Brazil-led, targets USD 125 billion; pays for protecting tropical forests.
    • Belém 4x Pledge: quadruple sustainable fuels by 2035 vs 2024; 23 countries endorsed; IEA tracks.
    • India: climate finance a legal obligation, demanded USD 1.3 trillion/year; opposed EU's CBAM.

    Memory aid Mutirão (Brazil) ≈ Shramdaan (India): a community coming together for shared work.

    Don't confuse Belém Health Action Plan = first international climate adaptation plan only for health (USD 300 million); Belém Action Mechanism = just transition. Don't mix.

    हिंदी: Climate finance (जलवायु वित्त) · Shramdaan (श्रमदान) · Just transition (न्यायसंगत परिवर्तन)

    From the magazine

    COP30, held in Belém in the Amazon region, became strongly associated with an “implementation-first” framing. Alongside the political track, COP30 also showcased a large-scale implementation architecture through the COP30 Global Climate Action Agenda (GCAA)—a renewed framework built on the Marrakech Partnership and the Global Stocktake response, organized into six thematic axes and driven by 30 activation groups (482 initiatives).

    Key Highlights

    • COP30 took place in Belem from November 10-22, 2025.
    • In parallel, the COP30 Global Climate Action Agenda (GCAA) operationalized this “implementation turn” through a four-step activation cycle–Coordinate, Measure, Showcase, Scale.
    • Coordinate: 30 activation groups with 482 initiatives aligned toward 30 key objectives.

    COP30’s “Implementation Shift” and the Belém Package

    • Unlike earlier COPs that leaned heavily toward announcing new pledges, COP30 marked a clear shift toward implementation.
    • The central political outcome was widely described as the Belém Package—around 29 decisions functioning less as a new “target set” and more as an implementation toolkit to deliver the Paris Agreement.
    • The package’s conceptual foundation was the Global Mutirão decision.
    • “Mutirão” (a Brazilian term) implies the community coming together for shared work—similar in spirit to India’s concept of “Shramdaan.”

    Accelerating Action: Mitigation, Adaptation, and Finance (with Finance the Most Contested)

    (1) Climate Finance: reinforcing obligations + tracking and delivery tools

    • A major achievement attributed to COP30 was strengthening the interpretation of Paris Agreement Article 9.1 (developed countries “shall provide” financial resources to developing countries).
    • A two-year “Climate Finance Work Programme” was launched.
    • Tropical Forest Forever Facility (TFFF): Brazil-led blended finance mechanism targeting USD 125 billion, designed like a “scholarship for forests,” delivering performance-based payments for protecting tropical forests (monitored via satellite data). (2) Adaptation: operationalizing the GGA and scaling resilience delivery
    • COP30 decisions treat the Baku Adaptation Road Map as an ongoing work stream with a defined first phase (2026-28). (3) Mitigation & Transition: the Belém 4x Pledge and sectoral scaling
    • To curb emissions and accelerate system transitions, COP30 advanced the implementation of the Belém 4x Pledge. The pledge was launched at the Pre-COP.
      • Target: quadruple the use of sustainable fuels by 2035 relative to 2024 (including green hydrogen, advanced biofuels, and e-fuels).
      • Tracking: IEA to track progress.
    • 23 countries officially endorsed the pledge, with broad non-state support (including major industry actors).

    Just Transition

    • Belém Action Mechanism (BAM): adopted to support a socially fair transition away from fossil fuels—focused on worker reskilling and social dialogue, though without a large dedicated fund.
    • The Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative announced its 18th nation-state supporter (Cambodia) and presented a PAS with next steps through the Climate Action Agenda.

    Health

    • Belém Health Action Plan: launched to build climate-resilient health systems to tackle heatwaves and vector-borne diseases.
    • The Belém Health Action Plan is described as the world’s first international climate adaptation plan dedicated entirely to health, launched with an initial USD 300 million investment from a coalition of 35+ philanthropies, funding research, policy, solutions for extreme heat/air pollution/ infectious diseases, and strengthening health systems via climate-data integration.
    • COP30 also marked “Race to Zero for health care hits 100”: The campaign has reached 100 institutions representing 14,000+ hospitals/ health centers across 28 countries.

    India’s position at COP30 (as reflected in negotiations and blocs)

      • Finance is an obligation: India emphasized that under Article 9.1, climate finance is a legal obligation, not charity, and demanded USD 1.3 trillion/year.
      • Opposition to CBAM: India strongly opposed unilateral trade measures like the EU’s CBAM, arguing they violate CBDR-RC and resemble “green protectionism.”
    • Looking ahead: COP31 (Türkiye, 2026) and the “Belém Mission to 1.5°C”

    Minimum Wage Revision in Uttar Pradesh Must knowPDF p. 161

    UP revised minimum wages by a notification of 17 April (effective 1 April 2026), dividing the State into three categories by area.

    • Notified April 17 as an interim step; retrospective from April 1, 2026.
    • Under Minimum Wages Act, 1948, using powers of the United Provinces Industrial Disputes Act, 1947.
    • Category I: Gautam Buddha Nagar and Ghaziabad (high industry, high living cost).
    • Category II: districts with municipal corporations; Category III: all other districts.
    • Wages set by skill (unskilled, semi-skilled, skilled): basic amount plus Variable Dearness Allowance (VDA).
    • Category I monthly wages: ₹13,690 unskilled, ₹15,059 semi-skilled, ₹16,868 skilled.

    Don't confuse Minimum Wages Act is of 1948; the UP powers used are under the 1947 Industrial Disputes Act.

    हिंदी: Minimum wage (न्यूनतम मजदूरी) · Dearness allowance (महंगाई भत्ता)

    From the magazine

    • The Uttar Pradesh Government issued a notification on April 17, regarding revision of minimum wages in the state as an interim step, with retrospective effect from April 1, 2026.
    • The notification revises existing minimum wage rates under the Minimum Wages Act, 1948, using powers under the United Provinces Industrial Disputes Act, 1947.
    • An important provision is the division of the state into three categories, depending upon geographical and economic factors.
    • Gautam Buddha Nagar and Ghaziabad are categorised as Category I because of the concentration of industrial activity and the high cost of living in these areas.
    • Category II encompasses districts with municipal corporations, while Category III overs the rest.
    • In each case, wages are set based on skill levels — unskilled, semi-skilled, and skilled.
    • The wage structure comprises a basic amount and a Variable Dearness Allowance (VDA).
    • In Category I, monthly wages are fixed at ₹13,690 for unskilled labour, ₹15,059 for semi-skilled labour, and ₹16,868 for skilled labour.

    • In 2024–25, Uttar Pradesh’s GSDP at constant prices is estimated to grow by 9%, which is higher than the estimated 6.5% GDP growth for India in the same year.
    • The structure of the state’s economy in 2024–25 shows that agriculture contributes 27%, manufacturing contributes 26%, and services contribute 47% of the economy. This means services remain the largest sector, but agriculture continues to hold a very significant share in Uttar Pradesh’s economy.
    • Uttar Pradesh’s per capita GSDP in 2024–25 is estimated at ₹1,24,366, which is an increase of 11.6% over 2023–24. It is noted that India’s per capita GDP is estimated at ₹2,34,859 in 2024–25.

    Revenue Surplus, Fiscal Deficit, and Primary Deficit Must knowPDF p. 165

    UP Budget 2026–27 shows a revenue surplus of ₹64,458 crore (1.6% of GSDP) and a fiscal deficit of ₹1,18,481 crore (3% of GSDP).

    • Revenue surplus 2026–27: ₹64,458 crore = 1.6% of GSDP.
    • 2025–26 RE surplus was bigger: ₹74,348 crore (2.4% of GSDP).
    • Fiscal deficit 2026–27: ₹1,18,481 crore = 3% of GSDP.
    • 3% matches the 16th Finance Commission's limit for States (2026–31).
    • Primary deficit ₹49,560 crore = 1.2% of GSDP.

    Don't confuse UP has a revenue surplus (1.6%) and a fiscal deficit (3%) at the same time.

    हिंदी: Revenue surplus (राजस्व अधिशेष) · Primary deficit (प्राथमिक घाटा)

    From the magazine

    • The budget estimates a revenue surplus of ₹64,458 crore, which is 1.6% of GSDP, in 2026–27. This means the state expects its revenue receipts to exceed its revenue expenditure.
    • However, this revenue surplus is lower than the revised estimate for 2025–26, when revenue surplus was estimated at ₹74,348 crore, or 2.4% of GSDP. This suggests that while the state remains in surplus on the revenue account, the cushion is becoming smaller.
    • The fiscal deficit for 2026–27 is budgeted at ₹1,18,481 crore, which is 3% of GSDP. This is the same ratio as the revised estimate for 2025–26 and aligns with the 16th Finance Commission’s recommended annual limit of 3% of GSDP for states for 2026–31.
    • The primary deficit is estimated at ₹49,560 crore, or 1.2% of GSDP, in 2026–27. This is significantly higher than the revised estimate for 2025–26, indicating a larger gap even before interest payments are considered.

    From the magazine

    • Capital outlay is budgeted at ₹1,77,744 crore, which is an increase of 11% over the revised estimate of 2025–26. Capital outlay is important because it creates assets such as roads, buildings, and infrastructure.
    • The rise in revenue expenditure is being driven by higher spending on pension, general education, rural development, grants to local bodies and Panchayati Raj institutions, and energy.

    हिंदी: Revenue receipts (राजस्व प्राप्तियाँ) · Non-tax revenue (गैर-कर राजस्व)

    From the magazine

    • Revenue receipts for 2026–27 are estimated at ₹7,28,928 crore, which is 26% higher than the revised estimate for 2025–26.
    • Of the total revenue receipts, roughly 50% will be raised by the state from its own resources and the remaining 50% will come from the Centre, either as the state’s share in central taxes or as grants.
    • State’s own tax revenue is estimated at ₹3,34,491 crore in 2026–27, which is 48% higher than the revised estimate for 2025–26.
    • State’s own non-tax revenue is estimated at ₹26,754 crore, which is almost double the revised estimate for 2025–26. The budget attributes this mainly to increases in concession fees, rent, royalty, share capital receipts from Uttar Pradesh Power Corporation for rural electrification, and interest income.
    • The state’s share in central taxes is estimated at ₹2,68,911 crore, while grants from the Centre are estimated at ₹98,772 crore.

    हिंदी: Micro, small and medium enterprises (सूक्ष्म, लघु एवं मध्यम उद्यम) · Capital subsidy (पूंजीगत सब्सिडी)

      • Establish four Technology/Extension Centres in Kosi, Bhagalpur, Munger and Purnea.
    • Incentives Proposed in the Draft-
      • Capital subsidy: Provide 25% in Category A districts and 30% in Category B districts, capped at ₹25 lakh, ₹1.5 crore and ₹5 crore for micro, small and medium enterprises, respectively.
      • Additional support: Provide 10% additional capital subsidy to women, SC, ST, BC, Divyang and transgender entrepreneurs.
      • Employment support: Reimburse employers’ EPF contributions for three years, capped at ₹24,000 per employee annually, subject to employment thresholds.
      • Electricity subsidy: Reimburse 20% of eligible low-tension power charges for three years.
      • Rooftop solar subsidy: Provide 25% of installation cost, capped at ₹5 lakh, for systems up to 300 kW.
      • Stamp duty: Provide 100% reimbursement on land purchases by new manufacturing enterprises. Note: These detailed targets and incentives are from the July 2026 draft.

    Overall Budget Size and Fiscal Framework PDF p. 174

    Bihar's 2026–27 net budget is ₹3,47,589.76 crore, with a fiscal deficit of 2.99% of GSDP (within the 3% limit) and a small revenue surplus.

    • Net expenditure ₹3,47,589.76 crore; ₹30,694.74 crore above 2025–26 BE (₹3,16,895.02 crore).
    • Scheme outlay ₹1,22,155.42 crore (35.14%); establishment/committed ₹2,25,434.34 crore (64.86%).
    • GSDP 2026–27 projected at about ₹13.09 lakh crore, about 15% growth.
    • Revenue surplus ₹1,143.19 crore; fiscal deficit ₹39,111.80 crore = 2.99% of GSDP.
    • Debt repayment about ₹22,665 crore; spending excluding it ₹3,24,925 crore.
    • Appropriation Bill gross ₹3,53,045.15 crore: voted ₹3,02,242.13 crore, charged ₹50,803.02 crore.

    Memory aid 35.14 + 64.86 = 100: scheme vs committed spending.

    Don't confuse Fiscal deficit is 2.99% of GSDP (within the 3% limit), yet the budget still shows a revenue surplus.

    हिंदी: Fiscal deficit (राजकोषीय घाटा) · Revenue surplus (राजस्व अधिशेष)

    From the magazine

    • For 2026–27, Bihar’s net budget expenditure is estimated at ₹3,47,589.76 crore, which is ₹30,694.74 crore higher than the Budget Estimate of ₹3,16,895.02 crore for 2025–26.
    • The annual scheme outlay is ₹1,22,155.42 crore, while establishment and committed expenditure is ₹2,25,434.34 crore.
    • Thus, scheme expenditure forms 35.14% of total expenditure and establishment/committed expenditure forms 64.86%.
    • The Gross State Domestic Product (GSDP) for 2026–27 is projected at about ₹13.09 lakh crore, showing an estimated growth of about 15% over 2025–26.
    • The Budget targets a revenue surplus of ₹1,143.19 crore and a fiscal deficit of ₹39,111.80 crore, equal to 2.99% of GSDP, which is within the 3% limit set under the Bihar Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management framework.
    • The expenditure excluding debt repayment is estimated at ₹3,24,925 crore, while debt repayment is about ₹22,665 crore.
    • In the Appropriation Bill, the state proposes gross expenditure of ₹3,53,045.15 crore, out of which ₹3,02,242.13 crore is voted expenditure and ₹50,803.02 crore is charged expenditure.
    • The net expenditure figure used in the budget summary is ₹3,47,589.76 crore.

    Revenue Receipts and Borrowings PDF p. 174

    Bihar expects ₹2,85,277.12 crore of revenue receipts in 2026–27, about ₹2,10,074 crore of it from the Centre, showing heavy dependence on central transfers.

    • Revenue receipts ₹2,85,277.12 crore: own sources ₹75,202.99 crore; Centre about ₹2,10,074 crore.
    • Own tax revenue ₹65,800 crore; State GST is the largest source at ₹38,000 crore.
    • Commercial taxes ₹50,000 crore; stamps and registration ₹10,000 crore; transport tax ₹5,000 crore.
    • Own non-tax revenue ₹9,402.99 crore, including ₹4,200 crore from mining.
    • Share in central taxes ₹1,58,178.32 crore; central grants ₹51,895.81 crore.
    • Borrowing proposed ₹61,939.48 crore; debt repayment ₹22,664.83 crore.

    Don't confuse ₹1,58,178.32 crore = share in central taxes; ₹51,895.81 crore = grants-in-aid. Together about ₹2,10,074 crore from the Centre.

    हिंदी: Tax devolution (कर हस्तांतरण) · Grants-in-aid (सहायता अनुदान)

At constant (2011–12) prices, Bihar’s growth rate is estimated at 8.6 percent, which is higher than India’s 6.5 percent. These figures place Bihar among the fastest-growing states in the country.
    • For 2024–25, quick estimates show that the Gross State Value Added (GSVA) of the secondary sector grew by 11.1 percent at constant (2011–12) prices and 15.5 percent at current prices.

    हिंदी: Outstanding debt (बकाया ऋण)

    From the magazine

    • Bihar’s fiscal development path reflects disciplined financial management, as the state government’s total expenditure increased from ₹1.66 lakh crore in 2020–21 to ₹2.82 lakh crore in 2024–25. The state government maintained fiscal prudence through moderate borrowing and effective debt servicing while consistently prioritising developmental expenditure in sectors such as education, health, energy, transport, irrigation, and agriculture.
    • This structural change reflects the government’s focus on long-term investment, infrastructure development, and asset creation.
    • Revenue receipts of the state government increased from ₹1.28 lakh crore in 2020–21 to ₹2.18 lakh crore in 2024–25, with tax revenue as the main source. The share of tax revenue increased from 70 percent to 84 percent, while the share of non-tax revenue declined from 5 percent to 2 percent and the share of grants-in-aid declined from 25 percent to 14 percent.
    • The structure of revenue expenditure remained largely stable over the last five years, with social services having the highest share at 46 percent. The share of economic services increased slightly from 21 percent in 2020-21 to 22 percent in 2024-25, while the share of general services declined slightly from 33 percent in 2020-21 to 32 percent in 2024- 25.
    • This distribution reflects the government’s commitment to both welfare expansion and strengthening productive sectors.
    • The share of plan expenditure in total expenditure increased from 38.3 percent in 2020–21 to 39.9 percent in 2024–25, while the share of establishment and committed expenditure declined from 61.7 percent to 60.1 percent.
    • This trend indicates a gradual shift towards welfare-oriented activities and policy-driven development priorities.
    • Developmental expenditure remained around two-thirds of the total budget, reaching 67.4 percent in 2024–25. It increased from ₹1,12,122 crore in 2020– 21 to ₹1,89,892 crore in 2024–25, indicating a stronger focus on development and welfare expenditure.
    • Receipts from the central government increased from ₹91,625 crore in 2020–21 to ₹1,59,298 crore in 2024–25, mainly due to transfers from the divisible tax pool, which increased from ₹59,861 crore in 2020-21 to ₹1,29,435 crore in 2024-25.
    • In 2024–25, grants-in-aid from the central government amounted to ₹29,863 crore.
    • The state’s own revenue increased from ₹36,543 crore in 2020–21 to ₹59,360 crore in 2024–25, with tax revenue as the major contributor.
    • As of 31 March 2025, the outstanding debt of the state government was ₹3,74,134 crore, which was 37.7 percent of the GSDP.
    • At the end of 2024–25, 84.6 percent of the total outstanding debt consisted of public debt. Out of total public debt, 83.8 percent came from internal borrowings, while 16.2 percent came from loans and advances from the central government.
    • Market loans and loans from financial institutions are the main components of internal debt.

    Narendra Modi Must knowPDF p. 178

    PM Modi completed 25 continuous years heading a government (Gujarat CM from October 7, 2001, then PM in 2014) on October 7, 2026.

    • June 10, 2026: became longest-serving elected PM for consecutive terms, surpassing Jawaharlal Nehru.
    • Nehru first took oath as elected PM on May 13, 1952 and served until May 27, 1964.
    • Modi's continuous PM tenure, May 26, 2014 to June 10, 2026: 4399 days.
    • March 22, 2026: longest-serving head of an elected government (CM + PM combined): 8,931 days.
    • Uzbekistan's 'Oliy Darajali Do'stlik' Order (Order of Highest Friendship) from President Shavkat Mirziyoyev, August 30, 2026.
    • 2026 honours: Indonesia's Bintang Adipurna, Seychelles' Guardian of the Blue Horizon (first time given), FAO's Agricola Medal.
    • Also: Royal Norwegian Order of Merit, Sweden's Royal Order of the Polar Star, Israel's Medal of the Knesset.

    Memory aid Award-country pairs: Bintang Adipurna = Indonesia; Blue Horizon = Seychelles; White Double Cross = Slovakia; Polar Star = Sweden; Knesset = Israel; Nishan = Ethiopia; Agricola = FAO.

    Don't confuse Two different records: 4399 days = continuous PM tenure; 8,931 days = CM + PM tenure combined.

    हिंदी: Prime Minister (प्रधानमंत्री) · Highest civilian honour (सर्वोच्च नागरिक सम्मान)

    From the magazine

    • Prime Minister Narendra Modi completed 25 continuous years as the head of a government on October 7, 2026.
    • Prime Minister Narendra Modi was conferred with the “Oliy Darajali Do’stlik” Order (Order of Highest Friendship) by the President of Uzbekistan, Shavkat Mirziyoyev on August 30, 2026.This is Uzbekistan’s highest honour for foreign leaders. The award was conferred for his contribution to the strengthening of friendship between the two countries.
    Awards to PM Narendra Modi Awards Country Date Remarks ‘Bintang Adipurna of the Republic of Indonesia’ Indonesia July 7, 2026 Highest civilian honour of Indonesia ‘Guardian of the Blue Horizon’ Seychelles June 28, 2026 This was the first time that this honour was bestowed “The Order of the White Double Cross, First Class” Slovakia June 15, 2026 Slovakia’s highest State honour Agricola Medal Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) May 20, 2026 Award conferred by Dr. Qu Dongyu, Director General of FAO Royal Norwegian Order of Merit Norway May 18, 2026 Norway’s highest honour bestowed on foreign Heads of Government Royal Order of the Polar, Star, Degree Commander Grand Cross Sweden May 17, 2026 Sweden’s highest honour conferred on foreign Heads of Government Medal of the Knesset Israel February 25, 2026 Highest honour of the Knesset, the Israeli Parliament Order of Oman (First Class) Oman December 18, 2025 Highest civilian honour of Oman Great Honour Nishan of Ethiopia Ethiopia December 16, 2025 Highest civilian honour of Ethiopia
    • He became the Chief Minister of Gujarat on October 7, 2001 and then became Prime Minister in 2014.
    • Prime Minister Narendra Modi has become the longest-serving elected the Prime Minister of India for consecutive terms on June 10, 2026.
    • He has surpassed the record of Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru, who first took the oath as an elected Prime Minister on May 13, 1952, and served until May 27, 1964.
    • From May 26, 2014 to June 10, 2026, Prime Minister Modi’s continuous tenure is 4399 days.
    • Prime Minister Narendra Modi has achieved a historic milestone in Indian politics by becoming the longest-serving head of an elected government in the country on March 22, 2026.
    • He has now completed 8,931 days (as of March 22, 2026) as head of government, combining his tenure as Chief Minister of Gujarat and as Prime Minister.

    • Chennai will become the first Indian city to implement a comprehensive ring-main solution.

    Don't confuse Chile = leprosy; Fiji = trachoma.

    • It has become the first country in the Americas – and the second globally – to be officially verified as having eliminated leprosy disease.
    • The United States Government formally exited from the World Health Organization on January 22, 2026.
    • The World Health Organization (WHO) has validated Fiji for eliminating trachoma as a public health problem on October 20, 2025.

    Exercises and Operations

    Exercises and Operations Must knowPDF pp. 213–215

    India's military exercises and operations of 2025-26 with partner countries and venues, from SIMBEX and VARUNA to MALABAR and Operation Sagar Bandhu.

    • Navy: 33rd SIMBEX-2026 (Singapore) at Visakhapatnam; 24th VARUNA 2026 (France) at Toulon Naval Base.
    • Army: KAZIND 2026 (Kazakhstan) at Oskemen; 15th MAITREE 2026 (Thailand) at Surat Thani.
    • 23rd Yudh Abhyas 2026 (India-US): Auli, Uttarakhand and Mahajan, Rajasthan; Udara Shakti 2026 (IAF–RMAF): Subang.
    • Operation Cy-Vajra 2026 (July 7-13, 2026): conducted by Uttar Pradesh Police.
    • Sudarshan Shakti-V: counter-hijacking and counter-terrorism mock exercise at IGI Airport, New Delhi.
    • 29th MALABAR-2025: India, Japan, Australia, US, around Guam; 19th SURYA KIRAN-2025 (Nepal) at Pithoragarh.
    • Operation Sagar Bandhu (November 28, 2025): India's help to Sri Lanka after Cyclone Ditwah.

    Memory aid Partner pairs: KAZIND = Kazakhstan; KHANJAR = Kyrgyzstan; Yudh Abhyas and VAJRA PRAHAR = USA; VINBAX = Vietnam; CINBAX = Cambodia; MAITREE = Thailand; SIMBEX = Singapore; AJEYA WARRIOR = UK; Harimau Shakti = Malaysia; GARUDA SHAKTI = Indonesia; LAMITIYE = Seychelles.

    Important Days/Week · National

    Important Days/Week Must knowPDF p. 215

    Important national days of India with dates and themes, such as National Space Day, National Science Day and National Voters' Day.

    • National Space Day: 23 August; National Sports Day: 29 August; Indian Akshay Urja Day: 20 August.
    • National Science Day 2026: 28 February; theme 'Women in Science: Catalysing Viksit Bharat'.
    • National Voters' Day 2026: 25 January, theme 'My India, My Vote'; National Tourism Day also 25 January.
    • National Girl Child Day: 24 January; National Youth Day: 12 January.
    • National Statistics Day 2026: 29 June; theme 'Data for Development'.
    • National Handloom Day: 7 August; Kargil Vijay Diwas: 26 July; National Flag Day: 22 July.
    • Good Governance Day: 25 December; National Mathematics Day: 22 December; National Education Day: 11 November.

    Memory aid 25 January double: National Voters' Day + National Tourism Day; Girl Child Day comes just before (24 January).

    Books & Authors Must knowPDF p. 220

    Recent books and their authors, including works by Ram Nath Kovind, Sonia Gandhi, Sudha Murty, Kailash Satyarthi and General Manoj Mukund Naravane.

    • Ram Nath Kovind: 'Triumph of the Indian Republic: My Life, My Struggles' (autobiography).
    • Sonia Gandhi: 'Belonging: A Journey of Love' (memoir); Kiran Desai: 'The Loneliness of Sonia and Sunny'.
    • Manoj Mukund Naravane: 'Four Stars of Destiny'; CDS General Anil Chauhan: 'Ready, Relevant and Resurgent II'.
    • Sudha Murty: 'Tides of Time: Bharat's History through Murals in Parliament'; Kailash Satyarthi: 'Karuna: The Power of Compassion'.
    • Shikhar Dhawan: 'The One: Cricket, My Life and More'; Anupam Kher: 'Different But No Less'.
    • Justice D.Y. Chandrachud: 'Why the Constitution Matters'; Srinath Raghavan: 'Indira Gandhi and the Years that Transformed India'.
    • Shivraj Singh Chouhan: 'Apnapan: Narendra Modi Sang Mere Anubhav'; Bandaru Dattatreya: 'Janata Ki Kahani, Meri Aatmakatha'.

    India at Aichi-Nagoya Must knowPDF p. 237

    India finished fourth at the Asian Games 2026 (Aichi-Nagoya) with 85 medals, including 21 gold: its second-highest tally after 2022.

    • Opening flag-bearers: Manu Bhaker (shooting) and Pawan Sehrawat (kabaddi); closing: Neeru Dhanda (shooting).
    • Fourth in the medal table: 85 medals, 21 gold; India's second-highest Asian Games tally after the 2022 edition.
    • Athletics gave the most medals (24) but just one gold; archery gave nine medals, including five gold.
    • First Indian women: Pranavi Urs (individual golf gold), Kumkum Mohod (recurve individual gold), Anahat Singh (squash singles silver).
    • India's first-ever medals: Baranica Elangovan (Asian Games pole vault, bronze) and Jay Meena (soft tennis).
    • National records: Sawan Barwal (marathon silver); Vithya Ramraj (400m hurdles bronze) broke P.T. Usha's 42-year-old mark.

    Sports and New Compact Model Must knowPDF pp. 237–238

    Glasgow 2026 used a compact model: only 10 sports (19 at Birmingham 2022), reused venues and 2715 athletes; India finished 4th with 39 medals.

    • Only 10 sports, compared with 19 at Birmingham 2022.
    • Existing venues were reused instead of building large new stadiums; only 2715 athletes.
    • Sports included athletics, swimming, gymnastics, track cycling, netball, weightlifting, boxing, judo, bowls, 3 × 3 basketball.
    • Top three: Australia (70 gold, 171 total), England (29 gold), Canada (19 gold).
    • India 4th: 13 gold, 17 silver, 9 bronze = 39; Scotland 5th, also 13 gold and 39 total.

    Don't confuse India and Scotland both had 13 gold and 39 medals; India was 4th, Scotland 5th.
